article_title: The Quality of Intellectual Work in Chicago Schools
citation: Newmann, F. M., Lopez, G., & Bryk, A. S. (1998). The Quality of Intellectual Work in Chicago Schools: A Baseline Report. Consortium on Chicago School Research.
title: Apply authentic intellectual work standards across almost any content at any grade level to bridge curricular disagreements
description: The report argues that because the standards define the nature of intellectual work needed for vocation, citizenship, and personal life rather than specific content, they provide a common intellectual mission across disciplines. It states that "one virtue of the standards for authentic intellectual work is that they can be applied to the teaching of almost any content at any grade level," bridging otherwise divisive preferences about what to teach.
requirements: Scoring against grade-level expectations and trained scorers using the developed rubrics
constraints: The standards deliberately avoid prescribing precise curriculum content, which the report notes remains contested among schools, districts, states, and professional organizations
target_learners: students at any grade level, illustrated here in grades three, six, and eight
target_learning_goals: authentic intellectual work across writing and mathematics content
examples: The report applied the same standards to score writing and mathematics assignments and student work in grades three, six, and eight in 12 Chicago schools
key_sources: Newmann, F. M., Lopez, G., & Bryk, A. S. (1998). The Quality of Intellectual Work in Chicago Schools: A Baseline Report. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/quality-intellectual-work-chicago-schools-baseline-report

article_title: ATS Field Note — Using AI in Prototyping
citation: McGurl, C. & Maisscotte, B. (2026). ATS Field Note: Using AI in Prototyping. In ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/298
title: Pair AI-supported prototyping with clear team roles, recurring review cycles, and systematic educator feedback
description: The article reports that AI prototyping is most effective when embedded in workflows with clear roles, regular review cycles, and ongoing educator input. Its team established weekly sessions with practicing educators and weekly sessions with internal experts, creating a "build → review → refine" cycle that let them respond quickly, as when teachers called a dashboard "overwhelming" and a revised version was tested the following week.
requirements: Clarified team roles, frequent team check-ins, consistently and systematically gathered educator feedback, and clear guidance on the development process
constraints: Progress slowed when there was no clear system for getting feedback, even though AI enabled rapid generation of multiple feature variations
target_learners: K-2 educators using the literacy decision support tool
target_learning_goals: Usable, classroom-fit literacy workflow and decision support tools refined through educator feedback
examples: The team held weekly sessions with practicing educators and weekly sessions with internal experts; after teachers said a prototype dashboard felt overwhelming, the team simplified the design and tested a revised version the following week
key_sources: McGurl, C. & Maisscotte, B. (2026). ATS Field Note: Using AI in Prototyping. In ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/298

article_title: An Ethical and Equitable Vision of AI in Education: Learning Across 28 Exploratory Projects
citation: Noakes, S., Shell, A., Murillo, A., Van Nostrand, P., Ruiz, P., Cornick, S., and Karim, S. (2024, October). An Ethical and Equitable Vision of AI in Education: Learning Across 28 Exploratory Projects. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/232
title: Build educator AI literacy through professional learning that explains how AI is trained, fine tuned, and functions, equitably distributed across districts
description: The report recommends professional learning focused generally on AI literacy rather than only on operating a specific tool. Educators need to understand which tools incorporate AI, what the tools use AI to do, and how AI is trained and fine tuned, so they can continually evaluate the accuracy of AI-generated content. The report stresses that AI literacy support "needs to be equitably distributed among educators," with high-quality professional learning accessible regardless of the zip code in which teachers work.
requirements: Professional learning that covers how AI is trained and fine tuned and how it functions
Equitable distribution of AI literacy support across all districts
target_learning_goals: Understanding how AI tools function and evaluating the accuracy of AI-generated content
examples: The cohort unearthed a need for the focus to be more generally on AI literacy so educators understand how AI is trained and fine tuned
key_sources: Noakes, S., Shell, A., Murillo, A., Van Nostrand, P., Ruiz, P., Cornick, S., and Karim, S. (2024, October). An Ethical and Equitable Vision of AI in Education: Learning Across 28 Exploratory Projects. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/232

article_title: AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology
citation: Mills, K., Ruiz, P., Lee, K., Coenraad, M., Fusco, J., Roschelle, J., & Weisgrau, J. (2024). AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/218
title: Non-linear AI literacy learning journey cycling through Understand, Evaluate, and Use
description: The report illustrates the framework in action through a high school lesson on AI chatbots, 'following a winding pathway of the three Modes of Engagement.' Students first learn how chatbots work, then responsibly tinker with prompting while noting questions, research those questions with evidence, center human judgment through Socratic seminar discussion, center justice through an Ethics Matrix of stakeholders and values, and optionally design a chatbot for a community problem. The report states 'engagement in AI literacy is non-linear and intertwined, where each mode of engagement builds and strengthens on each other to foster overall AI literacy.'
requirements: Builds on existing curriculum materials such as Common Sense Media AI Literacy Lessons for Grades 6-12
constraints: Illustrated for a high school audience
target_learning_goals: evaluate chatbot outputs and design for bias and transparency
use AI chatbots responsibly and creatively
examples: The lesson uses an Ethics Matrix (building off MIT RAISE) where students identify stakeholders invested in AI chatbots and the values of each stakeholder
key_sources: Mills, K., Ruiz, P., Lee, K., Coenraad, M., Fusco, J., Roschelle, J., & Weisgrau, J. (2024). AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/218

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology: Educator Guide
citation: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org
title: AI builds learner agency when students have opportunities to set goals and make choices about their learning
description: The guide's agency principle holds that AI should expand, not replace, students' capacities to act: "AI should expand students' capacities to act, think, decide, and connect, not replace them." It states that "AI can build agency among students when students have opportunities to set goals and make choices about their learning," and that AI can increase agency by personalizing content and connecting learning to students' goals, interests, and identities. Teachers are urged to help students identify interests and questions that matter to them.
requirements: Tools should allow students to choose when and how to use the AI, including opting out
Students need opportunities to set goals and make choices about their learning
constraints: When AI tools support personalization, privacy is often a trade-off; discuss with students what information is appropriate to share with an LLM and how their data could be used
target_learners: K-12 classroom students using AI tools
examples: The guide recommends building in stop-and-reflect moments about when students should use AI and what decisions they should have the freedom to make, and using AI to weave connections meaningful to students into content to increase relevance.
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology: Educator Guide
citation: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org
title: Design learning so students do the cognitive work themselves when AI tools are in use
description: The guide's metacognition principle states that "AI can support thinking, but it is critical for teachers to design learning so that students do the cognitive work themselves." It warns that when the judgment about the right level of challenge is outsourced to LLMs, student thinking can be undermined, and that research has found some AI tools inhibit productive struggle by reducing cognitive effort. Teachers can foster metacognition by supporting planning, self-monitoring, reflection, and revision.
requirements: Give students space to bring their own thinking and ideas to the table before introducing AI
Build in ample opportunities for human-to-human connection, since relationships, mentorship, and modeling promote productive struggle and metacognition
constraints: Rapid access to large amounts of information may interfere with a learner's ability to notice gaps in their own understanding, an essential process for metacognition and self-regulated learning
target_learning_goals: Metacognition, productive struggle, and self-regulated learning
examples: The guide suggests stop-and-reflect prompts such as: What thinking are you doing? What thinking is the AI doing? Is AI helping you understand, or helping you avoid thinking?
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology: Educator Guide
citation: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org
title: Use AI accessibility features such as captioning, transcription, and translation to reduce barriers, but not for higher-stakes decisions
description: The guide's accessibility principle says AI's "capacity to support accessibility" is one of its current strengths: "AI can support features such as automatic captioning, transcription, translation, text-to-speech, and more, opening access to materials that were previously out of reach for some students." It also notes AI lets students express ideas across multiple modes, consistent with research that all learners benefit from multiple means of representation and expression. Benefits are not automatic, and the guide sets explicit limits for higher-stakes work.
requirements: Use accessibility features in ways that support access without changing what some students are asked to learn
Follow district policies, especially regarding sensitive and identifiable student information
constraints: The potential to broaden accessibility does not make AI a good fit for higher-stakes work, such as making decisions about accommodations or IEP goals
The theory that people have different learning styles has been debunked; the benefit comes from multiple means of representation, not matching styles
target_learners: Students with diverse access needs, including multilingual learners and students with IEPs
target_learning_goals: Access to content and multiple forms of expression
examples: The guide notes some tools allow learners to move objects around physically as well as write to express their understanding, rather than just using one modality.
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology: Educator Guide
citation: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org
title: AI erodes critical thinking when outputs are accepted without background knowledge, but sharpens it when outputs are critiqued, compared, or verified
description: The guide's critical-thinking principle is two-sided: "AI can erode critical thinking when students accept AI outputs without background knowledge or the ability to judge the quality of the content." Conversely, "AI can sharpen their thinking skills when they use AI output as an object to critique, compare, or verify." It stresses that critical thinking is taught within meaningful subject matter, not as a generic skill isolated from content, and that AI can generate false but confident outputs.
requirements: Students need sufficient background knowledge and skill to use AI meaningfully and evaluate whether its output is accurate
Teach students basic information about AI before learning with AI, and integrate learning about AI while using AI tools
constraints: Critical thinking should be built into topics of study rather than taught in isolation only when using AI
target_learners: K-12 students using AI in subject-matter coursework
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking and evaluation of AI-generated content
examples: The guide recommends questions that consider multiple perspectives or missing information: What evidence supports this? What might be missing? Whose perspective is absent?
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org

article_title: AI in Education: A Set of Four Essential Resource Briefs for Educators
citation: Prado, Y.; Ruiz, P.; Fusco, J.; DuVall, D.; Hinkel, D.; Perkoff, M.; Rocha, O. (2026). AI in Education: A Set of Four Essential Resource Briefs for Educators. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/291
title: AI literacy framework: knowledge, skills, and dispositions for critically understanding, evaluating, and responsibly using AI
description: The briefs define AI literacy as "the knowledge, skills, and dispositions needed to critically understand, evaluate, and responsibly use AI systems in learning environments." The framework enumerates components for educators: identifying when AI is used, understanding how AI systems generate outputs, writing effective prompts, evaluating responses critically, recognizing bias and errors, and making informed instructional and ethical decisions. It is positioned as the foundation for ethical AI adoption in schools.
requirements: Educators need enough understanding to know what AI can and cannot do and to guide students, without becoming computer scientists
target_learning_goals: responsible and ethical use of AI tools
examples: The briefs were developed with the U-GAIN Reading National Leadership Educator Cohort as foundational knowledge for K-12 reading contexts
key_sources: Prado, Y.; Ruiz, P.; Fusco, J.; DuVall, D.; Hinkel, D.; Perkoff, M.; Rocha, O. (2026). AI in Education: A Set of Four Essential Resource Briefs for Educators. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/291

article_title: What States Say about Evaluating AI in Education
citation: Ruiz, P., Prado, Y., Roschelle, J., & Fusco, J. (2025). What States Say About Evaluating AI in Education: Reviewing Guidance From 32 States and Puerto Rico. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/280
title: Center educational goals and student outcomes, equity, human oversight, and safety in AI evaluation
description: The report identifies common priorities across state AI evaluation guidance: prioritizing human agency and oversight, centering educational goals and student outcomes in evaluation activities, committing to equity and accessibility, and ensuring compliance, safety, security, and privacy. These shared commitments frame evaluation as systematic assessment of impact that helps leaders move beyond hype to informed adoption decisions.
requirements: Evaluation that accounts for the non-deterministic, constantly evolving nature of generative AI systems with no stable versions to assess
target_learning_goals: Meaningful returns on educational technology investments in service of student learning
examples: North Carolina requires vendors to adhere to stringent security standards; Oklahoma requires vendors to provide evidence of effectiveness and impact before procurement.
key_sources: Ruiz, P., Prado, Y., Roschelle, J., & Fusco, J. (2025). What States Say About Evaluating AI in Education: Reviewing Guidance From 32 States and Puerto Rico. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/280

article_title: Integrating AI-Enabled EdTech in PK16 Education: Five Recommendations
citation: Ruiz, P., Peters Hinton, V., Prado, Y., Noakes, S., Liberman, B., Chillmon, C., Van Nostrand, P., Shell, A., Karim, S., Dallas, D., & Zachariah, I. (2025). Integrating AI-enabled edtech in PK16 education: Five recommendations for state and district leaders. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/273
title: AI-Enabled EdTech Adoption Cycle (vision and planning, implementation, ongoing evaluation, scaling and sustaining)
description: Appendix 1 of the brief outlines a four-phase adoption cycle for AI-enabled edtech: vision and planning, implementation, ongoing evaluation, and scaling and sustaining, each with key challenges and recommendations. It states that "Planning for AI-enabled edtech requires districts to move beyond reactive purchasing decisions and establish strategic frameworks that align technology with clear learning objectives and pedagogical goals." AI-enabled tools require specialized evaluation criteria including algorithmic transparency, bias mitigation, and data privacy.
requirements: Cross-functional teams, formal planning processes, and data-driven needs assessments
Comprehensive support systems including professional learning, clear usage guidelines, and usage tracking
constraints: Key challenges listed include siloed processes, insufficient measurement, delayed data availability, funding constraints, capacity limitations, market fragmentation, too many unused tools, and lack of vendor support
target_learners: District and state leaders adopting AI-enabled edtech for PK16 learners
target_learning_goals: Sustainable, student-centric adoption of AI-enabled educational technologies
examples: The ongoing evaluation phase recommends usage dashboards, adverse incident reporting systems, and early quality indicators including keyword detection at the input and output layers
key_sources: Ruiz, P., Peters Hinton, V., Prado, Y., Noakes, S., Liberman, B., Chillmon, C., Van Nostrand, P., Shell, A., Karim, S., Dallas, D., & Zachariah, I. (2025). Integrating AI-enabled edtech in PK16 education: Five recommendations for state and district leaders. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/273

article_title: Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators
citation: Ruiz, P. & Fusco, J. (2024). Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators. Educator CIRCLS Blog. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: AI built two primary ways: human-given rules versus machine learning
description: The glossary presents AI as "a branch of computer science" in which systems use hardware, algorithms, and data to create "intelligence" to do things like make decisions, discover patterns, and perform actions. It organizes the field by two primary build approaches: rule-based systems where human programmers give the rules, and machine learning algorithms that discover their own rules. This distinction anchors the rest of the glossary, including neural networks, LLMs, and generative AI.
requirements: Understanding the rule-based versus machine-learning distinction is needed to follow related entries such as algorithm, black boxes, and training data.
target_learning_goals: Understanding how AI systems are built and how machine learning differs from rule-based systems
examples: The algorithm entry explains that machine learning algorithms "can discover their own rules ... or be rule-based where human programmers give the rules."
key_sources: Ruiz, P. & Fusco, J. (2024). Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators. Educator CIRCLS Blog. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/ed330bf1-6697-4cb7-9189-79eba8eb0a1e

article_title: A Series of Briefs: Implementing AI Literacy Across Learning Environments
citation: Ruiz, P., Liberman, B., Karim, S., Dallas, D., Zachariah, I., Peters Hinton, V., Chillmon, C., & Gonzales, L. (2025). Implementing AI literacy across learning environments: A series of briefs. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/268
title: AI literacy as a set of foundational skills and competencies spanning understanding, evaluation, and effective human-centered use
description: The briefs define AI literacy as "a set of foundational skills and competencies that enable individuals to understand how AI works, responsibly evaluate AI systems, and use AI effectively as a human-centered tool across various contexts, including learning, work, and civic applications, while adapting to its ongoing evolution." This definition synthesizes several prior frameworks (CSTA & AI4K12, OECD, EDSAFE AI Alliance, Mills et al., Long & Magerko) and organizes the brief series' recommendations for learners and leaders across settings.
requirements: Adoption requires adapting to AI's ongoing evolution, so the definition is framed as dynamic rather than fixed
constraints: The authors note the brief may not capture every recent advancement and should be treated as foundational guidance while readers stay informed
target_learning_goals: using AI effectively as a human-centered tool
examples: The definition anchors four audience-specific briefs: PK-12, postsecondary, workforce, and informal learning environments
key_sources: Ruiz, P., Liberman, B., Karim, S., Dallas, D., Zachariah, I., Peters Hinton, V., Chillmon, C., & Gonzales, L. (2025). Implementing AI literacy across learning environments: A series of briefs. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/268

article_title: An Evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures Grant
citation: Fong, A., Chen-Gaddini, M., & Huang, M. (2025). An evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures grant. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Air Tutors virtual high-dosage math tutoring program
description: Air Tutors is an online high-dosage math tutoring program for upper elementary and early middle school grades, delivered via "dynamic video conferencing and interactive whiteboards" at a ratio of four students per tutor. It offers 45-minute sessions four to five times per week over 10 weeks (30 intended hours), uses the i-Ready curriculum's scope and sequence, employs tutors with at least a bachelor's degree and 3 years of experience, and structures instruction within the gradual release of responsibility framework alongside an Ubuntu professional learning community.
requirements: Tutors with at least 3 years of math teaching experience and a bachelor's degree or higher
Sufficient scheduling, budget, and calendar time to deliver the intended 30-hour dosage over at least 10 weeks
constraints: In this evaluation, District B schools delivered far fewer hours than planned due to budget reductions, scheduling limits, late starts, and cancellations
target_learners: 4th through 6th grade students needing foundational math support
target_learning_goals: Foundational math skills including decimals, fractions, proportions, and basic geometry
examples: In the 2023–24 evaluation, 1,210 students across two districts attended at least one Air Tutors session, with tutors delivering instruction via the online platform
key_sources: Fong, A., Chen-Gaddini, M., & Huang, M. (2025). An evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures grant. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673538

article_title: An Evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: A 1-Year Follow-Up on Math Achievement. Findings from an Arnold Ventures Grant
citation: Fong, A., Chen-Gaddini, M., & Huang, M. (2026). An Evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: A 1-Year Follow-Up on Math Achievement. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Air Tutors high-dosage math tutoring program
description: Air Tutors is a high-dosage math tutoring program evaluated in two districts (Colorado and Texas). The implementation plan "called for students to attend 45-minute sessions 4–5 times per week for at least 10 weeks, totaling approximately 30 hours of tutoring", with adequate participation defined as at least 24 hours (80 percent of full dosage). This follow-up evaluation found no measurable long-term effects on statewide math assessments 1 year after tutoring concluded.
requirements: Students were intended to receive approximately 30 hours of tutoring via 45-minute sessions 4–5 times per week for at least 10 weeks.
constraints: In District B, student participation remained far below the intended 30 hours because scheduling disruptions and session cancellations limited consistent exposure.
target_learners: Students in grades 4, 5, and 6 in two school districts (District A in Colorado, District B in Texas)
target_learning_goals: Math achievement as measured by statewide standardized summative assessments
examples: The evaluation matched treatment students to observationally similar non-tutored comparison students in District A (CMAS) and District B (STAAR).
key_sources: Fong, A., Chen-Gaddini, M., & Huang, M. (2026). An Evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: A 1-Year Follow-Up on Math Achievement. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681370

article_title: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Students
citation: Miao, Fengchun; Shiohira, Kelly; Lao, Natalie. (2024). AI competency framework for students. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-competency-framework-students
title: Four dimensions of student AI competency: human-centred mindset, ethics of AI, AI techniques and applications, AI system design
description: The framework organizes its 12 competencies under four dimensions: "A human-centred mindset", "Ethics of AI", "AI techniques and applications", and "AI system design". These dimensions define the domains in which students are expected to develop AI-related competence, ranging from values and ethics to technical understanding and design capability.
requirements: Used as the organizing structure for the framework's 12 competencies
key_sources: Miao, Fengchun; Shiohira, Kelly; Lao, Natalie. (2024). AI competency framework for students. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-competency-framework-students

article_title: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Students
citation: Miao, Fengchun; Shiohira, Kelly; Lao, Natalie. (2024). AI competency framework for students. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-competency-framework-students
title: Three progression levels of AI competency: Understand, Apply, Create
description: The framework structures competency development across three progression levels: "Understand", "Apply", and "Create". This progression moves students from comprehension of AI concepts, through application, toward creation, and is used to organize the framework's curricular goals and pedagogical methodologies across the four competency dimensions.
requirements: Applied across the framework's four competency dimensions to structure curricular goals
target_learning_goals: Progression from understanding AI, to applying AI, to creating with AI
key_sources: Miao, Fengchun; Shiohira, Kelly; Lao, Natalie. (2024). AI competency framework for students. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-competency-framework-students

article_title: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers
citation: Miao, Fengchun; Cukurova, Mutlu. (2024). AI competency framework for teachers. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org
title: Three progression levels — Acquire, Deepen, Create — structure teacher AI competency development
description: Within the framework, the 15 competencies are "categorized into three progression levels: Acquire, Deepen, Create." This progression axis describes how teachers advance from initial acquisition of AI-related competencies through deepening them to creating new applications and practices. It complements the five-dimension structure and is intended to inform the design of teacher training programmes and assessment parameters.
requirements: Training programmes and assessment parameters should be designed to reflect the three progression levels
target_learning_goals: progressive development of AI competencies from acquisition to creation
examples: The publication presents Acquire, Deepen, and Create as the levels into which all 15 competencies are categorized
key_sources: Miao, Fengchun; Cukurova, Mutlu. (2024). AI competency framework for teachers. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-competency-framework-teachers

article_title: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers
citation: Miao, Fengchun; Cukurova, Mutlu. (2024). AI competency framework for teachers. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org
title: Develop teacher AI competency frameworks on principles of protecting teachers' rights, enhancing human agency, and promoting sustainability
description: The framework was "Developed with principles of protecting teachers' rights, enhancing human agency, and promoting sustainability." This principle holds that teacher AI competency frameworks and training should be designed so that teachers' rights are protected, their human agency is enhanced, and sustainability is promoted, rather than treating AI adoption as a purely technical matter.
requirements: National AI competency frameworks and teacher training programmes built on this framework should embed these three principles
target_learning_goals: ethical and human-centred use of AI in education
examples: The publication states the framework itself was developed with these three principles
key_sources: Miao, Fengchun; Cukurova, Mutlu. (2024). AI competency framework for teachers. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-competency-framework-teachers

article_title: AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle
citation: Ruiz, P., and Noakes, S. (2025). AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/272
title: Four-phase AI-enabled edtech adoption cycle for districts
description: The article organizes district adoption of AI-enabled edtech into a cycle of four phases: vision and planning, implementation, ongoing evaluation, and scaling and sustaining. Each phase pairs a goal statement with key challenges and recommendations, e.g. planning requires districts to "move beyond reactive purchasing decisions and establish strategic frameworks that align technology with clear learning objectives and pedagogical goals." The cycle frames adoption as continuous rather than a one-time purchase.
requirements: Districts must establish strategic frameworks aligned with learning objectives and pedagogical goals before purchasing
constraints: The framework addresses AI-enabled edtech specifically, with criteria such as algorithmic transparency, bias mitigation, and data privacy
target_learners: K-12 district leaders and procurement staff
target_learning_goals: Effective selection, implementation, and sustained use of AI-enabled educational technology
examples: The brief lists per-phase challenges such as siloed processes, reliance on sales pitches, insufficient measurement, unused tools, funding constraints, and market fragmentation
key_sources: Ruiz, P., and Noakes, S. (2025). AI-Enabled Edtech Adoption Cycle. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/272

article_title: School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices
citation: Jackson, T., Pakhira, D., Fusco, J., Ruiz, P., Lekshmi Narayanan, A. B., Glazer, K., Eaglin, P., & Eguchi, A. (2021). School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices. CIRCLS. https://circls.org/reports/ai-policy
title: AI developers must be transparent about what their algorithms learn and how data is collected, used, and stored
description: The brief urges developers to commit to designing with educators and clearly communicating design context, data collection, and use. It states "AI developers must be transparent about what their algorithms will learn and how they will use that information to partner with educators to adapt, promote equitable instructional practices."
requirements: Developers should identify and communicate how the AI was designed, its intended context, and data handling
target_learning_goals: equitable instructional practices and educator advocacy
examples: The brief recommends using interpretable models such as decision trees and support-vector machines and disclosing interpretability
key_sources: Jackson, T., Pakhira, D., Fusco, J., Ruiz, P., Lekshmi Narayanan, A. B., Glazer, K., Eaglin, P., & Eguchi, A. (2021). School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices. CIRCLS. https://circls.org/reports/ai-policy

article_title: Agentic AI and Pedagogical Best Practice: The Tension Between Automation and Learning
citation: Steve Woollaston, Brendan Flanagan, Isanka Wijerathne, and Hiroaki Ogata. (2026). Agentic AI and Pedagogical Best Practice: The Tension Between Automation and Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04543
title: Exercise AI usage restraint: prioritise Modification and Redefinition over Substitution and Augmentation
description: The article urges educators to critically assess which learning tasks genuinely benefit from AI support and which are better served through traditional methods that prioritise human interaction and internal cognitive processing. Applying the SAMR model it cites, educators should avoid using AI merely for Substitution or Augmentation, where the technology adds little pedagogical value, and instead prioritise instances where AI can facilitate true Modification or Redefinition of the learning experience. The article notes that sometimes the most effective tool for deep learning remains a conversation or a blank page.
requirements: Educators must critically assess each learning task's suitability for AI support before deployment
constraints: The article presents this as a recommendation applying the SAMR model, not as an empirically tested allocation rule
target_learners: educators and AI stakeholders designing learning tasks
target_learning_goals: pedagogical integrity and deep human learning over task-completion efficiency

article_title: AI Agents, Joyful Assessment, and Third Space: Rethinking Assessment in the GenAI Era
citation: Eliana Khoury & Xiaoyan Ma. (2026). AI Agents, Joyful Assessment, and Third Space: Rethinking Assessment in the GenAI Era. Journal of Teaching and Learning, 20(4). https://doi.org/10.22329/jtl.v20i4.11850
title: AI-mediated third space assessment environments connecting formal curriculum with students' interests, experiences, and learning needs
description: Drawing on third space theory, the paper argues that AI agents implemented "within relational and ethically governed environments" can help mediate assessment settings that "connect formal curriculum with students' interests, experiences, and learning needs". Third space here names a hybrid assessment environment shaped jointly by formal curriculum and learner experience.

constraints: The paper presents this mediation as an argument to be examined further, listing relational assessment practice and equity among its future research directions.

target_learning_goals: connecting formal curriculum to student interests and experiences

article_title: AI-Assisted Autonomous Learning and Reduced Academic Accomplishment in Vocational Higher Education: The Mediating Role of Hardiness

title: Integrate AI as a supportive scaffold that preserves moderately challenging tasks and independent decision-making
description: The article recommends that AI tools be integrated "as supportive scaffolds rather than replacement systems": teachers should "intentionally retain moderately challenging tasks in AI-supported courses" and design activities requiring students to explain, reflect, revise, and decide independently. AI should provide prompting questions, step-by-step hints, alternative perspectives, or reflective feedback rather than complete solutions, so students keep a sense of control, persistence, and ownership while benefiting from AI support.

constraints: The recommendation rests on cross-sectional correlational evidence, not on a test of the designed activities themselves

examples: The authors suggest AI systems be designed or used to provide prompting questions, step-by-step hints, alternative perspectives, or reflective feedback rather than complete solutions

article_title: AI chatbot design principles to enhance the collective efficacy in collaborative learning
citation: Minji Kim, Cheolil Lim. (2025). AI chatbot design principles to enhance the collective efficacy in collaborative learning. Asia Pacific Education Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12564-025-10080-z
title: Four-element design framework for AI chatbots enhancing collective efficacy in collaborative learning
description: The article proposes a design framework for educational AI chatbots organized into four design elements: group cohesion support, affective cohesion support, support for collaborative learning activities, and inducing conversation (facilitation of dialogue). These elements are operationalized through ten design principles and 46 sub-guidelines. The framework is grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, Social and Emotional Learning, Social Presence Theory, and Transactional Distance Theory, and positions chatbots as "dynamic members of collaborative teams" that scaffold both social and cognitive processes.
requirements: The chatbot must automatically deliver team-specific feedback by analyzing accumulated conversation logs, without requiring learner prompts
constraints: The principles were developed as general guidelines across age groups; the authors state context-specific principles for project-based, maker, and discussion-based learning require further research
target_learners: learners working in collaborative learning teams across age groups
examples: The final framework comprises four components operationalized through ten actionable design principles and 46 sub-guidelines, refined through three expert validation rounds and a usability test
key_sources: Minji Kim, Cheolil Lim. (2025). AI chatbot design principles to enhance the collective efficacy in collaborative learning. Asia Pacific Education Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12564-025-10080-z

article_title: AI chatbot design principles to enhance the collective efficacy in collaborative learning
citation: Minji Kim, Cheolil Lim. (2025). AI chatbot design principles to enhance the collective efficacy in collaborative learning. Asia Pacific Education Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12564-025-10080-z
title: Address data privacy and algorithmic bias when deploying educational AI chatbots
description: The article recommends that researchers and educators consider ethical factors when using AI chatbots in education. It identifies data privacy risks around storage and use of user logs and algorithmic bias such as cultural insensitivity or emotionally inappropriate responses as significant concerns, and prescribes informed consent, active bias monitoring, institutional policy standards for student data governance, and ethical guidelines for chatbot development and deployment to support responsible implementation and user trust.
requirements: Prior and informed consent from users; institutional policy standards governing collection, storage, and use of student data
target_learners: all learners interacting with educational AI chatbots
target_learning_goals: safe and responsible AI-supported learning environments
examples: The article recommends increasing awareness of implicit bias, actively monitoring chatbot behavior, and staying up to date with the evolving capabilities and limitations of generative AI in education

article_title: Artificial intelligence as a cognitive partner: a developmental framework for human-AI co-regulation in learning
citation: S P, Joseph J, Jose M, S M A, N R and Joseph J (2026) Artificial intelligence as a cognitive partner: a developmental framework for human–AI co-regulation in learning. Front. Dev. Psychol. 4:1835258. https://doi.org/10.3389/fdpys.2026.1835258
title: AI integration should complement rather than replace human cognition, preserving human engagement in critical thinking and self-regulation domains
description: The article argues educators must distinguish domains where AI can productively support cognition (information processing, feedback, scaffolding, routine problem-solving) from domains requiring sustained human engagement (critical thinking, ethical reasoning, decision-making under uncertainty, self-regulation development). Its stated goal: "the goal of AI integration should not be to replace human cognition but to complement it, ensuring that external support enhances rather than substitutes the development of core cognitive competencies."
requirements: Deliberate domain-level decisions about where AI support is permitted and where human effortful processing is preserved
constraints: Over-reliance on AI in domains requiring effortful processing may limit opportunities for independent reasoning essential for long-term cognitive growth
examples: The article identifies information processing, feedback provision, scaffolding, and routine problem-solving as domains where AI is particularly effective

article_title: 'Artificial Intelligence and Communities of Inquiry: Reimagining Educational Experiences'
citation: Stenbom, S., & Garrison, D. R. (2026). Artificial Intelligence and Communities of Inquiry: Reimagining Educational Experiences. The International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 27(2), 114–131. https://doi.org/10.19173/irrodl.v27i2.9314
title: A five-role taxonomy of AI within a community of inquiry: instructional design support, independent learner resource, instructor analytics, discussion participant, and dialogical partner
description: The article enumerates the potential roles AI can assume within a community of inquiry: "supporting instructional design, guiding learners as an independent resource, assisting instructors through analytics, participating in discussions, and sustaining dialogical partnerships with students." These roles, the authors state, "highlight the capacity of AI to enrich learning communities," while also carrying risks when reflective inquiry is bypassed. The taxonomy organizes how AI participation can be designed across the teaching, cognitive, and social dimensions of a community of inquiry.
requirements: AI roles must be designed so that reflective inquiry is not bypassed
constraints: Roles are outlined as potential; the article does not report empirical evaluation of any role
target_learning_goals: meaningful integration of AI in learning communities
examples: The article examines each role—from design support to dialogical partnership—as a distinct way AI may participate in a community of inquiry

article_title: 'Artificial Intelligence and Communities of Inquiry: Reimagining Educational Experiences'
citation: Stenbom, S., & Garrison, D. R. (2026). Artificial Intelligence and Communities of Inquiry: Reimagining Educational Experiences. The International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 27(2), 114–131. https://doi.org/10.19173/irrodl.v27i2.9314
title: Adopt AI in education only within a coherent conceptual perspective emphasizing skeptical engagement, collaborative reflection, and preservation of human purpose
description: The article's central design recommendation is that "AI can contribute to worthwhile educational experiences only when framed within a coherent conceptual perspective that emphasizes skeptical engagement, collaborative reflection, and the preservation of human purpose." Adoption should therefore be organized around a framework such as CoI rather than around tools, so that AI strengthens rather than supplants collaborative inquiry.
requirements: A coherent conceptual framework (the article proposes CoI) must frame AI adoption
constraints: The article states this as a necessary condition for worthwhile educational experiences with AI; it does not claim tool-level adoption without a framework is impossible
examples: The article argues for framing AI adoption within the CoI framework, emphasizing skeptical engagement and collaborative reflection

article_title: The dark side of AI in education: AI dependency as a mediator linking academic self-efficacy and teacher support to learning burnout among university students
citation: Huang Q, Tu S, Lin J, Lu L and Lv C (2026). The dark side of AI in education: AI dependency as a mediator linking academic self-efficacy and teacher support to learning burnout among university students. Front. Psychol. 17:1889053. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1889053
title: Resource-depletion mediation framework: AI dependency as the mechanism linking personal and contextual resources to learning burnout
description: The article proposes an integrated framework in which academic self-efficacy (a personal psychological resource) and teacher support (a contextual resource) shape AI dependency, which in turn is associated with learning burnout. Grounded in Conservation of Resources, Cognitive Offloading, and Social Cognitive Theory, it treats AI dependency as "a comprehensive psychological phenomenon that encompasses emotional, cognitive, and behavioral dimensions". Dependency may temporarily conserve cognitive resources but gradually deplete internal learning resources such as critical thinking and autonomous learning competence, intensifying burnout.
requirements: Measurement of academic self-efficacy, teacher support, AI dependency, and learning burnout as distinct validated constructs
Theoretical framing in Conservation of Resources, Cognitive Offloading, and Social Cognitive Theory
constraints: The cross-sectional design limits the ability to establish causal relationships among the variables
The proposed model may capture only part of the mechanisms underlying AI dependency, indicating that its explanatory scope is not exhaustive
Reciprocal relationships may exist, such as higher burnout leading to greater AI dependency
target_learners: university students in AI-assisted learning environments
target_learning_goals: promoting responsible and autonomous AI use
examples: The study tested the framework with a cross-sectional survey of 276 university students using PROCESS Model 4 mediation analysis with 5,000 bootstrap resamples.
key_sources: Huang Q, Tu S, Lin J, Lu L and Lv C (2026). The dark side of AI in education: AI dependency as a mediator linking academic self-efficacy and teacher support to learning burnout among university students. Front. Psychol. 17:1889053. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1889053

citation: Wang J and Li P (2026). AI-driven educational reform: enhancing talent cultivation in computer-related majors for the digital era. Front. Psychol. 17:1790916. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1790916
title: AI-driven talent cultivation reform framework with five interconnected components
description: The article proposes a comprehensive reform framework for computer-related majors grounded in the new engineering philosophy, integrating AI across curriculum, pedagogy, and practical training. As printed, "The framework is structured around five core components: curriculum restructuring, smart teaching integration, interdisciplinary and collaborative talent cultivation, practice-based learning enhancement, and multi-dimensional evaluation." The components form an interconnected system intended to deliver AI-empowered talent cultivation with academic depth and industrial relevance, and the framework was phased in across four undergraduate programs as a replicable model.
requirements: AI technologies must be systematically embedded across curriculum structures, instructional processes, and practice-oriented modules rather than confined to isolated courses
constraints: Implemented in computer-related majors at one Chinese institution under the new engineering education paradigm
target_learning_goals: technical proficiency in AI and computing
examples: The reform framework was phased in across four undergraduate programs, with new courses such as Artificial Intelligence and Big Data Analysis and partnerships such as the Huawei Cybersecurity Laboratory

citation: Wang J and Li P (2026). AI-driven educational reform: enhancing talent cultivation in computer-related majors for the digital era. Front. Psychol. 17:1790916. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1790916
title: AI-enhanced course set spanning compulsory, elective, and practice categories
description: Table 1 of the article catalogs representative reformed courses. As printed, "the integration of AI into the curriculum is demonstrated through a selection of representative courses that highlight the breadth of the reform." Compulsory courses such as Network Security Technology introduce AI-driven intrusion detection with machine learning models for abnormal network traffic; electives such as Artificial Intelligence and Big Data Analysis introduce Python, TensorFlow, and big data frameworks; practice courses such as Enterprise Software Development Practice use AI-powered automated testing and code quality assessment tools.
requirements: Courses embed AI tools, industry datasets, and case studies into both theoretical and practical instruction
constraints: Course examples are drawn from one college's computer-related programs

article_title: AI-Driven Educational Reform: Enhancing Talent Cultivation in Computer-Related Majors for the Digital Era
citation: Wang J and Li P (2026). AI-driven educational reform: enhancing talent cultivation in computer-related majors for the digital era. Front. Psychol. 17:1790916. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1790916
title: Three-phase AI smart teaching loop of pre-class diagnosis, in-class adaptation, and post-class analytics
description: The smart teaching integration organizes AI support across the instructional cycle. Before class, "AI-powered diagnostic systems analyze historical learning records, course performance data, and individual cognitive profiles to assess knowledge readiness" and generate personalized preparation materials. During class, AI-enabled assistants monitor engagement in real time and can push supplementary explanations, mini quizzes, or instructor alerts. After class, intelligent grading systems provide immediate formative feedback and dashboards feed a closed-loop mechanism connecting learning design, implementation, and continuous improvement.
requirements: An integrated AI-LMS platform connecting data from classrooms, laboratories, and online learning environments
constraints: The article notes existing research remains largely focused on tool- or course-level functional performance with limited attention to curriculum-level alignment
examples: Instructors receive dashboard-based overviews highlighting learning gaps across the class cohort, allowing them to customize lesson emphasis

citation: Wang J and Li P (2026). AI-driven educational reform: enhancing talent cultivation in computer-related majors for the digital era. Front. Psychol. 17:1790916. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1790916
title: AI teaching technology stack: dashboard, reinforcement-learning feedback, and LLM-based semantic assessment
description: The article specifies the implemented technologies behind the smart teaching ecosystem. As printed, "The intelligent dashboard was implemented in a Python 3.10 environment using Dash and Plotly for visualization, and integrated with a PostgreSQL database to store students' activity logs and analysis results." Adaptive feedback loops use a reinforcement learning model in PyTorch to adjust learning tasks and personalized exercises; open-ended assignments are evaluated by converting text to vectors with the Qwen-7B pre-trained large language model and computing cosine similarity against reference documents.

constraints: Described as employed within this study's computing-related majors
examples: Semantic similarity analysis converts student submissions into vectors with the Qwen-7B pre-trained large language model and computes cosine similarity against reference documents

article_title: Artificial and Emotional Intelligence: Two Key Forces for Teachers' Professional Development in an Era of Uncertainty
citation: Aponte ML, Vargas Sánchez AD, Chiappe A and Martínez-Pérez S. (2026). Artificial and emotional intelligence: two key forces for teachers' professional development in an era of uncertainty. Front. Psychol. 17:1935683. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935683
title: Taxonomy of five AI-mediated functions in teacher professional development with differentiated ethical and pedagogical risks
description: The article treats educational AI as a heterogeneous family of systems rather than one technology, distinguishing "coordination systems, recommendation tools, analytics, conversational agents, and emotional AI" and examining their differentiated risks. Emotional AI is defined in a restricted sense as systems "that claim to recognize, infer, simulate, respond to, or classify emotions through computational means," deserving particular caution because they intervene directly in the socio-emotional domain. The taxonomy underpins the article's claim that critique should target substitutive, data-extractive uses rather than AI-mediated support in general.
requirements: Risk analysis and governance must be matched to the specific AI-mediated function, since a scheduling tool and an emotion-inference system raise different ethical concerns
constraints: The critique is directed only at uses that individualize wellbeing, replace human relationships, intensify data extraction, infer affective states without safeguards, or connect emotional information to managerial decisions
target_learners: AI system designers for professional development
target_learning_goals: ethical AI use in professional development
examples: The article contrasts a scheduling tool protecting collaboration time with a system inferring stress from facial expression, and a chatbot routing teachers to human mentoring versus one acting as an always-available emotional companion

article_title: When AI threatens my future career: growth mindset and perceived employability in Chinese college students' career decision making anxiety
citation: Chen H (2026) When AI threatens my future career: growth mindset and perceived employability in Chinese college students' career decision making anxiety. Front. Psychol. 17:1933842. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1933842
title: Cognitive-appraisal-based moderated mediation framework linking AI employment threat, perceived employability, growth mindset, and career decision-making anxiety
description: The article proposes and tests an integrated model drawing primarily on cognitive appraisal theory, in which "AI employment threat perception represents an appraisal of potential career threat, whereas perceived employability reﬂects students' evaluation of whether they possess suﬃcient career resources to respond to that threat." Growth mindset is positioned as a personal resource shaping this appraisal process, so that students who view abilities as developable interpret AI-driven change as opportunity for skill renewal rather than denial of their employment value. The framework integrates threat appraisal, resource appraisal, and a moderator explaining heterogeneity in students' responses.
requirements: Self-report measures of AI employment threat perception, perceived employability, career decision-making anxiety, and growth mindset from students facing AI-related labor market change
constraints: Cross-sectional single-time-point design limits causal and temporal inference
Sample drawn from a single institutional context in China, limiting generalizability
Model emphasizes threat-oriented appraisal and captures only part of the broader response process
target_learners: College students approaching career decisions in an AI-driven labor market
target_learning_goals: Accurate appraisal of AI-related employment change
examples: The author tested the framework with hierarchical regression, bootstrap mediation, moderation, simple slope, and moderated mediation analyses on survey data from 526 students.

article_title: From AI literacy to AI-integrated inquiry-based science teaching: the serial mediating roles of AI-TPACK and science teaching self-efficacy among Chinese pre-service science teachers
citation: Zou J, Li N, Wang X and Du J (2026) From AI literacy to AI-integrated inquiry-based science teaching: the serial mediating roles of AI-TPACK and science teaching self-efficacy among Chinese pre-service science teachers. title: AI-TPACK as a professional knowledge bridge linking general AI literacy, science teaching self-efficacy, and AI integration intention
description: The study positions AI-TPACK — pre-service science teachers' perceived ability to integrate AI tools, science content, inquiry-based pedagogy, and ethical judgment — as the central construct of a serial mediation model. Rather than a comprehensive measure of AI competence, the article frames it as "a professional knowledge bridge between general AI literacy and AI integration intention". target_learning_goals: AI-integrated pedagogical competence for inquiry-based science teaching
confidence in using AI to support inquiry, experimentation, data interpretation, and scientific explanation
examples: The study modeled AI-TPACK as a first-order serial mediator between AI literacy and intention in a PLS-SEM analysis of 548 Chinese pre-service science teachers.

article_title: Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance
citation: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816
title: AI learning companions framework: three interrelated design foundations
description: The paper defines AI learning companions as "adaptive, pedagogically informed, LLM-powered agents designed for integration into learning environments" and organises their design into three foundations. The pedagogical foundation addresses how students learn with AI, fostering cognitive engagement, metacognitive awareness, and agency. The adaptive foundation addresses how AI learns about students, modelling cognitive, affective, and behavioural data to tailor feedback and instruction. The responsible design foundation ensures systems remain transparent, accountable, inclusive, and secure, upholding human oversight, equity, and trust.
requirements: Deliberate engineering that prioritises durable learning over short-term performance, rather than repurposing LLMs built for work
constraints: The framework is illustrated through five case studies said to reveal both promise and current limitations of existing tools; the supplied text is truncated before the case studies
target_learners: students across diverse educational contexts and levels
examples: The paper states the framework is illustrated through five case studies spanning diverse educational contexts, levels, and tool designs
key_sources: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816

article_title: Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance
citation: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816
title: Nine-dimension contrast between AI for work and AI for learning
description: Figure 1 formalises the contrast between AI designed for professional productivity and AI designed to support learning across nine dimensions, including purpose, nature of interaction, relationship to cognitive effort, error, measures of success, failure mode, and design principle. In work contexts AI performs the task and success is output quality; in learning contexts AI must "scaffold and challenge the learner to produce their own understanding", interactions are developmental and cumulative, and success is measured by retention, transfer, and metacognitive growth. The key failure mode for learning AI is performance gains masking absent learning.
requirements: Design intent must deliberately withhold direct answers and preserve productive struggle
constraints: The paper frames this as a conceptual contrast, not an empirically tested taxonomy
examples: The paper states AI for work fails when productivity gains mask skill atrophy, while AI for learning fails when task scores improve while knowledge retention declines

article_title: Defining AI Fatigue in Academic Contexts: Dimensions, Indicators, and a Stage-Based Model Using Grounded Theory
citation: Miranda, J. P. P., Parreño, E. B., & Rivera, J. G. (2026). Defining AI Fatigue in Academic Contexts: Dimensions, Indicators, and a Stage-Based Model Using Grounded Theory. International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research, 25(5), 91–107. https://doi.org/10.26803/ijlter.25.5.5
title: AI Fatigue Model: a six-stage framework describing how AI-related strain accumulates and reinforces itself
description: The AI Fatigue Model is a stage-based conceptual framework explaining how the five dimensions of AI fatigue develop across repeated academic AI interaction. It proposes "six progressively intensifying stages": Initial Effort Reduction, Expansion of AI Roles, Accumulation of Strain, Disruption of Self-Regulation, Fatigue Consolidation, and a Feedback Loop in which continued AI use returns students to earlier stages and intensifies all pressures. The stage sequence was derived from the order in which participants described pressures in their accounts.
requirements: Requires empirical validation; the authors state the model "requires empirical validation before broader application".
constraints: Findings are exploratory, drawn from three universities in one academic region and self-reported data.
target_learners: university students using AI chatbots for academic work
target_learning_goals: recognizing and managing strain from sustained academic AI use
examples: In the Accumulation of Strain stage, students reported pressures across the five dimensions, e.g., "I feel mentally exhausted after checking so many outputs" (n = 72).

article_title: Beyond Tool Adoption: A Practical Five-Stage Developmental Continuum for AI Literacy in Higher Education
citation: Liu, J. P., & Levy, R. (2026). Beyond Tool Adoption: A Practical Five-Stage Developmental Continuum for AI Literacy in Higher Education. North Carolina State University.
title: The five-stage AI Literacy Continuum (Stages 0–4) describing developmental orientations toward AI use
description: The article proposes a five-stage developmental continuum: "0) Not Yet Engaged, 1) Uncritical Use, 2) Informed Use, 3) Critical Evaluation, and 4) Improvement". It complements dimensional competency frameworks by providing a diagnostic and instructional pathway describing how learners progress from avoidance or passive consumption toward responsible engagement, analytical judgment, and active contribution to AI systems. Stages are predominant orientations rather than rigid categories, and progression is generally sequential but not strictly linear.
requirements: Educators use observable indicators (Table 1) to diagnose learners' current stage and design instruction matched to it
constraints: The continuum is descriptive rather than normative at the individual level; stage is domain-dependent and learners may regress under unfamiliar conditions
target_learning_goals: responsible and critical engagement with AI systems
examples: Table 1 operationalizes each stage with observable indicators and possible assessment evidence, described as practical heuristics rather than psychometrically validated cut scores

article_title: The Main Barrier to AI Adoption in the Public Sector is Lack of Training
citation: Vinicius Santana Gomes. (2026). The Main Barrier to AI Adoption in the Public Sector Is Lack of Training: How a Structured Method Accompanied Productivity Gains in Two Brazilian Government Cases. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01517
title: The AI House: a four-layer pedagogical method for public-sector AI adoption (Foundation, Walls, Finishing, Roof)
description: The AI House is the article's named four-layer pedagogical method for adopting generative AI in the public sector, described as "a four-layer pedagogical method for the adoption of Artificial Intelligence in the public sector". The Foundation teaches what generative AI is and how the model produces text; the Walls teach prompt construction (the PACTO method, Chain of Thought, zero-/one-/few-shot modes); the Finishing ties AI functionalities to the public servant's concrete document tasks and marks where human review is mandatory; the Roof integrates data-protection law, procedural confidentiality, public-administration principles, and international AI governance frameworks. The layer order is deliberate: skipping a layer generates a specific, predictable mode of failure, and "the house collapses entirely if the foundation is unstable".
requirements: All four layers must be taught in order; the article states each layer fulfills a function and skipping any generates a specific, predictable mode of failure.
constraints: The method was designed to operate on free-tier versions of commercial AI platforms, without corporate licensing or proprietary infrastructure.
target_learners: Public servants in government control and administrative units, with or without legal training
target_learning_goals: Safe, methodical, legally compliant use of generative AI for official document production, including prompt construction and data-protection compliance
examples: The method was materialized as a 20-hour, five-class official EGOV-DF course, 'Artificial Intelligence in the public sector: techniques, risks, and applications', with classes mapped to the four layers.
key_sources: Vinicius Santana Gomes. (2026). The Main Barrier to AI Adoption in the Public Sector Is Lack of Training: How a Structured Method Accompanied Productivity Gains in Two Brazilian Government Cases. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01517

article_title: AI Assistance for Discretionary Work: Increasing Feedback Provision in Higher Education
citation: Mahinpei, R., Dean, V., Fong, R., Liu, L. T., & Ribeiro, M. H. (2026). AI Assistance for Discretionary Work: Increasing Feedback Provision in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03095
title: AI drafts as editable scaffolds that lower initiation barriers for discretionary work
description: The article proposes that AI-assisted drafts function as "editable scaffolds" for discretionary work: they provide personalized starting points that help workers begin a task they intend to do but often skip, rather than reducing the total effort of producing the output. Interviews show TAs use drafts to articulate implicit judgments, verify interpretations, and refine tone, treating them as "intermediate artifacts" rather than final outputs. The framework distinguishes increasing participation (whether work happens) from improving efficiency (how well required work is done).
requirements: The human must retain full control to use, edit, or ignore the draft at their discretion
constraints: Preserving human oversight may constrain how much total effort AI can remove, as the article notes drafts did not reduce measured time per unit of feedback
target_learning_goals: increasing provision of personalized feedback to students
supporting TA articulation and verification of feedback
examples: In the field experiment, TAs described drafts as helping them "get started with a template and then fine-tune it as we go on" and as an "attention check" catching errors they missed
key_sources: Mahinpei, R., Dean, V., Fong, R., Liu, L. T., & Ribeiro, M. H. (2026). AI Assistance for Discretionary Work: Increasing Feedback Provision in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03095

article_title: AI-Driven Assessment of Human Tutors: Linking Training Performance to Real-Life Practice
citation: Thomas, D. R., Kamikazi, M. C. A., Brandt, C., Borchers, C., & Koedinger, K. R. (2026). AI-Driven Assessment of Human Tutors: Linking Training Performance to Real-Life Practice. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18617
title: AI-driven tutor training and real-life assessment system linking scenario-based lessons to transcript-based evaluation
description: The article introduces a pipeline that trains tutors on research-supported "tutor moves" via immersive scenario-based lessons, then uses generative AI (Gemini-2.5-pro) to evaluate real-life application in tutoring transcriptions. A two-stage prompting strategy first uses "an 'opportunity prompt' identified relevant moments where a tutor move was applicable (0/1)" and then "an 'evaluation prompt' scored the quality of the tutor action" (0-ineffective, 1-effective). The system maps three validity types to stages: content validity via expert judgment, predictive validity via training-to-transcript correlation, and construct validity via AI scoring accuracy. If proficiency is not met, a remediation loop of self-reflection or lesson retake is triggered.
requirements: LLM prompts derived from expert-validated human scoring rubrics, with documented inter-rater reliability procedures
Transcripts of authentic tutoring sessions (audio processed via Whisper and merged with chat logs)
constraints: The article states LLM prompts require continuous auditing given the wide range of IRR scores
Manual session uploads may introduce selection bias where more confident tutors submitted more data
target_learners: undergraduate volunteer and paraprofessional math tutors tutoring middle school students remotely
target_learning_goals: pedagogical tutor moves such as praising, reacting to errors, determining what students know, affirming correct attempts, guiding thinking, and prompting explanation
examples: 86 undergraduate tutors completed six scenario-based lessons within a three-phase interrupted time series design, with audio transcriptions and Zoom chat logs collected in the resumed tutoring phase
key_sources: Thomas, D. R., Kamikazi, M. C. A., Brandt, C., Borchers, C., & Koedinger, K. R. (2026). AI-Driven Assessment of Human Tutors: Linking Training Performance to Real-Life Practice. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18617

article_title: What Changes When the Interlocutor Is an AI? Interactional Fluency and Linguistic Uptake in L2 Spoken Dialogue
citation: Russell Scheinberg, Ameeta Agrawal, Tetyana Sydorenko, Kalab Kahsay, Nina Vyatkina, Griet Boone. (2026). What Changes When the Interlocutor Is an AI? Interactional Fluency and Linguistic Uptake in L2 Spoken Dialogue. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22225
title: Complementary-affordances account: AI dialogue as supported monologue versus human dialogue as interactional-competence practice
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that AI and human dialogue "create distinct but complementary conditions for L2 practice." AI dialogue "structurally approximates supported monologue": sustained output with fewer, longer turns, slower responses, less floor competition, and more fluent within-turn production, shifting learners "from reactive turn management to more deliberate, content-focused production." Human dialogue instead exercises interactional competence through rapid turn exchange, floor competition, and negotiation sequences. The framework predicts AI's pedagogical contribution is specifically structural (syntactic priming), while human partners scaffold turn competition, clarification requests, repair, and collaborative floor management.
requirements: An AI interlocutor configuration whose verbose, syntactically regular input creates favorable conditions for short-term structural alignment
constraints: The AI condition reflects one system configuration (model, voice, prompt, VAD setting, and task interface) with university German learners performing one task type
Uptake measures cannot fully separate priming from parallel activation driven by shared task context
target_learners: second- and third-year university L2 German learners
examples: The spot-the-difference study showed human dialogue rapid and interactive versus AI dialogue with fewer, longer turns and more within-turn fluency
key_sources: Russell Scheinberg, Ameeta Agrawal, Tetyana Sydorenko, Kalab Kahsay, Nina Vyatkina, Griet Boone. (2026). What Changes When the Interlocutor Is an AI? Interactional Fluency and Linguistic Uptake in L2 Spoken Dialogue. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22225

article_title: 'A bit of chaos and madness: The AI Assessment Scale and the work of assessment reform'
citation: Perkins, M., Postma, D., Roe, J., Sisay, S., & Holdcroft, C. (2026). 'A bit of chaos and madness': The AI Assessment Scale and the work of assessment reform. Preprint.
title: The AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) as a structured framework for embedding GenAI into assessment design
description: The AIAS is a scale-based framework providing structured guidance for embedding generative AI into assessment design across the dimensions of integrity, equity, and pedagogy. It assigns levels that specify permitted GenAI use, functioning in practice as "a shared language" through which faculty, students, and institutions negotiate expectations. This study examines its enactment at two universities, showing its value depends on implementation conditions rather than framework choice alone.
requirements: Requires interpretation by staff and students, who must negotiate limits, declarations, and appropriate levels of use
constraints: Can degrade into a compliance layer when disconnected from learning outcomes, disciplinary context, and staff capacity
Levels can be read as permissions attached to unchanged tasks rather than specifications of task type and evidence
target_learners: higher education academic staff implementing GenAI assessment guidance
university students using GenAI in assessed work
target_learning_goals: assessment design aligned with learning outcomes
examples: A private international university in Vietnam adopted the first AIAS version institution-wide; a UK public university adopted the revised version in one school
key_sources: Perkins, M., Postma, D., Roe, J., Sisay, S., & Holdcroft, C. (2026). 'A bit of chaos and madness': The AI Assessment Scale and the work of assessment reform. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26729

article_title: Mapping the Emerging Curriculum for AI-Assisted Software Engineering via Syllabus Analysis
citation: Francis Geng, Anshul Shah, Mia Chen, Paul Denny, Juho Leinonen, Bill Griswold, Gerald Soosai Raj, and Leo Porter. (2026). Mapping the Emerging Curriculum for AI-Assisted Software Engineering via Syllabus Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05898v1
title: AI-assisted software engineering as an emerging curricular design space layering AI-mediated practices on software engineering foundations
description: The article frames AI-assisted software engineering education as a design space rather than a standardized curriculum. It argues that emerging courses "build on familiar software engineering education foundations" — project work, programming, debugging, design and deployment — with newer AI-mediated practices such as prompting, agentic development, AI evaluation, and managing context layered on top. The documented variation across courses in tools, topics, and assessment structures supports treating this as an evolving curricular area without a settled model.
requirements: Courses must explicitly frame generative AI as part of software engineering practice, with graded coursework requiring GenAI use for software engineering tasks, as in the analyzed dataset.
constraints: The article states findings should not be generalized to courses where AI use is optional, peripheral, or documented only as a policy issue.
examples: The 23 analyzed courses combined foundational AI/ML concepts, AI-assisted development practices, and selected software engineering lifecycle topics in differing configurations.
key_sources: Francis Geng, Anshul Shah, Mia Chen, Paul Denny, Juho Leinonen, Bill Griswold, Gerald Soosai Raj, and Leo Porter. (2026). Mapping the Emerging Curriculum for AI-Assisted Software Engineering via Syllabus Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05898

article_title: Mapping the Emerging Curriculum for AI-Assisted Software Engineering via Syllabus Analysis
citation: Francis Geng, Anshul Shah, Mia Chen, Paul Denny, Juho Leinonen, Bill Griswold, Gerald Soosai Raj, and Leo Porter. (2026). Mapping the Emerging Curriculum for AI-Assisted Software Engineering via Syllabus Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05898v1
title: Dataset of 23 publicly available U.S. AI-assisted software engineering course syllabi and materials
description: The study's dataset comprises 23 publicly available syllabi and course materials from U.S.-based, credit-bearing, upper-division university courses offered between Fall 2023 and Fall 2026. Courses were identified through structured Google searches and screened for three content criteria: explicit GenAI framing, software engineering lifecycle coverage across at least two SDLC domains, and required GenAI use in graded software engineering tasks. The dataset yielded 32 institutionally eligible candidates, of which 23 met all content criteria.
requirements: Public availability of course materials; courses must satisfy the three content criteria including required GenAI use for graded software engineering tasks.
constraints: Courses behind login systems, with unpublished materials, non-indexed pages, or different terminology may be missing from the dataset.
examples: Included courses range from AI-Assisted Software Development (Kalamazoo College, Fall 2023) to Applied Agentic Software Engineering (University of Michigan, Fall 2026).
