article_title: AI-Guided Learning: Research on Knowledge and Skill Acquisition Support Methods Using Deep Learning Audio-Video Processing Techniques
citation: Kazuki Kawamura. (2025). AI-Guided Learning: Research on Knowledge and Skill Acquisition Support Methods Using Deep Learning Audio-Video Processing Techniques. Doctoral dissertation, The University of Tokyo. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08990
title: AI-Guided Learning: integrated support for the Consume-Understand-Imitate cycle
description: The dissertation proposes AI-Guided Learning, an integrated approach in which deep learning systems provide adaptive support at each of three interrelated stages of learning from audio and video: Consume (efficient content consumption), Understand (deep comprehension), and Imitate (skill acquisition). The author states the framework "provides necessary support at each stage as learners progress through three interconnected phases" and stresses that AI functions as a guide that reduces cognitive load while maintaining learner autonomy, rather than automating tasks wholesale. Three subsystems (AIxSpeed, FastPerson, Profy) instantiate the stages.
requirements: Deep learning models capable of extracting features from audio, video, and text streams for each stage
Coordination among subsystems so learners can move cyclically between stages
constraints: The author notes the CUI model is an organizing framework proposed in the dissertation rather than an empirically established sequence
Current limitations include the need for long-term effect validation and extension beyond audio-visual domains
target_learners: Self-directed online learners of long-form audio and video content
target_learning_goals: Efficient consumption of long-form audio-visual content
Skill acquisition through imitation of expert models
key_sources: Kazuki Kawamura. (2025). AI-Guided Learning: Research on Knowledge and Skill Acquisition Support Methods Using Deep Learning Audio-Video Processing Techniques. Doctoral dissertation, The University of Tokyo. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08990

article_title: AI-Guided Learning: Research on Knowledge and Skill Acquisition Support Methods Using Deep Learning Audio-Video Processing Techniques
citation: Kazuki Kawamura. (2025). AI-Guided Learning: Research on Knowledge and Skill Acquisition Support Methods Using Deep Learning Audio-Video Processing Techniques. Doctoral dissertation, The University of Tokyo. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08990
title: Design AI learning support around adaptivity, integration, and transparency
description: The dissertation states that AI-Guided Learning rests on three design principles: "Adaptivity: Dynamic adjustment according to learners' individual needs, comprehension speed, and skill levels"; "Integration: Seamless coordination and mutual support between Consume-Understand-Imitate stages"; and "Transparency: Presentation of AI's judgments and recommendations in a form learners can understand". The principles position AI as a guide that reduces cognitive load at each stage while maintaining learner autonomy, in line with augmentation-rather-than-replacement perspectives.
requirements: AI subsystems capable of per-stage adaptation and of explaining their judgments to learners
constraints: Many current educational technologies are point solutions focused on a single stage and lack integrated support across the whole learning process
target_learners: Self-directed learners using AI-supported audio-visual learning systems
target_learning_goals: Efficient knowledge acquisition and skill development from audio-visual content
examples: The three subsystems instantiate the principles: AIxSpeed adapts speed to estimated listening difficulty, FastPerson integrates multimodal summarization, and Profy visualizes model-derived feedback
key_sources: Kazuki Kawamura. (2025). AI-Guided Learning: Research on Knowledge and Skill Acquisition Support Methods Using Deep Learning Audio-Video Processing Techniques. Doctoral dissertation, The University of Tokyo. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08990

article_title: Large Scale AI Grading of Handwritten Physics Assessments: Score Agreement and Olympiad Team Selection Outcomes
citation: Praveen Pathak, Siddharth Tiwary, Charudatt Kadolkar, Vijay Singh, David Rakestraw, Shirish Pathare, and Anwesh Mazumdar. (2026). Large-scale AI grading of handwritten physics assessments: Score agreement and Olympiad team selection outcomes. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20521
title: Use AI grading of handwritten physics assessments as a second reader or audit tool under examiner control, not as the grader of record
description: The article's central design recommendation is that multimodal AI can support high-stakes physics grading but should not replace examiners. Because "The main difficulty remained exact partial-credit grading, especially in experimental work," the authors conclude AI "should be used as a second reader or audit tool under examiner control." In this role AI can flag submissions with large differences from official scores, provide additional comments, and help examiners check grading consistency, while expert examiners remain central to final marks.
requirements: Detailed, physics-specific marking rubrics specifying award conditions, common deductions, alternative valid solutions, and carried-forward-error rules
constraints: Exact partial-credit grading, especially in experimental work, remained the main difficulty
Some high-confidence AI parts still differed from official scores by more than one point
target_learners: Olympiad candidates and university physics students whose handwritten examinations are graded
target_learning_goals: Accurate, reliable scoring of handwritten physics examinations including partial credit
examples: In both rounds the AI top five for OE2 contained the same five students as the human top five, and RII matched 34 of 40 QM course grades exactly

article_title: AI-Assisted Assessment of Experimental Physics Laboratory Reports: Potential, Limitations, and Support for Teaching Practice
citation: Marcos Abreu, Cecilia Stari, Arturo C. Martí. (2026). AI-Assisted Assessment of Experimental Physics Laboratory Reports: Potential, Limitations, and Support for Teaching Practice. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22417
title: Treat AI-generated scores as input for guiding review, not as grades interchangeable with teacher grades
description: The article recommends incorporating AI as a support tool that organizes and focuses review while professional teacher judgment guides interpretation and final assessment decisions. It reports that "AI-generated scores are not interchangeable with teacher grades" even when the model uses the same rubric criteria, so system output "should be considered an input for guiding the review rather than a definitive grade." The instructor confirms, modifies, or rejects the model's observations, retaining responsibility for assessment decisions.
requirements: Teachers must verify evidence, contextualize observations, and determine whether AI observations are appropriate for assessment and feedback.
constraints: AI feedback reliability varies by evidence type: descriptive criteria are more useful for initial review, while criteria requiring interpretation of equations, graphs, units, or uncertainties need careful teacher verification.
target_learners: higher education instructors assessing laboratory reports
target_learning_goals: reliable assessment and feedback on student laboratory work
examples: AI produces a first structured reading identifying possible strengths and difficulties organized by rubric criteria, which the instructor then confirms, modifies, or rejects.
key_sources: Marcos Abreu, Cecilia Stari, Arturo C. Martí. (2026). AI-Assisted Assessment of Experimental Physics Laboratory Reports: Potential, Limitations, and Support for Teaching Practice. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22417

article_title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
citation: Amin Jalali. (2026). AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06207
title: AI-decision checkpoints framework: one explicit AI-adoption decision point per BPM lifecycle phase
description: The framework uses the BPM lifecycle to structure explicit, phase-related decisions about AI adoption across identification, discovery, analysis, redesign, implementation, and monitoring. At each checkpoint students "identify AI-candidate subprocesses, establishing the baseline, evaluating expected benefits and risks using the analytical instruments of the corresponding lifecycle phase, and documenting a reasoned decision to adopt, adapt, postpone, or reject specific AI components". It decomposes AI adoption from a monolithic yes/no judgment into locally grounded assessments producing a traceable decision trail.
requirements: Each checkpoint aligns with one of the six BPM lifecycle phases and uses that phase's analytical instruments
constraints: The framework does not prescribe a correct answer at any checkpoint; it foregrounds reasoning quality
individual checkpoints can be weighted or combined without disrupting the logic
target_learners: Master-level Business Information Systems or Computer Science students
target_learning_goals: reasoning about AI as a first-class design element of end-to-end processes
justifying AI adoption decisions with phase-appropriate evidence
examples: In the Master-level course, CP1 yielded an AI opportunity register, CP3 a baseline performance report, CP4 a comparative redesign-and-simulation dossier, CP5 an implementation feasibility and governance dossier, and CP6 a mining-based evaluation summary
key_sources: Amin Jalali. (2026). AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06207

article_title: Artificial intelligence in mathematics education: A PRISMA-based systematic literature review (2021-2025)
citation: Omirzakova, F. N., & Tileubay, S. (2026). Artificial intelligence in mathematics education: A PRISMA-based systematic literature review (2021-2025). European Journal of STEM Education, 11(1), Article 43. https://doi.org/10.20897/ejsteme/19221
title: AI integration as a tensioned system in which educational value emerges only when pedagogical goals, ethical safeguards, and contextual constraints are addressed together
description: The review's integrative analytical perspective conceptualises AI in mathematics education not as separate domains of innovation and risk but as "a tensioned system in which educational value emerges only when pedagogical goals, ethical safeguards, and contextual constraints are addressed together". This framework explains why technologically advanced solutions may yield uneven or counterproductive results without instructional and institutional adaptation, and it underpins the review's caution that technical performance alone is insufficient evidence of instructional effectiveness.
requirements: Pedagogical goals, ethical safeguards, and contextual constraints must be addressed together for educational value to emerge
constraints: The framework is a review-level interpretation, not a directly tested model; the review avoids causal wording unless supported by direct evidence
target_learners: mathematics learners at school and higher education levels
target_learning_goals: effective and ethically responsible implementation of AI in mathematics education

article_title: Artificial Intelligence in Science and Chemistry Education: A Systematic Review
citation: Ali Kürşat Erümit, Rabia Özdemir Sarıalioğlu. (2025). Artificial intelligence in science and chemistry education: a systematic review. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-025-00622-3
title: Five-theme taxonomy of learning outcomes of AI applications in science and chemistry education
description: The review organizes the effects of AI applications in science and chemistry education into five themes: prompt engineering, learning, vocational skills development, active participation, and technology. The learning theme alone covers "contributing to the online learning process", "facilitating learning", "providing a multimodal (auditory) learning environment for the science laboratory class", "providing an interdisciplinary learning experience", and "promoting personalized learning". Each theme aggregates outcomes coded from the 18 included studies, with frequencies of 6, 9, 5, 2, and 3 respectively.
requirements: Content analysis coding of included studies by trained coders reaching consensus, as the review describes its four-coder coding system.
constraints: The taxonomy reflects the 18 studies included under the review's eligibility criteria (primary research, journal articles, English, 2014–2024, effectiveness-measuring).
target_learning_goals: characterizing effects of AI applications on science learning outcomes
examples: Table 6 lists codes per theme, e.g., under learning: contributing to online learning (A2), facilitating learning (A2, A11), successful construction of knowledge (A3).

article_title: An AI-supported E-mentoring model to develop EFL pre-service teachers' self-efficacy and emotional intelligence
citation: Ismael I, Luo X and Li S (2026). An AI-supported E-mentoring model to develop EFL pre-service teachers' self-efficacy and emotional intelligence. Front. Psychol. 17:1853510. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1853510
title: AI-supported e-mentoring model integrating human mentoring with AI-driven support across engagement, analysis, feedback, and reflection cycles
description: The article proposes a dynamic, iterative e-mentoring system in which pre-service teachers generate inputs through learning activities, teaching practice, and reflective interaction; an AI system analyzes these inputs to provide personalized feedback, while human mentors offer contextual guidance and socio-emotional support. The authors state it is 'a dynamic, iterative system integrating human mentoring with AI-driven support to enhance both pedagogical and emotional development'. AI is positioned as augmenting, not replacing, the human mentor.
requirements: Human mentors must provide contextual guidance, professional judgment, and socio-emotional support alongside AI-driven feedback
constraints: AI does not replace the human mentor but augments the mentoring process, per the article's own framing

title: Use AI to augment rather than replace human mentors, dividing feedback by level (AI for task and process, mentors for self-regulation and self)
description: The article recommends integrating AI within mentoring so that each source handles the feedback levels it serves best. Per the article, 'AI-generated feedback mainly addresses the task and process levels through immediate, strategy-specific suggestions, while human mentor feedback works more at the self-regulation and self-levels'. This division follows Hattie and Timperley's feedback model and is intended to enhance the quality, consistency, and scalability of support.

article_title: AI Teaching Innovation Behavior Among College Teachers: A Structural Equation Modeling Analysis Based on the AI-TPACK Framework, Teaching Self-Efficacy, Professional Identity, and AI Literacy
citation: Bai X and Hsieh T-S (2026) AI teaching innovation behavior among college teachers: a structural equation modeling analysis based on the AI-TPACK framework, teaching self-efficacy, professional identity, and AI literacy. Front. Psychol. 17:1834827. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1834827
title: AI-TPACK framework: seven interconnected knowledge domains for AI-supported teaching
description: The AI-TPACK framework extends TPACK to GenAI contexts by conceptualizing AI-related competence as "seven interconnected knowledge domains": CK and PK as disciplinary and pedagogical foundations, AI-TK for knowledge of AI principles and applications, PCK, AI-TCK for AI use within disciplinary contexts, AI-TPK for aligning AI tools with instructional strategies, and integrative AI-TPACK. The article uses it as the core analytical framework, retaining the seven dimensions separately because different domains may contribute differently to innovative practice. It emphasizes evaluating AI-generated content, understanding algorithmic logic, and coordinating human–AI collaboration.
requirements: Teachers must be able to integrate AI with pedagogy and subject content, not merely operate AI tools, for the framework's integrative capacity to be exercised
constraints: The article notes the framework could theoretically be modeled as a higher-order construct but retains seven separate dimensions, and that structural coherence among some TPACK dimensions showed very small, occasionally negative correlations warranting caution
target_learners: college teachers in GenAI-supported higher education contexts
target_learning_goals: teachers' capacity to integrate AI into pedagogy and subject content for innovative instruction
examples: The study measured the seven dimensions with Ning et al.'s 42-item scale and tested each dimension's association with AI teaching innovation behavior separately

citation: Li Y (2026) Beyond output metrics: reframing AI-assisted vocal pedagogy through human learning and educational value. Front. Psychol. 17:1844841. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844841
title: Position AI as human-centered support for interpretation and dialogue, not as an autonomous evaluator of singing quality
description: The article's central design recommendation is that AI in vocal pedagogy "should support human evaluative judgment, pedagogical dialogue, reflective uptake, and learners' capacity for self-regulation rather than function as an autonomous evaluator of singing quality." Teachers mediate AI feedback by explaining it, filtering irrelevant indicators, contextualizing genre and task demands, and helping learners decide whether a measured pattern should be corrected, explored, or temporarily accepted as part of development.

examples: The article concludes that AI should be positioned as a human-centered support for interpretation, reflection, teacher–student dialogue, and pedagogically responsible decision-making

citation: Habeeb Yusuf, Arthur Money, Damon Daylamani-Zad. (2026). title: AIvaluate: an emotionally intelligent LLM-augmented pedagogical AI conversational agent for oral performance-based assessments
description: AIvaluate is a disembodied chatbot deployed in a browser for oral performance-based assessments, with three functionalities: a conversational interface for student–teacher dialogue, student emotional state self-reporting, and LLM augmentation that uses emotional state data to generate suggested replies for the educator. article_title: It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction
citation: Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Küchemann, David J. Rakestraw, & Patrik Vogt. (2026). It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction.
title: AIRIS: a three-phase framework for cognitively activated AI augmentation in physics instruction
description: AIRIS (Activate – Inquire – Reflect with Intelligent Support) is a three-phase instructional framework that structures student activities before, during, and after AI use in science education. It is not tied to a specific tool and focuses on when and how AI enters the learning process. The authors state: "We propose a simple but powerful three- phase instructional framework for AI -augmented science education that structures student activities before, during, and after AI use". It draws on self-regulated learning, cognitive load, multiple representations, and hybrid intelligence research.
requirements: Requires prior direct instruction establishing the conceptual knowledge students need for meaningful Phase 1 predictions
Requires teachers able to design tasks that resist AI completion and evaluate AI outputs in their domain
constraints: Presented as a design proposal grounded in established learning science principles, not as an empirically validated intervention
Designed for inquiry-based instruction and problem-solving settings; does not replace direct instruction
target_learning_goals: epistemic practices of physics: predicting, evaluating evidence, coordinating representations
examples: The Shard elevator ride task, in which students sketch predicted a-t, v-t, and s-t diagrams before AI use, delegate data visualization and integration to AI, then interpret and reflect on the outputs
key_sources: Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Küchemann, David J. Rakestraw, & Patrik Vogt. (2026). It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13812

article_title: It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction
citation: Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Küchemann, David J. Rakestraw, & Patrik Vogt. (2026). It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction.
title: Three-phase lesson pattern: epistemic grounding before AI, guided delegation during, epistemic responsibility after
description: A reusable lesson-level pattern in which each AI-integrated task passes through three phases. Before AI use, students activate prior knowledge and establish expectations that serve as a reference point; during AI use, computational tasks are delegated while epistemic judgment stays with students; after AI use, learning is consolidated through interpretation and reflection on what the AI contributed. The authors note it "shares the three-phase structure of established inquiry cycles such as 5E1" and is "an AI -specific adaptation of existing inquiry cycles, not a replacement for them".
requirements: Phase 1 tasks must require genuine prior-knowledge activation rather than surface recall
Phase 3 must make the human-AI division of cognitive work explicit, e.g. via a written reflection
constraints: Applies to any phenomenon that can be measured, modelled, and interpreted, such as smartphone recordings of a bouncing ball, rolling cylinder, or pendulum
target_learners: introductory physics students in inquiry-based labs
examples: In the elevator task, Phase 1 asks students to sketch expected diagrams and justify expectations; Phase 2 asks them to compare AI-generated diagrams with their sketches; Phase 3 includes a 150–200 word written reflection on what the AI and the student each contributed

citation: Alvaro Becerra, Diego Gomez, Ruth Cobos. (2026). AISSA: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-based Student Slides Analysis tool for Academic Presentations. LASI Spain 26: Learning Analytics Summer Institute Spain 2026. https://orcid.org/0009-0003-7793-2682
title: Structured LLM feedback pattern: rubric-driven prompt with strict JSON output producing overall and item-by-item feedback in three pedagogical paragraphs
description: AISSA's AI Module dynamically builds a restrictive prompt using an adapted version of the GePeTo framework, combining evaluation instructions, scoring rules, rubric criteria, and presentation metadata. The prompt's functional blocks are a System Role framing the model as an expert university evaluator, Calculation Rules, Input Data, an Expected Output JSON Schema, and Strict Output Constraints enforcing valid JSON only. The returned feedback is bilingual (Spanish and English) and organized into a general assessment of three paragraphs — strengths, areas for improvement, and concrete actions — "following well-established pedagogical feedback structures", plus criterion-level explanations for each rubric item.
requirements: A teacher-defined rubric specifying the meaning of each level of the 1–5 Likert scale, extracted slide features as input data, and a backend able to parse the predefined JSON structure
constraints: The pattern was implemented with ChatGPT 5.2 via the OpenAI API; the article plans but has not yet performed comparisons with other proprietary and open-source LLMs
target_learners: higher education students preparing oral presentations

examples: The prompt constrains the model to return a predefined JSON structure containing 1–5 Likert scores per rubric item and bilingual qualitative feedback

article_title: Modeling AI-TPACK in Practice: Insights from Teachers'' Multi-Agent Workflow Design
citation: Sun, Y., Xin, H., Li, S., Niu, Q., Chai, C. S., Huang, L., & Chen, G. (2025). Modeling AI-TPACK in Practice: Insights from Teachers' Multi-Agent Workflow Design. https://cocorobo.cc
title: AI-TPACK framework operationalized as four AI-specific knowledge dimensions for analyzing generative-AI-era teacher design
description: The AI-TPACK framework extends traditional TPACK for AI integration. The article operationalizes it, "as specified for the generative AI context by Ning et al. (2024)", as an a priori coding scheme with four dimensions: "AI-Technological Knowledge (AI-TK), AI-Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (AI-TPK), AI-Technological Content Knowledge (AI-TCK), and the overarching AI-TPACK (Integration)". The framework addresses the gap that traditional TPACK inadequately addresses architectural thinking for coordinating agent logic, because AI agents' generative and conversational nature differs from prior educational technologies. The study used it to code both design artifacts and interview transcripts.
requirements: Requires coding schemes and analyses that capture AI-specific dimensions beyond operational tool proficiency, including prompt engineering and AI affordance understanding
constraints: The article notes traditional TPACK inadequately addresses multi-agent architectural thinking, so the framework is specific to AI integration contexts
target_learning_goals: Integrating AI technologies, pedagogy, and content knowledge when designing AI-powered instructional tools
examples: The researchers used the four dimensions as the a priori coding scheme for thematic analysis of 15 workflow artifacts and 12 interviews, achieving Cohen's kappa=0.81 on artifact coding

article_title: AI-Driven Analytics of Team-Teaching Talk: Acoustic Patterns across Experience, Cohorts and the Learning Design
citation: Yuchen Liu, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Riordan Alfredo, Paola Mejia-Domenzain, Dwi Rahayu, and Sadia Nawaz. (2026). AI-Driven Analytics of Team-Teaching Talk: Acoustic Patterns across Experience, Cohorts and the Learning Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09831
title: AI-based speech processing pipeline for multi-teacher classroom audio
description: An automated pipeline for analysing team-teaching talk: multi-channel headset recordings are processed with a weighted fusion of spectral masking and ECAPA-TDNN speaker-embedding-based masking to reduce cross-channel interference, transcribed with WhisperX, and used to extract 88 acoustic features with openSMILE from fixed 1-second segments. Quality was verified via word error rate: "The WER decreased from158%before cross-talk mitigation to21%after processing, which is considered acceptable". Standardised features were reduced by Varimax-rotated PCA into five rotated components explaining 58% of cumulative variance.
requirements: Wireless headset microphones per instructor for audio capture; cross-talk mitigation before transcription; z-score normalisation of features before dimensionality reduction
constraints: In two of the 36 sessions a microphone placement issue rendered one instructor's audio unusable, so analyses included 34 sessions with complete recordings
target_learning_goals: scalable automated analysis of how team teaching is enacted in classroom talk
examples: Applied to 36 recorded undergraduate and postgraduate database-course sessions at Monash University, yielding five rotated components used for group comparisons

article_title: AiAWE: An Open-Source LLM Automated Writing Evaluation System Using LoRA-Adapted Instruction-Tuned Models
citation: John Maurice Gayed. (2026). AiAWE: An Open-Source LLM Automated Writing Evaluation System Using LoRA-Adapted Instruction-Tuned Models. A PREPRINT. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12801
title: AiAWE open-source automated writing evaluation platform
description: AiAWE is a Django web application, publicly accessible at https://app.awade.gec.waseda.ac.jp, that serves students and educators with "real-time essay scoring, rubric-referenced qualitative feedback, batch processing, and custom-rubric configuration." It runs llama.cpp inference of a Q4_K_M-quantised LoRA-adapted Gemma-3-27B model on a single RTX 3090, with average inference latency below two seconds per essay. Educator-facing features include batch user creation via Excel upload, batch essay processing (batches of over 1,000 essays in a single run), admin-defined custom rubric configurations with temperature settings, and token-based authentication with per-model daily request quotas. An experimental AWADE mode runs the base Gemma model without a LoRA adapter against instructor-defined rubrics for formative feedback.

constraints: The experimental AWADE custom-rubric mode "is not evaluated against any benchmark" and is presented only as a demonstration of extensibility
The article specifies bartowski GGUF files for replication, since quantisation provenance affects quality
target_learners: Adult L2 English learners preparing for TOEFL Independent Writing
University students in argumentative writing courses
examples: In production the platform has served thousands of scored essays, including individual submissions and batches of several hundred essays, without service degradation

article_title: AI Literacy for Legal Translation: Developing Digital Resilience
citation: Łucja Biel. (2026). AI Literacy for Legal Translation: Developing Digital Resilience. University of Warsaw. https://uw.edu.pl
title: AI-related risk profile of legal translation: five interrelated risk categories
description: The chapter proposes an analytical framework mapping how AI creates professional risk in legal translation. As printed: "I propose an AI-related risk profile of legal translation comprising five interrelated categories according to the aspect of professional practice they affect: linguistic, technical, legal, ethical and cognitive". Linguistic risks cover terminology, mistranslations and genre conventions; technical risks cover hallucinations and unpredictable performance; legal risks cover data protection, confidentiality, copyright and liability; ethical risks cover algorithmic bias, transparency and access to justice; cognitive risks cover illusions of quality, automation bias, cognitive surrender and deskilling. The framework grounds the argument that legal accountability requires human-centred augmentation.
requirements: Applied for analytical purposes to legal translation's high-risk setting, where translation errors may have severe consequences
constraints: The chapter notes many risks were first identified for NMT but apply equally, and in several respects more acutely, to GenAI
target_learning_goals: risk awareness in AI-assisted legal translation
examples: Figure 1 presents the five risk categories and their manifestations, from terminology and hallucinations to automation bias and deskilling
key_sources: Łucja Biel. (2026). AI Literacy for Legal Translation: Developing Digital Resilience. University of Warsaw. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04641

article_title: AI Literacy for Legal Translation: Developing Digital Resilience
citation: Łucja Biel. (2026). AI Literacy for Legal Translation: Developing Digital Resilience. University of Warsaw. https://uw.edu.pl
title: AI Literacy Framework for legal translation: four mutually reinforcing dimensions
description: The chapter's central framework adapts general AI literacy models (Ng et al. 2021; Long and Magerko 2020; Krüger 2024) to legal translation. It defines AI literacy for legal translators as the capacity to make informed, critical and ethically responsible decisions about the use and supervision of AI while preserving translation quality, legal certainty and professional accountability. As printed: "AI literacy is conceptualised here as a multidimensional construct comprising four mutually reinforcing dimensions: Foundational, Procedural, Critical and Strategic". Foundational covers understanding AI systems and data literacy; Procedural covers workflow integration and prompt engineering; Critical covers human oversight, verification and automation-bias awareness; Strategic covers professional judgement about whether, when and how AI should be used. The framework is presented as a transversal layer of legal translation competence supporting digital resilience.
requirements: Builds on existing legal translation competence models (strategic, thematic, linguistic/textual, instrumental, professional) rather than replacing them
constraints: The chapter states the framework "requires empirical validation" and that future research should evaluate the effectiveness of pedagogical interventions
examples: Figure 2 presents the AI Literacy Pyramid for Legal Translation and Table 1 maps each dimension to its function and knowledge/skills

article_title: Methodologies for Improving the Quality of AI Tutoring in K-12 Education
citation: Udeshi, T., Khazenzon, A., Khan, K., Breen, N., Corwin, R., DiGiano, C., Weatherholtz, K., Zaluski, M. (2026). Methodologies for Improving the Quality of AI Tutoring in K-12 Education. https://sites.google.com/khanacademy.org/aied2026supplementalmaterial/home
title: Theory of action linking AI tutor quality to engagement, skill acquisition, and transfer
description: The article grounds its measurement choices in an explicit causal chain: tutor quality drives cognitively engaged interaction, engagement predicts skill acquisition, and skill acquisition should generalize to standardized assessment performance. Metrics are chosen to span this chain, from proximal engagement measures to distal transfer. The cognitive engagement metric is "grounded in the ICAP framework (Chi and Wylie, 2014), which distinguishes four levels of cognitive engagement—Passive, Active, Constructive, and Interactive—predicting deeper learning as engagement deepens."
requirements: Metrics must be sensitive to change, moving after 1-2 weeks of experimentation as leading indicators of effective tutoring
constraints: The chain is stated as a motivating theory; the article measures proximal engagement and near transfer rather than standardized-assessment outcomes directly
target_learners: K-12 students using Khanmigo on Khan Academy
target_learning_goals: Skill acquisition in exercised skills, measured as near transfer to independently attempted next items
examples: Next-item correctness is described as capturing near transfer on a new item measuring the same underlying skill, counting only items attempted independently without further tutor help

article_title: AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency
citation: Kuhn, J., Gerjets, P., Trautwein, U., Greene, J. A., Malone, S., Vogt, P., & Fütterer, T. (2026). AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency in Hybrid Human-AI Cognition. https://osf.io/preprints
title: AIRIS: a multi-level control allocation architecture for preserving epistemic agency in hybrid human-AI cognition
description: AIRIS (AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems) is a theoretical framework, not a cognitive architecture like ACT-R, specifying what must remain in place for genAI-supported work to sustain understanding. It rests on three core principles: "human epistemic primacy", "complementary generative engagement", and "event-driven intervention". The article states that "AIRIS is a multi-level control allocation architecture specifying the conditions under which epistemic agency can be preserved in hybrid generative systems," and that "The architecture does not itself improve learning; it specifies what must remain in place for genAI -supported work to sustain understanding." It integrates distributed cognition, cognitive load theory, multimedia learning, and self-regulated learning.
requirements: Regulatory support must be enactable by a teacher, the learner's own internalized regulation, or a future technical implementation; the framework specifies functional regulatory requirements rather than a fixed instructional sequence.
constraints: The article states the architecture does not itself improve learning; it specifies conditions for sustaining understanding.
target_learners: learners using generative AI in educational and knowledge-work contexts
target_learning_goals: preserving epistemic agency and durable understanding during genAI-supported epistemic work
examples: The framework is presented as an episodic control-allocation layer that activates when destabilizing patterns emerge, with a Detect–Diagnose–Act cycle linking behavioral traces to targeted interventions.
key_sources: Kuhn, J., Gerjets, P., Trautwein, U., Greene, J. A., Malone, S., Vogt, P., & Fütterer, T. (2026). AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency in Hybrid Human-AI Cognition. https://osf.io/preprints

article_title: AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency
citation: Kuhn, J., Gerjets, P., Trautwein, U., Greene, J. A., Malone, S., Vogt, P., & Fütterer, T. (2026). AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency in Hybrid Human-AI Cognition. https://osf.io/preprints
title: Seven destabilizing mechanisms of hybrid cognition, from control redistribution to motivational-affective drift
description: AIRIS's diagnostic layer comprises seven mechanisms: control redistribution, germane effort attenuation, calibration drift, delegation drift, representational passivity, dual-threshold instability, and motivational-affective drift. The article frames them as hypotheses: "the following seven mechanisms specify those disturbances as theoretically derived, empirically testable hypotheses, not as established facts, nor as a claim that disturbance is inevitable." The mechanisms "are not independent failure modes but form a self -reinforcing system," interacting so that, for example, delegation drift feeds motivational-affective drift and deepens calibration drift.
requirements: Each mechanism is grounded in existing theoretical frameworks (distributed cognition, CLT/CTML, SRL) and requires empirical testing through the derived propositions.
constraints: The article states the mechanisms describe conditions of potential destabilization, not inevitable outcomes; direct experimental tests of the dual-threshold prediction remain scarce.
target_learners: learners and designers of genAI-integrated learning environments
target_learning_goals: diagnosing where hybrid human-AI cognition loses epistemic equilibrium
examples: Darvishi et al. (2024) is cited for behavioral evidence that students with genAI feedback access showed measurable reductions in independent evaluative reasoning that deepened across repeated interactions.
key_sources: Kuhn, J., Gerjets, P., Trautwein, U., Greene, J. A., Malone, S., Vogt, P., & Fütterer, T. (2026). AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency in Hybrid Human-AI Cognition. https://osf.io/preprints

article_title: AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency
citation: Kuhn, J., Gerjets, P., Trautwein, U., Greene, J. A., Malone, S., Vogt, P., & Fütterer, T. (2026). AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency in Hybrid Human-AI Cognition. https://osf.io/preprints
title: Five regulatory operators (Anticipate, Interrogate, Reflect, Integrate, Synthesize) activated by event-driven triggers
description: AIRIS's regulatory layer specifies five operators that target internal generative engagement at points of emerging instability. The article states: "AIRIS employs five complementary regulatory operators: Anticipate , Interrogate, Reflect, Integrate, and Synthesize." Operators are episodic, triggered by event-driven mechanisms rather than running continuously, and may be enacted as system prompts, instructor interventions, or internalized self-regulation strategies. Three trigger classes are distinguished from interaction traces: calibration discrepancy, delegation dominance, and reflection compression triggers.
requirements: Trigger operationalization requires disentangling genAI-assisted from independent performance, e.g., via brief probe tasks requiring independent knowledge construction without genAI access.
constraints: AIRIS-triggered regulation should be understood as a scaffold, not a substitute, for the learner's own regulatory awareness; the long-term goal is internalization of regulatory competencies.
target_learners: learners in genAI-integrated learning environments, instructors, and system designers
target_learning_goals: restoring equilibrium between human generative engagement and genAI-supported processes
examples: Calibration discrepancy triggers activate when confidence levels diverge strongly from performance outcomes; delegation dominance triggers activate when users consistently consult genAI before articulating their own ideas.
key_sources: Kuhn, J., Gerjets, P., Trautwein, U., Greene, J. A., Malone, S., Vogt, P., & Fütterer, T. (2026). AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency in Hybrid Human-AI Cognition. https://osf.io/preprints

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Sustainable Development: An Ethical Governance and Development Goals Framework
citation: Md. Masudul Islam, Mirza Niaz Morshed, Md. Shafiqul Islam. (2025). Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Sustainable Development: An Ethical Governance and Development Goals Framework. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7643-5420
title: AIRE Taxonomy: a six-level progression from AI awareness to governance foresight
description: The Artificial Intelligence Reasoning and Ethics (AIRE) Taxonomy is a six-tier model extending Bloom's hierarchy with ethical and governance tiers: Recognize, Comprehend, Apply, Analyze, Integrate, and Govern. The article states that "the study introduces a six-tier framework the AIRE Taxonomy that extends Bloom’s hierarchy (Kastberg, 2003) to encompass ethical synthesis and governance foresight." Each tier specifies a learning outcome, a governance competency, and a measurable indicator, and the taxonomy functions as both a pedagogical framework and a policy evaluation instrument across micro, meso, and macro levels.
requirements: Each tier specifies a learning outcome, a governance competency, and a measurable indicator, enabling evaluation across learner, institutional, and policy levels
constraints: In most academic contexts, particularly within undergraduate programs of two to three years, it is not feasible to achieve the full spectrum of competencies outlined in the higher tiers of the taxonomy; the framework should be interpreted as a multi-stage developmental model rather than a linear curriculum
target_learners: learners, educators, policymakers, and institutions engaged in AI education and governance
target_learning_goals: AI literacy progressing from foundational recognition to ethical reasoning and governance capability
examples: Table 1 pairs each AIRE level with illustrative indicators, e.g. percentage of institutions offering AI awareness modules for Level 1 and presence of national AI literacy benchmarks for Level 6
key_sources: Md. Masudul Islam, Mirza Niaz Morshed, Md. Shafiqul Islam. (2025). Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Sustainable Development: An Ethical Governance and Development Goals Framework. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7643-5420

citation: Md. Masudul Islam, Mirza Niaz Morshed, Md. Shafiqul Islam. (2025). Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Sustainable Development: An Ethical Governance and Development Goals Framework. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7643-5420
title: AI–SDG Nexus Framework positioning AI literacy as a meta-competency for all 17 SDGs
description: The AI–SDG Nexus Framework is a governance-oriented conceptual model that maps AI literacy competencies and governance levers onto all 17 Sustainable Development Goals. The article describes it as "a governance -oriented conceptual model that positions AI literacy as a meta -competency underpinning all 17 Sustainable Development Goals." It organizes the goals into People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, and Partnership clusters with AI literacy at the centre, and identifies five analytical dimensions: competency, ethical, governance, innovation, and measurement.
requirements: Mapping of each competency to SDG targets through relevance analysis, policy linkage, and indicator-based validation
constraints: The SDG linkage classification is a conceptual synthesis of literature on AI applications rather than a literature-count-based classification, since direct studies linking AI literacy to SDGs remain limited

target_learning_goals: ethical and sustainable AI decision-making supporting sustainable development goals

article_title: AI literacy over tool design: a mixed-methods study of scaffolded versus unrestricted generative AI in programming education
citation: Azimi, S. (2026). AI Literacy over Tool Design: A Mixed-Methods Study of Scaffolded versus Unrestricted Generative AI in Programming Education. Delft University of Technology.
title: AI Study Coach: a notebook-embedded scaffolded AI tutor with two modes and four session constraints
description: The AI Study Coach is an AI tool built into Jupyter-notebook laboratory sessions so students can consult it without leaving the task. It operates in two modes: Explainer mode, in which it "explained analytic outputs and the design choices behind the code", and Debugger mode, which gives stepwise hints from general to specific without generating code. Four constraints apply each session: a 25-hint budget, a fifteen-minute AI-use limit, an end-of-session written reflection, and tagging of AI-sourced code. Together these constituted the scaffold under study.
requirements: Integration into the notebook environment so consultation happens within the laboratory task
Teaching-team visibility of tagged AI-sourced code for the scaffold to be monitorable
constraints: The article's results say nothing about scaffolds in general, only that this particular scaffold did not produce the assumed learning advantage
target_learners: master's-level students in a data analytics and machine learning course with varied prior programming experience
target_learning_goals: data analysis and machine learning practice: understanding analytic outputs, debugging code, and responsible AI use
examples: In the pilot, Coach students used Explainer and Debugger modes under the four constraints, logged every interaction, and completed end-of-session reflections
key_sources: Azimi, S. (2026). AI Literacy over Tool Design: A Mixed-Methods Study of Scaffolded versus Unrestricted Generative AI in Programming Education. Delft University of Technology. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16784

article_title: AIfred: Augmented Learning through Functional Robotic Embodiment at the Desk
citation: Gregorio Orlando, Milan Groshev, Eduardo Castelló Ferrer. (2026). AIfred: Augmented Learning through Functional Robotic Embodiment at the Desk. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38737
title: AIfred: desk-based robotic arm with end-effector projector delivering spatially co-located generative AI assistance
description: AIfred is a prototype combining a robotic arm with a mini projector at its end-effector, an OptiTrack motion-capture system tracking a desk object, and an overhead camera. It operates through a three-stage spatial assistance pipeline: workspace perception (MediaPipe gesture detection triggering a screenshot), context-aware content generation (Gemini models interpreting the scene under the active interaction mode), and robot-mediated projection onto the indicated desk location. Three interaction modes were programmed: math homework (scaffolding hints rather than answer replacement), generate image, and draw. All code and materials are publicly available in the article's stated repository.
requirements: Requires workspace perception hardware: an overhead camera, a motion-capture system tracking the robot base and a trackable desk object, and an inverse kinematics solver to orient the projector
constraints: The OptiTrack motion-capture tracking limits deployment outside controlled lab settings, per the authors' limitations section
The current design prioritizes functional projection over expressive robot behavior
target_learners: university-campus adult participants across humanistic, social-science, business, and engineering backgrounds
target_learning_goals: math problem solving on quadratic equations
examples: In the user study, participants completed math assignments, image-generation from sketches, and drawing tasks with AIfred or laptop ChatGPT, including a crossover third drawing task

article_title: Ensuring Academic Integrity through Automated Online Exam Proctoring: A Decade-Long Systematic Review
citation: Malhotra, M., & Chhabra, I. (2026). Ensuring academic integrity through automated online exam proctoring a decade long systematic review. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-01224-3
title: AIPS four-feature integrity taxonomy: authentication, browsing tolerance, remote authorization and control, and report generation
description: The review describes Artificial Intelligence Proctoring Systems as ensuring system integrity through four main features: authentication (e.g., camera-based face verification so only registered students log in), browsing tolerance (restricting computer and internet use during tests), remote authorization and control (letting examiners initiate, stop, resume tests and investigate suspicious activity during live proctoring), and report generation (compiling summaries of student actions from exam recordings). This taxonomy organizes the review's classification of proctoring system functions.
requirements: Front and rear cameras and microphones already present on students' devices, which the review says these systems use to monitor actions
constraints: The review notes these surveillance measures may be perceived as violating privacy, requiring measures that assure users of safety and privacy
target_learners: higher education students in online examinations
target_learning_goals: maintaining academic integrity during online assessment
examples: The review states "AIPS ensures system integrity by looking at four main features: (1) authentication, (2) browsing tolerance, (3) remote authorization and control, and (4) generating reports."

citation: Benali Taouis, H., & Díaz García, A. (2026). Teaching with Generative Artificial Intelligence: Enhancing Critical Thinking and Ethical Awareness in Academic Writing. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice. https://doi.org/10.53761/28y4hw95
title: Have students use AI to rephrase, question, edit, or elaborate on key course concepts rather than as a shortcut, to reinforce understanding and promote deeper learning
description: The principle directs students to engage actively with course material through AI interactions instead of using AI to bypass the work. The article states: "By interacting with AI to rephrase, question, edit, or elaborate on key concepts, students become more conscious of the content, reinforcing understanding and promoting deeper learning." It is grounded in the article's aim of improving retention of course content by using AI "as a means to actively reflect, process, and engage with the material explained in class."
requirements: Course content must be explained in class so students have material to reflect on and process with AI
target_learners: higher education students in academic and professional communication courses
examples: Students used AI to rephrase, question, edit, or elaborate on key concepts from the class material

article_title: How generative AI guided-professional development supports teachers’ engagement with mathematical creativity, content knowledge, and pedagogical content knowledge
citation: Ali Bicer, Tugce Aldemir, Unggi Lee, Jewoong Moon, Karen Rambo Hernandez, Miriam Sanders. (2026). How generative AI guided-professional development supports teachers' engagement with mathematical creativity, content knowledge, and pedagogical content knowledge. ZDM–Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01816-1
title: Generative AI as a cognitive and instructional partner in teacher professional learning
description: The study conceptualizes generative AI not as a content-delivery tool but as "a cognitive and instructional partner" that supports teacher learning through contingent prompting, feedback, rehearsal, and guided reflection. Guided by Rhodes' 4P framework (person, process, press, product) and constructivist and socio-constructivist perspectives, the AI responds to teachers' ideas, prompts explanation and revision, simulates student reasoning, and scaffolds reasoning within teachers' zone of proximal development. Teachers experienced the system as a "knowledgeable partner" rather than a static content provider.
requirements: Interaction organized around clear pedagogical goals, discipline-specific tasks, and repeated cycles of explanation, feedback, and revision
Teachers retain interpretive authority and the system's role remains transparent and bounded
constraints: Open-ended AI coaching may produce generic feedback or overextend beyond teachers' professional judgment
target_learners: in-service K-6 mathematics teachers in rural and under-resourced districts
examples: The chatbot used GPT-4 via the OpenAI API, configured through module-specific system prompts, few-shot examples, and conditional prompt templates with guardrails against direct solution-giving

ZDM–Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01816-1
title: Ten-module AI-guided asynchronous PD program on proportional reasoning with eight designed AI-mediated mechanisms
description: The AI-guided PD comprised ten asynchronous modules completed across one academic semester, typically requiring 30-45 hours, each centered on rate and proportional reasoning. Eight intentionally designed AI-mediated mechanisms structured engagement: adaptive prompting, real-time feedback, progressive scaffold fading, simulated student reasoning, supportive nonjudgmental tone, flexible pacing, representational nudges, and cycles of creative challenge and reflection. Teachers solved tasks, generated multiple strategies, posed problems, interpreted simulated student thinking, and reflected on instruction.
requirements: Module-specific system prompts, few-shot examples, and conditional prompt templates constraining the AI to the intended mathematical and pedagogical focus
constraints: Designed for contexts with limited access to sustained, content-specific professional development
examples: When teachers provided correct solutions the AI asked for mathematical justification; when only one strategy was used it requested another representation or approach

article_title: A Capability–Decision Model of teacher readiness for AI integration in teaching
citation: Mnguni L (2026) A Capability–Decision Model of teacher readiness for AI integration in teaching. Front. Educ. 11:1897632. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1897632
title: Treat AI readiness as pedagogical capability rather than tool familiarity, and evaluate whether targeted mediators moved
description: From the capability-to-belief bridge (H6, H7) and mediated pathways (H10, H11), the article recommends that teacher-education programmes "treat AI readiness as pedagogical capability rather than tool familiarity, prioritising integrated AI-TPACK development through lesson-design tasks, prompt-evaluation activities, content-validity judgements, and artefact-based reflection." Programme evaluation should measure whether the targeted mediators (PBC and attitude) moved before intention, not only whether participants report greater willingness, because technological knowledge may align with perceived benefits while integrated competence lags.
requirements: Programme evaluation must measure whether the targeted mediators moved, not only stated willingness
constraints: Technological knowledge may align strongly with perceived AI benefits while pedagogical and content knowledge show weaker associations, producing confidence without integrated competence
examples: The article links this principle to the performance-based tasks operationalised in its Section 4.3.3

article_title: Students' experiences of using ChatGPT for English language learning: a qualitative study in a Malaysian higher education institution
citation: Annamalai N, Nasor M, Din Eak A and Ayoub Alkubaisy AA (2026) Students’ experiences of using ChatGPT for English language learning: a qualitative study in a Malaysian higher education institution. Front. Psychol. 17:1875727. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1875727
title: AI-mediated motivational ecology: an extension of Self-Determination Theory in which basic psychological needs are partly met through AI interaction
description: The article extends SDT, which conceptualizes autonomy, competence, and relatedness as human-centered constructs grounded in interpersonal and instructional contexts, by proposing that learner needs can be "partly met through AI interaction rather than solely through instructor and peersupport". In this account, ChatGPT's personalized feedback and conversational responsiveness reshape how autonomy, competence, and relatedness are negotiated in human–AI interactions, e.g. relatedness experienced as perceived communicative support rather than human connection. The study uses this lens to interpret Malaysian EFL undergraduates' experiences of ChatGPT-mediated English learning.
requirements: Learners actively engage with AI feedback and make informed decisions about their learning strategies for agency and self-regulation to be encouraged
constraints: Whether AI interaction fully satisfies the psychological need for relatedness remains debatable because authentic relatedness traditionally involves human interactions
target_learners: undergraduate EFL students with limited English proficiency (MUET Bands 2–3)
target_learning_goals: English language competence in grammar, writing, speaking, and vocabulary; learner motivation and self-directed learning
examples: The study interviewed 25 Malaysian undergraduates who used ChatGPT 3.5 or 4.0 voluntarily for course-related English activities over a 5-month semester, coding themes deductively against autonomy, competence, and relatedness

title: Large-scale field study dataset and code release for AI-generated exam evaluation

examples: In rare cases (less than 2%) of multiple submissions, responses were superscored by retaining the highest score per question

article_title: AICoFe: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-Based Collaborative Feedback System for Higher Education
citation: Alvaro Becerra, Alejandra Palma and Ruth Cobos. (2026). AICoFe: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-Based Collaborative Feedback System for Higher Education. LASI Spain 26: Learning Analytics Summer Institute Spain 2026. https://orcid.org/0009-0003-7793-2682
title: AICoFe: an AI-based collaborative feedback system for peer, self-, and teacher assessment in higher education
description: AICoFe is a human-centered AI system that supports peer and self-evaluation in educational settings using customized rubrics integrating quantitative scores and qualitative observations. It is "organised into four main modules": a Visualization Module with role-specific dashboards, a Management Module for data storage, a Feedback Generation Module orchestrating multi-LLM feedback production, and a Recording Module capturing student performances in video and audio. Video recordings of presentations support reflective learning and more thorough evaluation.

constraints: Participation in video recording is strictly opt-in via informed consent, and all audiovisual data are stored in compliance with GDPR

examples: Deployed at Universidad Autónoma de Madrid with approximately 80 students and 5 teachers across one undergraduate course and one master's course

title: Role-specific Learning Analytics dashboards for evaluators, students, teachers, and administrators
description: AICoFe's Visualization Module provides interactive Learning Analytics dashboards developed with the Dash framework, each tailored to the user's role. The Evaluator Dashboard supports Likert scoring with qualitative comments and captures interaction metadata such as timing of score selections to explore evaluation dynamics and detect potential biases. The Student Dashboard supports self-assessment against the same rubric and visualises differences between self-assessment and aggregated evaluations. The Teacher Dashboard supports feedback review and curation, and an Admin Dashboard handles configuration.

constraints: The Admin Dashboard is not visible to students or teachers during normal operation

examples: Students receive AI-supported collaborative feedback composed by the teacher and answer an embedded questionnaire on agreement and perceived usefulness of the feedback

citation: Alvaro Becerra, Alejandra Palma and Ruth Cobos. (2026). AICoFe: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-Based Collaborative Feedback System for Higher Education. LASI Spain 26: Learning Analytics Summer Institute Spain 2026. https://orcid.org/0009-0003-7793-2682
title: Hybrid SQL and MongoDB data infrastructure for traceability of feedback versions
description: AICoFe's Management Module integrates two complementary database technologies: a relational SQL database managing structured academic data such as courses, rubric definitions, user accounts, and evaluators' scores and comments; and a MongoDB document store for semi-structured data that varies in shape across evaluation instances, including multiple LLM feedback versions, teacher drafts and curations, per-sentence metadata with source LLM, and coherence/usefulness ratings. A File Service manages audiovisual recordings linked to evaluation instances.
requirements: The flexible document model is suited to a multi-LLM pipeline where each evaluation instance may generate a variable number of feedback versions with different internal structures

article_title: The Effortless Trap: Productive Struggle, AI, and the Illusion of Learning
citation: Mario Brcic, Stjepan Frljic. (2026). The Effortless Trap: Productive Struggle, AI, and the Illusion of Learning. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26181
title: Place AI by cognitive role: secure the first hard attempt and final unaided check, allow guarded AI in between
description: The article's central design rule is per skill, not per course: "AI belongs wherever it increases feedback, practice density, or professional realism without obscuring the evidence that the student can think and perform unaided." Concretely, teachers protect Probe and Test as AI-out moments, permit guarded AI (hints, examples, feedback, drill) in the middle moves, and open AI for authentic work once unaided competence is shown. The diagnostic is that if letting AI in makes the task feel effortless, it is in the wrong place.
requirements: A secured, AI-free check that shows the student can perform unaided; guarded rather than answer-giving AI during scaffolded moves
constraints: The rule is per skill, not per course; the same student may need AI kept out of one skill and welcomed into another in the same hour
target_learners: All students in AI-supported courses, from high school through higher education
target_learning_goals: Protecting productive struggle and unaided skill demonstration while scaling feedback and practice
examples: Mapped onto the six moves, the access pattern is protected attempt, guarded support, protected proof; the survivorship-bias lesson keeps AI out only at Probe and Test

article_title: ChatGPT as a Virtual Laboratory Teaching Assistant in Undergraduate Biology
citation: M. Said Doğru & Emily K. Faulconer. (2026). ChatGPT as a Virtual Laboratory Teaching Assistant in Undergraduate Biology. Research in Science Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11165-025-10271-z
title: Integrate AI laboratory support with human instructor guidance and a safety net against incorrect information
description: The article recommends that ChatGPT serve as a resource that lifts the burden of answering basic questions from TAs and instructors, while humans remain in the loop. Because "students must understand the error rate provided by the system, and a safety net must be in place to ensure students do not proceed with incorrect information," AI support should be balanced with the guidance of human instructors. Educators should develop a pedagogical approach providing learners strategies for fact-checking AI output.

constraints: The article states replacing human teachers with genAI technology is difficult at this stage of the technology's development.

citation: Yao Lyu, Leonymae Aumentado, Holden Winton, Jared Lee Katzman, Sparkle Berry, Zachary Rowe, Kimberly Sanders, and Tawanna R. Dillahunt. 2026. Co-Designing Community-Centered AI Education for Adults: A Midwestern Case Study. CSCW Companion '26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3785651.3831486
title: AI literacy as community capacity rather than individual technical competency
description: The article proposes reconceiving AI literacy through the lens of community capacity, defined by prior work it cites as "the collection and interplay among human, organizational, and social resources that enable a community to recognize and address problems". From its analysis, AI literacy was "less about mastering tools or technical mechanisms, but more about developing the capacity to recognize AI in everyday contexts, critically interpret its outputs, articulate concerns and expectations, and make informed decisions". The theory resists generic, top-down framings and holds that community members themselves should hold the power to define what AI means in their lives.

Evaluation methods that capture critical awareness, sense-making, and decision-making rather than technical mastery alone

target_learners: Adults outside formal educational systems in local communities
target_learning_goals: Critically interpreting AI outputs and articulating concerns and expectations
examples: The session surfaced tensions between utility and risk rather than framing AI as inherently beneficial or harmful, aligning with scholarship critiquing techno-solutionist narratives

citation: Alexei Kaltchenko and Gurnivaj Tiwana. (2026). ChatGPT Solves All Tested Qiskit Homework Assignments. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19707

description: Three complete take-home homework packages for an undergraduate quantum software course: HW1 (seeded basis-state circuits with bit flips and customized measurement mappings), HW2 (QFT followed by inverse-transform recovery with circuit metrics and an optional hardware extension), and HW3 (seeded Deutsch–Jozsa with customized oracle masks). Each used a deterministic student identifier so an instructor-side reference could regenerate the configuration, and layers included exact JSON submissions, hidden deterministic references, circuit metrics, reflections, and optional IBM Quantum execution.

article_title: A Scoping Review of AI for Sustainability and Sustainable AI in Higher Education
citation: Ben Kei Daniel, Nataliya Podgorodnichenko and Sarah Carr. (2026). A scoping review of AI for sustainability and sustainable AI in higher education. Discover Computing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10791-025-09861-2
title: Dual framework: AI for Sustainability versus Sustainable AI as the two dominant thematic orientations
description: The review organizes the literature into two complementary but distinct dimensions. AI for Sustainability uses AI technologies to advance environmental, social, and economic goals, while Sustainable AI focuses on reducing the environmental and social impacts of AI itself, including energy-efficient models, fairness, and transparency across the AI lifecycle. The review presents this as the field's dominant thematic orientation, summarized across definitions, objectives, applications, stakeholders, and ethical considerations.

constraints: The review notes the relationship between AI and Sustainability remains fragmented and inconsistently defined in the literature.

responsible AI adoption in higher education

citation: Davor I, Larbi E and Boateng FO (2026). Artificial intelligence-supported learning and higher-order cognitive outcomes: the mediating role of metacognitive self-regulation. Front. Educ. 11:1855869. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1855869

description: The article proposes a mechanism-based framework distinguishing three AI interaction dimensions: AI task scaffolding (supportive), AI verification literacy (evaluative), and cognitive offloading tendency (dependency-related), grounded in Self-Regulated Learning and Cognitive Load Theory. It shifts attention "from AI adoption to AI interaction mechanisms" and positions metacognitive self-regulation — planning, monitoring, and evaluating cognitive processes — as "the key pathway linking AI-supported learning to higher-order cognitive outcomes." The framework explains both beneficial and detrimental pathways of AI use.

Findings reflect AI-using university students in Ghana, not all students in Ghanaian higher education

citation: Patiño Hernández JF, Chiappe A and Ortega González E (2026). From digital competence to AI-responsive pedagogy: a scoping review of technology-supported teacher education. Front. Educ. 11:1949296. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1949296
title: AI-responsive pedagogy: maintaining pedagogical agency when deciding whether, when and how AI participates in teaching
description: AI-responsive pedagogy is the review's interpretive construct linking teacher digital competence with pedagogical enactment of AI. It denotes "the professional capacity to decide whether, when and how AI should participate in teaching and teacher learning, and to select, interrogate, adapt or constrain AI outputs in relation to pedagogical purposes, disciplinary knowledge, evidence of learning, ethical commitments and contextual conditions". The construct builds on UNESCO's AI Competency Framework for Teachers and extensions of TPACK to AI-related professional knowledge, and is explicitly not a synonym for AI adoption or tool proficiency. Its specific conditions are derived from patterns across the reviewed studies rather than imposed as a normative framework.

constraints: Responsiveness does not mean adapting education to technological change; the review derives its conditions from reviewed study patterns rather than a predetermined normative framework

article_title: Coach not crutch: Evidence that AI can improve writing skill despite reducing effort
citation: Benjamin Lira, Todd Rogers, Daniel G. Goldstein, Lyle Ungar, and Angela L. Duckworth. (2025). Coach not crutch: Evidence that AI can improve writing skill despite reducing effort. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02880
title: Effort versus learning-environment framework: AI can reduce effort while improving the learning environment, with skill depending on the net effect
description: This framework holds that a practice tool affects skill acquisition through two opposing channels: the effort learners expend and the quality of the learning environment. As the article's Figure 1 caption states, "Relying on AI may cause people to exert less effort but improve the learning environment," and "Post-practice writing skill depends on the net effect of effort and the quality of the learning environment." The article uses this framework to explain why AI practice, despite reducing effort, produced larger skill gains: AI supplies high-quality, just-in-time, personalized examples illustrating otherwise abstract writing principles, consistent with literature on learning by observation.
requirements: A learning tool must improve the quality of examples or feedback available to the learner, not merely reduce effort, for net skill gains to occur
constraints: The article notes it is not clear whether the benefits of AI examples would generalize to other domains like math or computer programming, where a single example may reveal less of the producing process
In the experimental paradigm, participants interacted with AI only once; long-term effects of repeated use remain an open question the authors flag
target_learners: adult learners practicing professional writing skills
examples: In Study 4, participants who only viewed an AI-generated example improved as much as those who practiced with the AI tool, supporting the examples mechanism

description: CyberAGENTS integrates the AISecKG cybersecurity ontology, which "defines valid entity types (e.g., tool, technique, attack, vulnerability, defense, system) and permissible relations among them (e.g., exploits, detects, counters, uses, can harm)." Outputs from the Challenge, Buddy, and Critic agents are checked against entity categories, relation patterns, and unsafe-content rules before learner exposure. The article reports that "Content that violates semantic constraints or safety thresholds is flagged and re-prompted under stricter conditions before presentation."

A re-prompting mechanism under stricter conditions when validation fails

citation: Luis P. Prieto, Yannis Dimitriadis. (2026). An emancipatory vision for designing (generative) AI for learner flourishing. International Workshop on Critical and More-than-human Perspectives on AI in Education (at EC-TEL 2026). https://luispprieto.com/
title: Emancipatory vision of AIED oriented to learner flourishing within nested complex systems
description: The paper proposes an alternative vision in which educational AI is designed to foster long-term learning, agency, and flourishing rather than performance alone. It holds that technology deployment is the beginning of appropriation, that systems should intervene only while necessary, that multiple values in tension should be elicited and navigated, and that education is a communal process of socialization into group knowledge and values. The article argues learners using such technologies will be more attuned to evidence-based notions of human flourishing, and expects flourishing learners to lead to more flourishing societies and environment.

citation: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263
title: AI Expert Feedback Ecology: a closed-loop cognition framework linking AI Twins, AI Tutors, dashboards, and learners
description: The article defines the AI Expert Feedback Ecology as "a closed-loop educational ecosystem in which AI Twins, AI tutors, dashboards, and learners continuously interact through cognition-aware feedback processes." AI Twins generate adaptive tasks; AI Tutors interpret behaviours into cognition reports; the ECD aggregates them; AI Twins reason through aggregated structures to generate interventions that start a new cycle. Cognition is treated as "an evolving interpretive structure continuously shaped through interaction, reflection, and intervention."

constraints: AI Twins perceive learners indirectly through cognition reports rather than raw behavioural logs

article_title: Mathematical Modelling of Ethical AI Use in Higher Education: A Coordination Game Framework for Future-Facing Learning
citation: Ndidi Bianca Ogbo, Zhao Song, Shatha Ghareeb, and The Anh Han. (2026). Mathematical Modelling of Ethical AI Use in Higher Education: A Coordination Game Framework for Future-Facing Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27400
title: Coordination-based evolutionary game-theoretic framework of student AI use in assessment
description: The framework models student generative-AI use in assessment as a two-player symmetric coordination game in a well-mixed finite population, in which the institution is not a strategic player but shapes payoffs through assessment design. Strategies span responsible use with meaningful reflection, responsible use with superficial reflection, opportunistic use, and clear misuse, with parameters for learning value, effort costs, legitimacy costs, reflection reward and effort, and misconduct penalties. Behavioural change follows the Fermi imitation rule with small mutation probability, and long-run dynamics are approximated by a Markov chain over homogeneous states. The article writes that "we model interactions at the student–student level using a two-player symmetric game in a well-mixed population".
requirements: Reflective assessment incentives must be calibrated so that the reward for meaningful reflection is proportionate to its effort cost
constraints: The model treats each assessment task as a one-shot decision context in a well-mixed population; the article notes extending to multi-player and networked interactions and empirical validation as future work
target_learning_goals: responsible and learning-oriented use of generative AI in assessment
examples: Simulations with population size N = 100 and Fermi updating, varying reflection reward r, peer sensitivity β, and reflection effort cost κ across Figures 1–3

citation: Harry Feng, Yuan Tian, and Erica Zhao. 2026. From Answer Generators to Reasoning Facilitators: Designing AI Tutors for Mathematical Reasoning in High-Stakes Environments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01692
title: AITutor: an LLM-based iPad tutoring app translating pedagogical mechanisms into UI features
description: AITutor is a React Native/Expo iPad app with a Python/FastAPI backend that orchestrates LLM calls, curriculum-constrained prompting, retrieval over digitized course materials, and telemetry logging. Rather than "treating the AI as an open-ended chatbot, we constrained the interaction, translating pedagogical mechanisms into explicit UI features." Its features are layered worked examples (overview, orientation, explanation, final-answer checkpoint, exam-format layer), step-linked visual grounding, a contextual follow-up dock, and a delayed retrieval/wrong-book loop.
