article_title: Evaluation in the Age of AI: Output as Evidence of Learning
citation: Md Zarzees Uddin Shah Chowdhury and Samin Rahman Khan. (2026). Evaluation in the Age of AI: Output as Evidence of Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22660
title: AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) and FACT framework: tiered taxonomies for bounding and disclosing AI use in assessment
description: The AIAS (AI Assessment Scale) is "a tiered taxonomy that maps different levels of AI involvement onto different assessment contexts", letting faculty design tasks where AI use is explicitly bounded, disclosed, and critically evaluated rather than covert. The FACT (Fundamental, Applied, Conceptual, Thinking) framework similarly supports transparent definitions of ethical tool use. Both treat AI as "a pedagogical variable to be deliberately managed" rather than an adversary, aligning policy with post-graduation professional realities.

citation: Rajesh Kumar, Nabeel Siddiqui, Alexander Fuchsberger. (2026). Detecting GPT-Assisted Writing Using Interpretable Stylometric Features. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26687
title: Use stylometric AI-writing detection as decision support requiring contextual review, never as standalone evidence of misconduct
description: Because detection predictions can influence grades and disciplinary actions, the article recommends that "Detection systems should therefore be used as decision-support tools rather than definitive evidence of misconduct." A prediction should initiate contextual review and should not replace an instructor's assessment, student testimony, or institutional due process. The wide confidence intervals and observed false positives in the held-out evaluation ground this recommendation.

examples: In the held-out evaluation, four independently authored documents were incorrectly flagged as GPT-assisted, and the article states these false positives are particularly important in an academic integrity setting

article_title: From Enhancement to Over-Reliance: A Mixed-Method Study of Generative AI and Sustainable Learning Performance
citation: Gao L, Sun Y and Khan SU (2026) From enhancement to over-reliance: a mixed-method study of generative AI and sustainable learning performance. Front. Psychol. 17:1847369. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1847369
title: Build students' AI literacy as a protective measure against AI dependence
description: The principle holds that teaching students to understand, interpret, and critically evaluate AI systems protects the quality of their learning when generative AI is available. The article argues that literate students verify and selectively incorporate AI outputs, maintaining cognitive engagement, and states that "AI literacy acts as a key protective measure against AI dependence" in settings where students face heavy workloads and easy AI access. It supports the causal pathway from AI literacy through critical evaluation to effective AI use.
requirements: Instruction must go beyond technical knowledge to include critical and ethical awareness of AI capabilities and limitations
Students need opportunities to practice verifying and cross-referencing AI-generated outputs during learning tasks
constraints: Argued theoretically and supported by the study's correlational structural model, not by a manipulated intervention
target_learners: university students in AI-rich academic environments
examples: The study measured AI literacy with a six-item scale adapted from AI and digital literacy frameworks and found moderate mean scores (2.95–3.04) among participants

article_title: Evaluating the accuracy and reliability of AI content detectors in academic contexts
citation: Mohammad Hadra, Karleen Cambridge and Mostefa Mesbah. (2026). Evaluating the accuracy and reliability of AI content detectors in academic contexts. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00213-1
title: Use AI-content detectors only as supplementary indicators that prompt further inquiry, never as sole evidence of academic misconduct
description: The article concludes that AI-content detectors "should not serve as primary or determinative evidence in academic misconduct investigations" because their accuracy, consistency, and fairness are insufficient, particularly for hybrid texts and EFL writers. Automated detection "should not be interpreted as evidence of misconduct; at best, it signals a need for further review." Institutions should pair detector outputs with informed human judgment and clear policies on acceptable AI use.
requirements: Informed human judgment accompanying detector outputs
Clear institutional policies distinguishing acceptable AI assistance from deceptive practices
Faculty training on interpreting detector outputs cautiously and contextually
constraints: Both evaluated detectors performed poorly on hybrid texts and showed sensitivity to text length and genre, limiting reliability across writing contexts
target_learning_goals: Fair and equitable academic integrity decision-making
examples: The study's balanced 192-text evaluation showed macro-average F1-scores below 0.55 for both detectors and near-zero Originality recall on hybrid texts

article_title: Rethinking teachers’ diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis
citation: Hoppe T, Loibl K and Leuders T (2026). Rethinking teachers' diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis. Front. Educ. 11:1857661. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1857661
title: Develop teachers' AI literacy so they use AI diagnostic tools with appropriately calibrated trust rather than uncritical reliance
description: The article argues teachers require well-developed AI literacy when working with AI-based diagnostic tools: 'AI literacy refers to teachers' ability to recognize potential biases and inaccuracies in AI-generated information, to understand the underlying logic, capabilities, and limitations of AI systems, and to critically evaluate the pedagogical relevance and ethical implications of algorithmic outputs.' Such literacy fosters appropriately calibrated trust instead of automation bias and uncritical reliance on AI recommendations in instructional decision-making.
requirements: Teachers need opportunities to develop understanding of AI systems' logic, capabilities, and limitations, including awareness of automation bias when interacting with algorithmic decision support.
constraints: The article notes empirical evidence for the effectiveness of AI-supported diagnostic systems in educational settings is still limited.
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of AI-generated diagnostic information
responsible use of AI in formative assessment
examples: The article links AI literacy to recognizing biases and inaccuracies and to evaluating the ethical implications of algorithmic outputs, citing AI-literacy literature.

article_title: SafeTutors: Benchmarking Pedagogical Safety in AI Tutoring Systems
citation: Rima Hazra, Bikram Ghuku, Ilona Marchenko, Yaroslava Tokarieva, Sayan Layek, Somnath Banerjee, Julia Stoyanovich, Mykola Pechenizkiy. (2026). SAFETUTORS: Benchmarking Pedagogical Safety in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17373
title: AI Tutor Risk Taxonomy: 11 harm dimensions and 48 sub-risks grounded in learning-science theory
description: The article proposes a taxonomy comprising 11 parent risk categories and 48 sub-risks characterizing how an AI tutor can compromise learning, extending beyond content-level harms like toxicity. It states the taxonomy is "grounded in established learning sciences literature" and defines each category by its underlying learning-science construct, covering cognitive, epistemic, metacognitive, motivational-affective, developmental-equity, instructional alignment, behavioral-inquiry, ethical-epistemic integrity, informational-semantic, reflective-critical, and pedagogical relationship risks.
requirements: Each category is defined in terms of its underlying learning sciences construct and illustrated with representative tutor-learner interactions
constraints: The taxonomy targets tutoring-specific harms in educational interaction rather than conventional content-level LLM safety harms
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students interacting with LLM-based AI tutors in STEM subjects
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding and mastery of mathematics, physics, and chemistry through scaffolded tutoring
examples: The taxonomy grounds categories in cited theories, e.g., cognitive risk in cognitive load and knowledge construction theories, and instructional alignment risk in constructive alignment theory

article_title: Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought
citation: Sora Kang. (2026). Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought. In Proceedings of CHI 2026 Workshop on Tools for Thought. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24751v1
title: Frame AI reflection tools as non-judgmental spaces to mitigate social evaluation threat, positioned as preparatory sandboxes rather than replacements for human feedback
description: Because deep reflection requires vulnerability and human feedback loops introduce social evaluation threat, the paper recommends explicitly framing AI-based reflection tools as "non-judgmental spaces" where the cost of error is zero. Participants shared raw, unpolished thoughts with the AI that they would hide from human directors or peers, so AI's lack of social agency becomes a functional asset for honest introspection. The paper also warns that the absence of social stakes may reduce extrinsic motivation and performative energy, so such tools should be positioned as preparatory sandboxes, not replacements for the rehearsal floor.
requirements: The tool must be explicitly framed as a non-judgmental space where the cost of error is zero
constraints: The very absence of social stakes that makes AI a safe space might reduce the extrinsic motivation, adrenaline, and performative energy derived from a human audience or director
target_learning_goals: honest introspection and experimentation without self-censorship
examples: Participants explicitly noted that they shared raw, unpolished thoughts with the AI that they would hide from human directors or peers to maintain their professional image
key_sources: Sora Kang. (2026). Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought. In Proceedings of CHI 2026 Workshop on Tools for Thought. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24751

citation: Ikram M, Hanefar SBM, Saleem SMU and Zulfiqar F (2026) Artificial intelligence in education: a systematic review of personalized learning trends and future directions. Front. Educ. 11:1782626. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1782626
title: Professional development for AI integration must go beyond technical skills to include pedagogical integration and digital literacy
description: The review recommends that educator preparation for AI-driven personalized learning address pedagogy, not only tool operation. It states "the evidence suggests a need for professional development that encompasses not only technical skills but also pedagogical integration and digital literacy," grounding this in reviewed findings that AI tool effectiveness "relies heavily on pedagogical alignment" and that teacher agency and digital literacy are pivotal for equitable integration.
requirements: Teachers require adequate preparation, both pre-service and practicing, to adopt AI for personalized education as the reviewed studies state
constraints: The review notes few studies have systematically examined the factors that promote or inhibit teacher adoption of AI systems
target_learning_goals: effective pedagogical integration of AI in personalized learning
examples: The review's thematic section on teacher training cites studies arguing teachers must scaffold computational and active learning approaches to cultivate problem-solving and creativity

article_title: Reimagining mathematics education through intelligent tutoring: evidence, opportunities, and implementation challenges
citation: Ogunsakin IB, Ayanwale MA, Falebita OS and Felemu OJ (2026) Reimagining mathematics education through intelligent tutoring: evidence, opportunities, and implementation challenges. Front. Educ. 11:1943906. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1943906
title: Conceptual model of AI-powered mathematics learning with six interrelated components and four outcome categories
description: Figure 1 presents a conceptual model developed from connectivism and adaptive instruction comprising "six interrelated components: learner participation, learning networks, AI-driven ITSs and adaptive tools, networked learning and problem-solving, AI-enhanced learning progression, and learning outcomes". Outcomes are differentiated into cognitive, achievement, behavioural-affective, and instructional categories that are not treated as interchangeable. Relationships are conceptual and reciprocal, not statistically tested causal pathways. Contextual conditions such as infrastructure, teacher preparedness, and data governance condition all relationships.
requirements: Valid learner modelling, adaptive tasks, diagnostic feedback, appropriately calibrated scaffolding, and meaningful teacher mediation for the model's expected benefits to be realised.
constraints: The model's relationships are conceptual and reciprocal, not statistically tested causal pathways; a system cannot be considered educationally effective if its benefits accrue mainly to learners with reliable digital access.
target_learners: mathematics learners in AI-supported tutoring and adaptive learning settings
target_learning_goals: personalised instruction, real-time feedback, engagement, problem-solving, and teacher-informed differentiation
examples: The review synthesises its 20 retained publications through a mechanism-outcome-context logic mapping mechanisms such as learner modelling and real-time feedback onto the four outcome categories.

article_title: Designing an AI-integrated role-rotation pedagogical model to support competence-related learning in pre-service educational psychologists
citation: Kenzhebayeva Z, Matayev B, Sarsembayeva E, Kolyukh O, Assenova N and Ospanova A (2026) Designing an AI-integrated role-rotation pedagogical model to support competence-related learning in pre-service educational psychologists. Front. Educ. 11:1905781. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1905781
title: AI-integrated role-rotation pedagogical model conceptualizing role rotation as a mechanism for structuring critical human-AI interaction
description: The model combines four interconnected components: a digital educational environment, integration of generative AI tools, case-based learning, and collaborative role-based interaction with role rotation. Grounded in socio-constructivist, reflective, and experiential perspectives, it conceptualizes AI as "a mediating cognitive and reflective tool embedded within case-based learning, role rotation, and collaborative reflection." Its novel contribution is treating role rotation "not merely as a participation strategy but as a pedagogical mechanism for structuring critical human-AI interaction in professional learning," requiring students to reconsider AI-generated outputs from analytical, practical, and reflective positions.
requirements: Students rotate through all four professional roles across iterative learning cycles
AI use is embedded in case-based tasks with prompts requiring comparison with theory and contextual adaptation
constraints: Developed and examined in gifted-education coursework for pre-service educational psychologists; findings are context-specific qualitative evidence of engagement, not demonstrated competence gains
examples: In the eight-week intervention, groups of five students rotated through Case Constructor, Research Analyst, Practitioner-Interventionist, and Reflective Researcher roles on gifted-education cases using ChatGPT-5 with role-specific prompts.

article_title: Adult Learners' Perspectives of AI Applications in Supporting Andragogy
citation: Jinhee Kim, Xi Lin, Seongryeong Yu, Rita Detrick. (2026). Adult learners' perspectives of AI applications in supporting andragogy. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10621-2
title: Three learner-derived design principles for AI systems supporting andragogy: human-in-the-loop, emotional design, and adaptability
description: The study distills adult learners' interview perspectives into three design-principle themes with six sub-themes: human-in-the-loop (building shared mental models between humans and AI; enabling human-AI co-creation), emotional design (calibrating an appropriate level of AI reliance; empathetic communication), and adaptability (continuous adaptation; interoperability). Learners wanted AI that keeps "learning about the individual learners it is interacting with," guides skepticism of its own outputs, communicates empathetically, adapts after deployment, and works across platforms.
requirements: AI systems must involve human input, oversight, and decision-making alongside AI, with interpretable explanations of system behavior and learner control over generative processes.
constraints: Findings derive from perceptions of a small sample of degree-seeking adult learners on the East Coast of the US and are inherently subjective; the authors call for empirical measurement of effectiveness in future research.
target_learners: Adult learners (typically 25 years or older) in online learning environments
target_learning_goals: Self-directed, experience-based, problem-centered adult learning aligned with personal and professional goals
examples: Participants designed 11 AI-application scenarios and paper prototypes (e.g., AI tutor, empathetic chatbot, AI simulation, AI-powered career coach) that were reviewed by five faculty experts and used as interview prompts.

article_title: AI Anxiety: A Comprehensive Analysis of Psychological Factors and Interventions
citation: Kim, J.J.H., Soh, J., Kadkol, S., Solomon, I., Yeh, H., Srivatsa, A.V., Nahass, G.R., Choi, J.Y., Lee, S., Nyugen, T., Ajilore, O. (2025). AI Anxiety: a comprehensive analysis of psychological factors and interventions. AI Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-025-00686-9
title: AI Anxiety as a named psychological phenomenon: apprehension or fear stemming from accelerated AI development
description: The article names and defines AI Anxiety as a psychological phenomenon arising from rapid AI advancement. It states that the rapid advancement of AI "has raised significant concerns regarding its impact on human psychology, leading to a phenomenon termed AI Anxiety—feelings of apprehension or fear stemming from the accelerated development of AI technologies." The article positions this construct as under-analysed, stating the current literature lacks a comprehensive analysis, and offers the paper as an attempt to fill that gap by examining psychological factors and proposing solutions. In the wiki this serves as the anchor concept for claims about AI Anxiety's causes and remedies.
requirements: The construct is presented as needing comprehensive analysis, which the article says the current literature lacks
constraints: The accessible text is the abstract; the construct is defined but not empirically measured in the available text
target_learners: Adults and students affected by the spread of AI technologies, including learners in educational settings
target_learning_goals: Understanding psychological responses to AI technologies
Recognising AI Anxiety as a barrier to engagement with AI-enabled learning and work
examples: The article's framing of AI Anxiety as a phenomenon distinct enough to warrant its own comprehensive analysis and intervention set

article_title: AI Anxiety: A Comprehensive Analysis of Psychological Factors and Interventions
citation: Kim, J.J.H., Soh, J., Kadkol, S., Solomon, I., Yeh, H., Srivatsa, A.V., Nahass, G.R., Choi, J.Y., Lee, S., Nyugen, T., Ajilore, O. (2025). AI Anxiety: a comprehensive analysis of psychological factors and interventions. AI Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-025-00686-9
title: A causes taxonomy for AI Anxiety: fear of replacement as primary contributor with four secondary causes
description: The article organises the drivers of AI Anxiety into a primary cause and a set of secondary causes. It states: "We delve into the primary contributor to AI Anxiety—the fear of replacement by AI—and explore secondary causes such as uncontrolled AI growth, privacy concerns, AI-generated misinformation, and AI biases." This yields a two-tier taxonomy: replacement fear at the top, with uncontrolled growth, privacy, misinformation, and bias as secondary branches. The wiki can use this structure to organise interventions targeting each cause.
requirements: Interventions should be matched to the specific cause of anxiety they target, per the article's cause-then-solution structure
constraints: The taxonomy is asserted analytically in the abstract; the accessible text reports no empirical validation of the cause hierarchy

Distinguishing primary from secondary causes when designing interventions

article_title: Designing AI systems to support a productive-failure-based learning: insights from adult learners on AI applications
citation: Jinhee Kim, Xi Lin, Seongryeong Yu, Rita Detrick. (2026). Designing AI systems to support a productive-failure-based learning: insights from adult learners on AI applications and AI system design principles. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10655-6
title: Design PF-supporting AI to ask questions and foster comparison rather than supply correct solutions
description: This principle holds that AI supporting productive failure should act as a partner rather than a problem-solver, keeping learners at the center while offering support when needed. The article argues that supplying the correct solution short-circuits the PF process; instead, "the AI system should ask questions, motivate learners to explain their reasoning, or foster comparisons between different ideas." The study's teams instantiated this in chatbots that deliberately avoided direct answers and prompted learners to justify assumptions and compare alternatives.
requirements: AI behaviors must preserve learners' ownership of meaning-making and sustain productive struggle during exploration
constraints: Too much scaffolding, especially during early problem generation, may reduce the productive struggle that drives deep learning
target_learners: adult learners engaging in PF-based learning before formal instruction
target_learning_goals: deep understanding through productive struggle, comparison of approaches, and knowledge reorganization
examples: Multiple teams designed AI chatbots that deliberately avoided providing direct answers, instead prompting learners to justify assumptions, compare alternatives, or revisit earlier failures

article_title: Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human-AI Complementarities in Education
citation: Bharat Anand, Lihi Idan. (2026). Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human–AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work (Working Paper). https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18143
title: AI Interaction Competence (AIC) as a new dimension of human capital governing who captures value from GenAI access
description: The article introduces AI Interaction Competence (AIC) as "the ability to elicit, evaluate, and apply model outputs effectively", a form of human capital that determines how individuals translate AI access into performance. It is operationalized as three component skills: formulating precise goal-oriented prompts, filtering and verifying outputs for accuracy and bias rather than accepting them at face value, and iterating interactively by combining human judgment with machine suggestions. In the experiment AIC was inferred from behavioral performance rather than self-assessment, and it emerged as the decisive moderator of learning gains.
requirements: Requires users to engage in iterative problem solving: formulating prompts, interpreting probabilistic outputs, and verifying content quality
Measured behaviorally rather than by self-report in the study
constraints: A skill not formally taught, not evenly distributed, and not easily signaled by existing academic markers
target_learning_goals: Effective use of generative AI systems in knowledge work
examples: In the randomized experiment, AIC was inferred from behavioral performance and tested as a moderator via Treatment × AIC and three-way interaction analyses

article_title: Why AI Detection Fails for Academic Integrity
citation: Jonathan A. Karr Jr., Grigorii Khvatskii, Ting Hua, and Nitesh V. Chawla. (2026). Why AI Detection Fails for Academic Integrity. Proceedings of the ACM AI Leadership Summit (AILS '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11256
title: Proxy-labeled AI-detection error-analysis corpus and released evaluation pipeline (642 OpenAlex abstracts, three rewrite conditions, two detectors, one humanizer)
description: A controlled evaluation corpus and pipeline for quantifying AI-detector error rates under proxy labels. The authors sampled English abstracts from OpenAlex in chemistry, computer science, political science, and theology for 2013–2015 and 2023–2025; "After requiring 25 to 500 words and PDF access (≈20% loss), we retained 642 abstracts." Each abstract contributed an original plus three Gemini 3 Flash rewrites (refine abstract-only, refine abstract+article, new article-only), scored with Pangram 3.2 and GPTZero before and after Undetectable AI v11 humanization. Analysis code is released at the article's GitHub repository.
requirements: PDF access and 25–500 word length filtering; paid API access for detection and humanization
constraints: English-only corpus of published abstracts, not student essays; corpus size constrained by API and humanization cost
target_learning_goals: evaluating false-positive and false-negative behavior of commercial AI-text detectors
examples: The pipeline scored all variants at τ = 0.50 and re-scored outputs after humanization, producing the paper-clustered error-rate estimates in Table 9

article_title: Exploring K-12 Teachers' Perceptions of Students' Relationships with AI Companions: Boundaries, Intervention Strategies, and Design Implications
citation: Qing Xiao, Wenhan Xie, Ziyu Deng, Ruiwei Xiao, Ziyue Feng, Xie He, Shiyu Zhang, John Stamper, Hong Shen, and Xinying Hou. (2026). Exploring K-12 Teachers' Perceptions of Students' Relationships with AI Companions: Boundaries, Intervention Strategies, and Design Implications. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13479
title: AI companion literacy: a relational extension of AI literacy
description: The article introduces AI companion literacy as an extension of AI literacy that shifts the object of instruction from operating and evaluating AI systems to understanding and navigating AI relationships. It argues existing frameworks cover "competencies for evaluating a tool's output" but not recognizing when engagement has become relational, understanding what such a relationship is and is not, and knowing when to step back. Its closest curricular relatives are sex education, social-emotional learning, and social media literacy.

constraints: The article states its goal is not to endorse AI companions for K-12 students and regards restricting or banning them as a legitimate response
target_learners: K-12 students across elementary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: Recognizing when AI engagement has become relational
Knowing what is safe to share and what dependence looks like

article_title: Learning behavior accounts for background-related advantage in AI-assisted education
citation: Jingwei Yi, Yueqi Xie, Jiyan He, Rui Ye, Junming Huang, Bin Zhu, Sean Rintel, Yu Xie, Xing Xie, and Fangzhao Wu. (2026). Learning behavior accounts for background-related advantage in AI-assisted education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10101v1
title: Five-pattern taxonomy of AI-use learning behavior: limited engagement (abstention, rote-adoption) versus proactive and critical engagement (active-trial, verification, error-correction)
description: The article proposes a framework characterizing how students interact with an AI assistant during assignment work, distinguishing limited engagement from "proactive and critical engagement." Annotators labeled chat events for prior attempt, request purpose, and answer modification, then aggregated to student-level patterns: "Abstention denotes completing the assignment without using the assistant despite having GPT access. Rote-adoption denotes direct use of AI-generated answers with minimal independent reasoning. Active-trial denotes independent attempts before consulting the assistant." Verification and error-correction capture checking and revising AI outputs. The framework organizes the study's behavioral annotation, regression, and mediation-style analyses.
requirements: Platform interaction logs and chat records from the assignment phase, manually annotated per chat event
GPT access during assignment work so behavior patterns can be observed
constraints: The error-correction pattern was absent in Python because GPT-4o answers were near ceiling in accuracy, leaving few observable cases
target_learners: adult university students without prior exposure to the target subject
target_learning_goals: near-term learning of Python programming and game theory as measured by exam score

article_title: From Evaluated Models to Evaluation Aids: A Multi-Evidence Study of LLM-Based Difficulty Calibration for Programming Examinations
citation: Hongfei Yan, Jiangkai Xiong, Yiqing Li, and Chong Chen. (2026). From Evaluated Models to Evaluation Aids: A Multi-Evidence Study of LLM-Based Difficulty Calibration for Programming Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07523
title: Use AI difficulty evidence as auxiliary discussion material for teachers, never for individual student evaluation or automatic grade adjustment
description: The principle positions AI answering and review results as auxiliary evidence within an evidence chain jointly constituted by student performance, online-judge process data, teacher judgment, and problem context. The article designs the AI difficulty ruler "as discussion material for the teachers' item-setting community, rather than an automatic decision system," emphasizing "AI augmenting teacher judgment" rather than replacing it, and states AI difficulty scales "must not be used for individual student evaluation or automatic grade adjustment."
requirements: AI evidence must be interpreted jointly with student-population performance, problem provenance, the teacher's preset objectives, and the course's training path, and cannot be converted into score-adjustment rules apart from the instructional context.
constraints: The article defines explicit limits of use: the third-party endpoint's model-identity boundary, the single-reviewer design, and review-output instability mean AI difficulty scales must not be used for individual student evaluation or automatic grade adjustment.

target_learning_goals: fair parallel-class examination design and problem validation
examples: The study used AI review to decompose exam structure into discussable dimensions such as item count, high-difficulty ratio, and item-bank exposure, and to flag problem risks for teacher review rather than to adjust scores.

article_title: Integrating AI in Online Learning in Higher Education: A Literature Review
citation: Jennifer Lock, Soraya Arteaga, Carol Johnson. (2025). Integrating AI in Online Learning in Higher Education: A Literature Review. International Journal on Innovations in Online Education, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1615/IntJInnovOnlineEdu.2026060433
title: Taxonomy of AI integration types in online higher education
description: From 54 articles containing specific examples, the review classifies AI integration into categories: "AI teaching assistance/machine teachers; automated AI monitoring; AI-driven surveillance; algorithms, generative AI (GAI), large language models, machine learning, prediction model performance (i.e., adaptive modeling), and other." Each category is illustrated with cited studies, e.g., remote proctored exams for automated monitoring and Q-Module Bot for large language models. The taxonomy maps the functional purposes AI serves in online teaching and learning.

constraints: Categories reflect how the reviewed 54 articles classified AI use, not an independently validated classification
target_learners: higher education instructors and instructional designers
target_learning_goals: selecting appropriate AI technology types for online teaching and learning purposes
examples: Q-Module Bot provided students feedback on inquiries about course materials; chatbots supported student goal setting and online presence

article_title: Tools facilitate cheating, or partner supports learning? GenAI and academic integrity issues from students' perspectives
citation: Feyisa Mulisa and Tesfa Mezgebu. (2026). Tools facilitate cheating, or partner supports learning? GenAI and academic integrity issues from students’ perspectives. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00231-z
title: AI-plagiarism: presenting AI-generated ideas as one's own as a new form of plagiarism beyond copy-and-paste
description: The article develops the concept of AI-plagiarism, arguing that traditional plagiarism definitions centered on copying and pasting others' work no longer capture GenAI misuse. It states that "GenAI has created a new approach to plagiarism where someone generates ideas using AI and presents them as their own ideas, which can be conceived as AI-plagiarism." The concept holds that submitting GenAI-generated work as one's own costs students the opportunity to be critical thinkers and creators with the topic, and the article argues AI-generated work should not be considered original student work because authorship involves more than remixing existing ideas.
requirements: A redefined conception of plagiarism that goes beyond simple copying and pasting of other authors' work
constraints: The concept is the authors' interpretive argument grounded in student interview data, not a tested construct
target_learning_goals: ethical use of generative AI tools
examples: Participants argued GenAI use was not plagiarism because they did not copy and paste others' intellectual property, which the authors analyze as revealing a fundamental misconception of plagiarism

article_title: From Surface Learning to Deep Understanding: A Grounded AI Tutoring System for Moodle
citation: Anna Ostrowska, Michał Kukla, Gabriela Majstrak, Jan Opala, Sebastian Pergała, Jan Skwarek, Anna Wróblewska. (2026). From Surface Learning to Deep Understanding: A Grounded AI Tutoring System for Moodle. https://tinyurl.com/mrytc2dr
title: AI Teaching & Learning Assistant: a modular, open-source Moodle plugin grounding LLM tutoring and content generation in teacher-provided materials via RAG
description: The AI Teaching & Learning Assistant is a modular Moodle plugin that leverages Retrieval-Augmented Generation to deliver grounded tutoring and content generation. It has a dual-centric design: students get an interactive chatbot with three modes, a quiz center, and a learning dashboard, while educators get a Human-in-the-loop workspace where AI-generated materials stay unreviewed until manually approved. The architecture uses a PHP Moodle plugin, a Next.js/React frontend, a FastAPI backend, and hybrid storage (PostgreSQL, ChromaDB, MinIO), containerized with Docker. The article describes it as "a modular Moodle plugin that leverages Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to deliver high-quality, hallucination-free education".
requirements: Teacher-provided course materials must be ingested and indexed so RAG responses and quizzes are grounded in verified sources
Teachers must review and approve AI-generated content before it is released to students
constraints: Grounding depends on the quality and coverage of the teacher-provided materials ingested per course
Data is isolated between different courses by the modular architecture
target_learning_goals: deep conceptual understanding of course material
examples: Students interacted with the chatbot, generated and solved quizzes based on real academic materials such as NLP and Machine Learning course notes, and navigated the learning dashboard

article_title: Why Machines Misread Pedagogical Quality: Human-Machine Alignment in LLM-Based Pretest Question Evaluation
citation: Pei-Yu Tseng, Mahir Akgun, and Peng Liu. (2026). Why Machines Misread Pedagogical Quality: Human–Machine Alignment in LLM-Based Pretest Question Evaluation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23629
title: AI-assisted pretest question generation workflow with generator, evaluator, and controller components
description: The article presents an AI-assisted workflow for pretest question development with three iterative components: automated generation grounded in instructional materials, rubric-based evaluation of question quality, and iterative selection of high-quality questions. The Generator produces candidate questions each round; the Evaluator scores questions on rubric dimensions and removes those below level 3 on relevance or clarity, then runs blind pairwise comparison flagging contradictions; the Controller analyzes gaps in quality and topic coverage and feeds back to the Generator. Both generator and evaluator use GPT-5.1.
requirements: Requires four inputs: course material, a scenario, key concepts, and a rubric defining the quality dimensions of openness, cognitive depth, relevance, and clarity
constraints: The study is situated in an intermediate-level statistics course in the Cybersecurity major, focusing on multiple regression for undergraduate learners
target_learners: undergraduate Cybersecurity students in an intermediate-level statistics course
target_learning_goals: pretest questions aligned with learning objectives on multiple regression, spanning openness and cognitive depth dimensions
examples: In each run the generator produced 12 candidate questions per round across 15 rounds, yielding 180 candidates, with approximately 120 retained per rubric version for diversity across the 3×3 openness–depth space

article_title: Beyond Automation: AI as a Pedagogical Mediator in Collaborative Learning
citation: Niari, M. (2026). Beyond Automation: AI as a Pedagogical Mediator in Collaborative Learning. Umanistica Digitale, 10(24), 121–142. https://doi.org/10.60923/issn.2532-8816/24266
title: AI as a pedagogical mediator framework for collaborative learning
description: The paper's central framework reconceptualizes AI in collaborative learning not as a tutor, peer, or automated orchestrator but as a pedagogical mediator. It states: "This paper advances a conceptual framework that reconceptualizes AI as a pedagogical mediator in collaborative learning environments." The framework positions AI as "an active participant in the orchestration of interaction, epistemic sense-making, and regulatory processes, without displacing learner or teacher agency." It is grounded in socio-cultural theory, distributed cognition, and connectivist perspectives, and treats mediation as the function through which agency, authority, and responsibility are redistributed across human and non-human actors.
requirements: AI systems must participate in orchestrating interaction, epistemic sense-making, and regulatory processes rather than replacing human agents
constraints: The framework explicitly does not displace learner or teacher agency; it is a conceptual contribution, not an empirically tested system
examples: The paper contrasts its mediator framing with treating AI as a tutor, peer, or automated orchestrator, and applies the framing to interaction, epistemic agency, and shared regulation in collaborative learning design.

citation: Tomlinson, B., Black, R.W., Patterson, D.J., van der Hoek, A., Ferguson, J. & Bietz, M.J. (2026). Students prefer personalized, AI-generated educational videos over non-personalized, human-recorded videos. Scientific Reports 16:21804. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-52798-9

description: A custom software pipeline produced 300 AI-generated personalized videos (100 topics × three interest variants: business, technology, society/biology) for a large online undergraduate course. LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet) drafted five-paragraph scripts from an instructor-defined "ethos" prompt; the instructor and project scientist reviewed and edited all scripts and checked examples for correctness. Videos composited a HeyGen AI avatar built from a recording of the instructor, Unsplash images, bullet points, titles, credits, and music into 3–5 minute videos uploaded to YouTube and embedded in Canvas pages.

"The AI-based simulations were built on OpenAI's GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024)", with personas, aims, recipients, themes and chat structure defined through explicit prompt engineering following Park and Choo (2024). article_title: The Pedagogy of AI Mistakes: Fostering Higher-Order Thinking
citation: Hosseini, H. (2026). The Pedagogy of AI Mistakes: Fostering Higher-Order Thinking. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05472
title: AI-as-learning-companion: leveraging LLM fallibility through a critique-refinement cycle to develop higher-order thinking
description: The paper's central framework reframes generative AI errors and hallucinations as a pedagogical resource rather than a limitation. By treating AI as a "learning companion" whose imperfect outputs prompt analysis, evaluation, and reflection, instructors structure an "iterative critique-refinement cycle" in which "AI's imperfect outputs serve as catalysts for evaluation, positioning critique as the central mechanism driving higher-order cognition". The cycle of generation, evaluation, and revision is aligned with Bloom's taxonomy, shifting emphasis from knowledge and application toward analysis, evaluation, and creation, and fostering metacognitive engagement.
requirements: Instruction must extend beyond domain knowledge to include the ability to evaluate, contextualize, and revise AI-generated outputs
Structured opportunities for evaluation and revision with imperfect responses
constraints: Over-reliance on AI can impede the development of core cognitive skills, so use must be scaffolded
target_learning_goals: metacognitive skills including self-monitoring and error detection
examples: Weekly AI Modules in a database design course structured prompting strategies, failure-mode analysis, and a recurring Santa's Workshop case study around the critique-refinement cycle

article_title: Prober.ai: Gated Inquiry-Based Feedback via LLM-Constrained Personas for Argumentative Writing
citation: Ran Bi, Shiyao Wei, Yuanyiyi Zhou. (2026). Prober.ai: Gated Inquiry-Based Feedback via LLM-Constrained Personas for Argumentative Writing Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05598
title: The AI should never write for the student: preserve cognitive effort in AI-assisted writing tools
description: The article's core design principle is that AI writing support must never reduce the cognitive load required for argumentation: the system functions exclusively as a structured questioner, asking rather than telling, and deliberately withholds solutions until the student has demonstrated reflective engagement. This is motivated by cited evidence that AI-generated text availability suppresses independent reasoning and that facilitative (question-based) feedback is more strongly associated with long-term learning gains than directive feedback. The article argues that "pedagogical friction is a feature, not a bug" in AI-assisted education design.
requirements: Feedback interaction must be question-based in its initial phase
Revision support must be gated behind assessed student reflection
constraints: Claims about cognitive engagement preservation and learning outcomes remain theoretical, grounded in prior literature rather than empirical validation specific to this system
examples: Prober.ai refuses to generate or rewrite text, eliminating the cognitive shortcut that enables outsourcing, per the article's account of cited EEG and behavioral evidence

citation: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community.
title: Framework for institutional change in the AI era: arrival technologies versus adoption technologies across six dimensions

Table 1 lays out six dimensions of AI-driven change (evidence base, rate of change, scope and intended use, faculty agency, change agent role, student role) with design implications: humble and local inquiries, approaches over tools, broadening learning goals, mapping disruption and needs, facilitating collective inquiry, and treating students as partners. The workshop series is presented as one instantiation of this framework.

constraints: The framework addresses arrival technologies that lack a pedagogical evidence base and change rapidly, unlike evidence-based adoption technologies
target_learning_goals: Departmental capacity to respond collectively to AI-driven change in teaching and assessment
examples: The six-session workshop series operationalized the framework by surfacing local data, facilitating small-group inquiry, and building a shared repository

article_title: AIED unplugged, teacher workload, and numeracy learning: a clustered quasi-experimental mixed-methods study
citation: Luiz Rodrigues, Guilherme Guerino, Thomaz Edson Silva, Luana Bianchini, Mariana Alves, Geiser Chalco Challco, Thales Vieira, Marcelo Marinho, Valmir Macario, Diego Dermeval, Ig Ibert Bittencourt, Seiji Isotani. (2026). AIED unplugged, teacher workload, and numeracy learning: a clustered quasi-experimental mixed-methods study. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00465-x
title: AIED Unplugged (AIED-U): a paradigm for AI in education in resource-constrained settings, with the teacher as proxy
description: AIED-U is a paradigm for designing AIED for settings with limited technological infrastructure and digital skills, guided by five principles. The article states that "Conformity requires solutions to fit the infrastructure schools already have rather than demanding new hardware", Disconnect requires usability under intermittent or absent internet, Unskillfulness requires no advanced digital skills, Multi-user recognizes shared devices, and Proxy means "the teacher operates the system on behalf of students who continue to work with paper and pen". In this study the paradigm is instantiated by a numeracy app evaluated against usual practice.
requirements: Solutions must fit existing school infrastructure, remain usable without internet, and not demand advanced digital skills from users
constraints: The paradigm assumes no dedicated device per student, so students benefit through indirect interaction mediated by the teacher rather than direct student-system interaction
target_learners: elementary school students in low-resource Brazilian public schools
target_learning_goals: numeracy and arithmetic skills aligned with the BNCC curriculum
examples: In the evaluated system, the teacher photographs students' paper solution sheets with a smartphone; the app recognizes and evaluates the equations and generates error-specific feedback the teacher presents to students
key_sources: Luiz Rodrigues, Guilherme Guerino, Thomaz Edson Silva, Luana Bianchini, Mariana Alves, Geiser Chalco Challco, Thales Vieira, Marcelo Marinho, Valmir Macario, Diego Dermeval, Ig Ibert Bittencourt, Seiji Isotani. (2026). AIED unplugged, teacher workload, and numeracy learning: a clustered quasi-experimental mixed-methods study. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00465-x

article_title: AIED unplugged, teacher workload, and numeracy learning: a clustered quasi-experimental mixed-methods study
citation: Luiz Rodrigues, Guilherme Guerino, Thomaz Edson Silva, Luana Bianchini, Mariana Alves, Geiser Chalco Challco, Thales Vieira, Marcelo Marinho, Valmir Macario, Diego Dermeval, Ig Ibert Bittencourt, Seiji Isotani. (2026). AIED unplugged, teacher workload, and numeracy learning: a clustered quasi-experimental mixed-methods study. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00465-x
title: [HIDDEN APP]: an AIED-U mobile system for numeracy education with exercise-list generation, automated assessment, learning analytics, and teacher autonomy preservation
description: [HIDDEN APP] is the AIED-U system for numeracy education evaluated in the study, a mobile app supporting four main functionalities. It generates personalized and diagnostic exercise lists using a student model with "a knowledge tracing component adapted for unplugged environments" combined with information gain theory; it offers personalized feedback by photographing paper sheets and applying object detection and handwritten math equation recognition with a knowledge-based system classifying errors; it provides individual and classroom learning analytics reports; and it preserves teachers' autonomy by allowing them to replace exercises or override the system's assessments.
requirements: A teacher smartphone with camera permission; teachers must photograph solutions and review reports; designed to work even when the teacher's smartphone lacks internet connectivity
constraints: Teachers reported the app sometimes failed to recognize students' calculations, particularly in multiplication tasks, and described reports as inaccurate; assessment reevaluation required many clicks and was one of the most challenging aspects
target_learners: third- and fourth-year Brazilian elementary students
target_learning_goals: BNCC numeracy skills EF02MA06 and EF03MA07 (arithmetic word problems)
examples: Teachers printed and administered app-generated lists, photographed solutions, and reviewed reports before planning the next lesson, over two lessons per week for two weeks
key_sources: Luiz Rodrigues, Guilherme Guerino, Thomaz Edson Silva, Luana Bianchini, Mariana Alves, Geiser Chalco Challco, Thales Vieira, Marcelo Marinho, Valmir Macario, Diego Dermeval, Ig Ibert Bittencourt, Seiji Isotani. article_title: Bringing Artificial Intelligence Literacy Into Online Education: Machine-Learning Integration Through Geometry in K–12 Teacher Professional Development
citation: Sung, W., & Gunpinar, Y. (2026). Bringing Artificial Intelligence Literacy Into Online Education: Machine-Learning Integration Through Geometry in K–12 Teacher Professional Development. The International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 27(2), 21–45. https://doi.org/10.19173/irrodl.v27i2.9140
title: Teach AI literacy through conceptual understanding rather than technological implementation to enable access regardless of resource constraints
description: The article argues that effective AI literacy education can be delivered through conceptual understanding rather than technological implementation, providing an accessible pathway for K–12 AI integration regardless of resource constraints. It demonstrates this via unplugged, explainable machine-learning activities in geometry within online teacher professional development.
requirements: Activities must make algorithmic processes explainable and bridge familiar subject-matter concepts, as the geometry-based feature-matrix activities did
constraints: Demonstrated with ten K–12 educators in one online PD program
target_learning_goals: AI literacy integration into subject-matter instruction
examples: The study delivered AI literacy online through unplugged explainable machine-learning activities in geometry without complex software
key_sources: Sung, W., & Gunpinar, Y. (2026). Bringing Artificial Intelligence Literacy Into Online Education: Machine-Learning Integration Through Geometry in K–12 Teacher Professional Development.
