article_title: Student Evaluation of Repeated AI Feedback Across a Semester of Writing
citation: Andres Karjus, Janika Leoste, Tiia Õun. (2026). Student Evaluation of Repeated AI Feedback Across a Semester of Writing. arXiv:2607.16115 [cs.CY]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16115
title: Design AI-feedback coursework so the intended learning work does not depend on the final text alone
description: The article argues that integrating AI feedback changes what a writing task becomes, and that AI feedback should not be evaluated only by whether students like it. Its educational value depends on the surrounding task: "whether students still have to write, and are motivated to interpret, question,andintegratefeedbackaspartoftheirownwritingprocess." The authors recommend requirements such as revision following feedback, comparison with reflection criteria, and follow-up rationales.
requirements: Assignments would need to directly incentivize reflection depth or require revision following feedback, comparison with explicit reflection criteria, follow-up questions, or a rationale for accepting or rejecting feedback
constraints: No single design feature completely prevents AI delegation of the parts meant to exercise student judgment; prohibition can be ignored and prescribed rationales, revisions, and self-reports can also be generated
target_learners: first-year humanities bachelor students in higher education
target_learning_goals: critical and selective use of AI feedback
examples: The course tied writing and feedback use to earlier in-class contexts and the authors suggest version histories or brief peer- or teacher-facing explanations to shift the task toward showing situated decisions
key_sources: Andres Karjus, Janika Leoste, Tiia Õun. (2026). Student Evaluation of Repeated AI Feedback Across a Semester of Writing. arXiv:2607.16115 [cs.CY]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16115

article_title: Do Not Copy/Paste: Soft Barriers for Copying in AI-Assisted Programming
citation: Iyiola E. Olatunji, Alberick Euraste Djire, Jacques Klein, and Tegawendé F. Bissyandé. 2026. Do Not Copy/Paste: Soft Barriers for Copying in AI-Assisted Programming. Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3834554
title: AI code handoff problem and handoff-aware AI-assisted programming as a design perspective
description: The paper identifies the AI code handoff problem: "the unmanaged transition from AI-generated text to executable or persistent software artifacts". It proposes handoff-aware AI-assisted programming, in which coding assistants explicitly shape how generated code is transferred, inspected, tested, or attributed, treating the handoff boundary as a software engineering design surface where transfer policies vary by context (education favors reconstruction; professional codebases require provenance, review, testing, or security checks).
requirements: A handoff-aware assistant applies a policy layer allowing direct transfer when appropriate or introducing explanations, metadata, review, tests, or soft barriers
constraints: Transfer policies should vary by context; educational and professional settings favor different defaults
target_learning_goals: responsible and reviewed use of AI-generated code
examples: The paper instantiates one point in this design space—soft-barrier handoff—using Unicode perturbations as a minimal technical probe
key_sources: Iyiola E. Olatunji, Alberick Euraste Djire, Jacques Klein, and Tegawendé F. Bissyandé. 2026. Do Not Copy/Paste: Soft Barriers for Copying in AI-Assisted Programming. Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3834554

article_title: Reconnecting relationships through technology: Developing feedback literacy capabilities through an AI automated feedback tool
citation: Laura Tubino, Chie Adachi. (2022). Developing feedback literacy capabilities through an AI automated feedback tool. ASCILITE 2022 Conference Proceedings. https://doi.org/10.14742/apubs.2022.39
title: AI automated feedback tool piloted university-wide for student feedback
description: An AI tool for automated feedback deployed in a University-wide teaching and learning pilot project at Deakin University. Higher education students interacted with the tool, and the authors analysed those interactions to discuss the tool's affordances for developing students' feedback literacy capabilities. The paper also presents "Implications for further refinement of this tool", indicating the tool was iteratively improved based on the pilot.
requirements: Deployment at scale within a university teaching and learning project; student interaction with the tool as feedback recipients
constraints: The reported evidence comes from a pilot project reflection rather than a controlled evaluation
examples: The tool was run as a University-wide T&L pilot project whose student interactions were reported in this paper
key_sources: Laura Tubino, Chie Adachi. (2022). Developing feedback literacy capabilities through an AI automated feedback tool. ASCILITE 2022 Conference Proceedings. https://doi.org/10.14742/apubs.2022.39

article_title: The AI guilt complex: Moral emotions and ethical dilemmas in academic technology adoption
citation: Diane Vassallo. (2026). The AI Guilt Complex: Moral Emotions and Ethical Dilemmas in Academic Technology Adoption. Journal of Academic Ethics (2026) 24:53. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09726-3
title: AI Guilt Index: a preliminary four-item measure of AI-related guilt in academic contexts
description: The AI Guilt Index is a four-item Likert-scale instrument developed for this study to measure AI-related moral distress among academics, covering credibility worry, feeling like cheating, feeling bad about task automation, and remorse after AI use. Exploratory factor analysis of ten moral-emotion items revealed a unidimensional structure accounting for 63.5% of variance (KMO = 0.93), and the four retained items showed "excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.88)" with item-total correlations from 0.68 to 0.80. Items were adapted from the GASP and State Shame and Guilt Scale. The mean score in the sample was 2.39 (SD = 1.01).
requirements: Requires validation in larger samples; the authors state it was not intended as a definitive measure of AI-related guilt but as an initial exploratory instrument
constraints: Developed and tested only in a single-institution exploratory sample of 109 academics; the item on teaching students about academic integrity was excluded on conceptual grounds
target_learners: University academic staff (lecturers to professors, postdoctoral researchers)
target_learning_goals: Measuring moral emotions (guilt) surrounding AI tool adoption in academic practice
examples: In the survey, 22.9% of participants (n = 25) exceeded the scale midpoint, indicating substantial guilt in about one quarter of the sample
key_sources: Diane Vassallo. (2026). The AI Guilt Complex: Moral Emotions and Ethical Dilemmas in Academic Technology Adoption. Journal of Academic Ethics (2026) 24:53. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09726-3

article_title: Beyond Perspectives: A Trio-Ethnography of Interpretation Evolution in LLM-Supported Programming Education
citation: Jennie Ren, Jordan H. McDowell, and Kyrie Zhixuan Zhou. (2026). Beyond Perspectives: A Trio-Ethnography of Interpretation Evolution in LLM-Supported Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22463
title: Reposition AI in programming education from a classroom-policy issue to a teachable component of pedagogy
description: The article argues programming education should shift from regulating AI use to designing learning environments where students learn with AI. Educators should make AI "a visible, legitimate, and teachable part of programming classrooms" by explicitly communicating when AI use is appropriate and positioning AI as a learning partner and tutor supporting conceptual understanding and independent reasoning.
requirements: Instructors must explicitly communicate AI expectations and provide guidance on productive AI-supported learning strategies
constraints: The recommendation arises from a single trio-ethnography with one highly motivated student participant, which the article says may not represent all programming students
examples: R2 spent about ten minutes in the first class telling students what is and is not allowed with AI use; R1 concluded AI usage transparency is very important
key_sources: Jennie Ren, Jordan H. McDowell, and Kyrie Zhixuan Zhou. (2026). Beyond Perspectives: A Trio-Ethnography of Interpretation Evolution in LLM-Supported Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22463

article_title: Assessment Design Through Co-Creation: Student-Staff Partnership in Evaluating the Impact of Artificial Intelligence
citation: Williams, A., & Ingle, E. (2025). Assessment design through co-creation: Student-staff partnership in evaluating the impact of artificial intelligence. International Journal for Students as Partners, 9(1), 214–226. https://doi.org/10.15173/ijsap.v9i1.5802
title: AI Co-Creators project
description: The AI Co-Creators project is a student-staff co-creation initiative exploring generative AI in higher education assessments. The article states the project "aimed to promote dialogue between students and staff on the impact of AI with the objective of using AI tools more effectively". Its partnership evaluated ChatGPT-generated output against diverse coursework assessments on an undergraduate medical sciences programme.
requirements: Dialogue between students and staff on the impact of AI, which the project aimed to promote
Coursework assessments from which ChatGPT-generated output can be produced and evaluated
constraints: The reported evaluation concerned ChatGPT-generated output on an undergraduate medical sciences programme
target_learning_goals: evaluating AI-generated output against co-designed assessment criteria
examples: Students and staff co-designed evaluation criteria and evaluated ChatGPT-generated output in response to diverse coursework assessments on an undergraduate medical sciences programme
key_sources: Williams, A., & Ingle, E. (2025). Assessment design through co-creation: Student-staff partnership in evaluating the impact of artificial intelligence. International Journal for Students as Partners, 9(1), 214–226. https://doi.org/10.15173/ijsap.v9i1.5802

article_title: Cultivating Agency and Responsible AI Use Through the AI-ARC Framework
citation: Wood, D., & Moss, S. (2026). Cultivating Agency and Responsible AI Use Through the AI-ARC Framework. Journal of Instructional Design and Technology, 1(1), 8–17. https://doi.org/10.65201/CJHS2205
title: AI-ARC framework: Ask, Reflect, Create as a student-facing scaffold for responsible AI use
description: AI-ARC is a three-stage, student-facing framework for ethical and reflective collaboration with generative AI, adapted from the AI-ICE evaluative model. The paper describes it as "a practical, student-facing model for cultivating ethical and reflective collaboration with AI" in which Ask emphasizes inquiry, Reflect emphasizes critical evaluation, and Create emphasizes originality and ethical authorship. It functions both as a roadmap students follow and as a design heuristic for instructional designers.
requirements: Students progress through the three stages of asking purposeful questions, reflecting critically on AI outputs, and creating original work, with student agency central at each stage
constraints: The paper presents AI-ARC as a conceptual framework with stated potential rather than an empirically tested intervention
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students using generative AI
examples: Table 1 outlines each stage with its focus, the role of student agency, and example questions students might use to guide engagement
key_sources: Wood, D., & Moss, S. (2026). Cultivating Agency and Responsible AI Use Through the AI-ARC Framework. Journal of Instructional Design and Technology, 1(1), 8–17. https://doi.org/10.65201/CJHS2205

article_title: Evaluation Indicator System for AI Certificate Programs
citation: Zijing Wu and Qiang Li. (2026). Evaluation indicator system for AI certificate programs. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00604-x
title: AI Certificate Pedagogical Transformation Effectiveness Evaluation Indicator System (20 indicators, S1–S20)
description: A structured indicator system (Table 1) operationalizing the five TPACK-mapped criteria dimensions through 20 sub-indicators coded S1–S20, each with 9-level Saaty scale anchors (e.g., S1 curriculum-AI frontier alignment: 1 = highly aligned, 9 = severely disconnected; S6 AI core competency achievement rate; S15 student data privacy protection technical compliance). Indicators were derived from the literature and refined through Delphi expert consultation. Pre-testing confirmed content validity: "88.89% (16 of 18) of experts judged the Saaty scale anchor settings to be consistent with educational realities".
requirements: Delphi expert consultation and pre-testing with the full expert panel for content validity
constraints: All indicators are expert-perceived proxies; the Impact (Effect) metric was not measured in this study and requires longitudinal or experimental data
target_learners: higher education students in AI certificate programs
target_learning_goals: evaluation of AI certificate program quality and pedagogical transformation potential
examples: The system was applied with 18 Chinese experts via two structured questionnaires: an AHP pairwise comparison survey on the 1–9 Saaty scale and a FAHP fuzzy assessment survey on a 5-point Likert scale, with three Delphi rounds at 10-day intervals.
key_sources: Zijing Wu and Qiang Li. (2026). Evaluation indicator system for AI certificate programs. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00604-x

article_title: Designing for AI literacy: psychological mechanisms and self-determination
citation: Yu S, Lin Y and Chen C (2026) Designing for AI literacy: psychological mechanisms and self-determination. Front. Psychol. 17:1937845. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1937845
title: AI literacy instruction should move beyond procedural prompting to include model principles, limitations, critical evaluation, and ethical responsibility
description: The article derives this principle from its finding that thinking-based instruction outperformed skills-based instruction on objective AI literacy performance. It states that "AI literacy instruction should move beyond procedural prompting and include model principles, limitations, critical evaluation, and ethical responsibility." TBI emphasized reasoning, evaluation, and reflective judgment rather than concrete procedures alone.
requirements: Instructional content must address AI principles, limitations, and ethical consequences, not only tool operation, as the TBI video did.
constraints: The supporting evidence comes from a brief, single-institution experiment with students who already had AIGC experience; the authors call for longer, multi-site replication.
target_learners: university students learning to use AIGC image-generation tools
target_learning_goals: AI literacy including critical evaluation and ethical responsibility
examples: The TBI video covered how AIGC generates images, limits of image-generation systems, critical evaluation and verification, bias and stereotypes, and copyright/privacy/responsibility.
key_sources: Yu S, Lin Y and Chen C (2026) Designing for AI literacy: psychological mechanisms and self-determination. Front. Psychol. 17:1937845. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1937845

article_title: Impacts of artificial intelligence on willingness to communicate and its key antecedents in EFL contexts: a systematic review (2015–2026)
citation: Zhang S, Zou B, Liu Y, Chen Z and Yan R (2026) Impacts of artificial intelligence on willingness to communicate and its key antecedents in EFL contexts: a systematic review (2015–2026). Front. Educ. 11:1927432. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1927432
title: Integrated multi-pathway framework of AI's impacts on EFL learners' WTC, extending MacIntyre et al.'s pyramid model
description: The review proposes an integrated framework in which AI directly enhances learners' WTC while also indirectly promoting WTC through four pathways: the Affective Foundation Pathway, the Motivational Propensity Pathway, the Communicative Capacity Pathway, and the Contextual Affordance Pathway. Anchored in MacIntyre et al.'s pyramid model, it "conceptualiz[es] AI as a dynamic, multi-layered affordance that shapes the affective, motivational, communicative, and contextual antecedents of communication". The framework was built by mapping synthesized evidence onto an extended theoretical model.
requirements: Evidence mapped from studies of AI use in EFL settings measuring WTC or its antecedents (anxiety, self-confidence, motivation)
constraints: The review states "all proposed pathways presented are theoretical syntheses derived from the included literature; only a small subset have been empirically validated through formal statistical mediation tests in primary studies"
target_learners: EFL learners across age groups and proficiency levels
target_learning_goals: oral communication in English as a foreign language
examples: The framework organizes Table 4's thematic mapping: 26 direct-impact studies and pathway categories of 46, 31, 39, 28, 20, and 14 studies respectively
key_sources: Zhang S, Zou B, Liu Y, Chen Z and Yan R (2026) Impacts of artificial intelligence on willingness to communicate and its key antecedents in EFL contexts: a systematic review (2015–2026). Front. Educ. 11:1927432. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1927432

article_title: Human-written and AI-generated revisions: An appraisal analysis of dialogic positioning in argumentative writing
citation: Zhao H and Ji J (2026) Human-written and AI-generated revisions: an appraisal analysis of dialogic positioning in argumentative writing. Front. Educ. 11:1904852. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1904852
title: Use AI-generated revisions as a complementary pedagogical resource rather than a substitute for human feedback
description: Because peer-feedback and AI-generated revisions display distinct dialogic positioning — peer revisions more contractive, AI revisions more balanced between Contract and Expand — the article concludes that "AI may be used in instruction as a complementary resource rather than a substitute for human feedback". Each feedback type exposes students to different stance-taking strategies, so combining them lets learners examine how alternative viewpoints are opened up or constrained.
requirements: Students need guidance to critically evaluate which linguistic choices suit the rhetorical purpose, so they do not equate greater assertiveness with stronger argumentation
constraints: Findings come from a small sample of fourteen undergraduates in one EFL context in China and one standardized ChatGPT-4 prompt, limiting generalizability
target_learning_goals: flexible, rhetorically motivated stance-taking in writing
examples: The study compared the same students' first drafts, peer-feedback revisions, and AI revisions across four writing tasks over nine weeks
key_sources: Zhao H and Ji J (2026) Human-written and AI-generated revisions: an appraisal analysis of dialogic positioning in argumentative writing. Front. Educ. 11:1904852. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1904852

article_title: Identifying the ethical values and norms for artificial intelligence in education: A systematic literature review
citation: Agarwal, B., Urlings, C., van Lankveld, G., & Klemke, R. (2022). Identifying the Ethical Values and Norms of Artificial Intelligence in Education: a Systematic Literature Review. Open University of the Netherlands. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7347-8465
title: Thematic grouping of AIED ethical value definitions into common-term themes
description: The review organises ethical value definitions collected from the literature into themes based on recurring key terms: "Data stewardship: definitions with the terms 'data' or 'information'", non-discrimination (bias, discrimination, diversity), explicability (explain, understand, justify), human oversight (people, someone, third party, self), and goodwill (well-being, consequences, harm, control). Second-level theme names were coined by the review's authors, except explicability, adopted from Floridi et al. (2018) as an umbrella term. Pedagogical appropriateness, fitting no theme, was placed in a theme on its own, later named educational aptness.
requirements: Articles must provide consolidated definitions of ethical values, identified via definitional phrases such as 'defined as', 'means', or 'refers to'
constraints: Based on literature published after 2010 and available in English; only 16 of 25 included articles provided value definitions
target_learners: students and teachers affected by AIED systems across K-12 and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: ethical design and use of AI in education
examples: Definitions such as privacy ('Individual's right to access and control the disclosure of their personal information') were collected per term and grouped into the mind-map themes
key_sources: Agarwal, B., Urlings, C., van Lankveld, G., & Klemke, R. (2022). Identifying the Ethical Values and Norms of Artificial Intelligence in Education: a Systematic Literature Review. Open University of the Netherlands. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7347-8465

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health
citation: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393
title: Artificial intelligence connectedness: definition and three-dimensional structure
description: The article defines artificial intelligence connectedness as 'A novel relational experience formed through sustained interactions with anthropomorphic AI, wherein individuals construct algorithms as responsive "quasi-subjects" and attain need satisfaction through asymmetric responsive confirmation.' Its three dimensions are demand identification, two-way behavioral engagement, and responsive confirmation, each with proposed self-report sample items for Likert-scale measurement. The construct is characterized as psychologically real yet ethically asymmetric, positioned as a digital subtype of connectedness coexisting with traditional interpersonal and self-connectedness in adolescents' relational ecosystems.
requirements: Measurement is proposed via self-report scales using Likert 5-point or 7-point scoring across the three dimensions.
constraints: The article states the construct is currently theoretical; its scientific validity and applicability remain to be verified through standardized measurement tools and systematic empirical research.
target_learning_goals: measuring and understanding adolescent human-AI relational bonds
examples: Sample items include 'I feel this AI truly understands my inner thoughts and feelings' for demand identification and 'I am willing to invest time to maintain the interactional relationship with this AI' for two-way behavioral engagement.
key_sources: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393

article_title: Effectiveness of AI-Supported Game-Based Learning: A Systematic Review of Outcomes, Challenges, and Future Directions
citation: Kaşarcı İsmail, Yurt Eyüp. (2026). Effectiveness of AI-Supported Game-Based Learning: A Systematic Review of Outcomes, Challenges, and Future Directions. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071050
title: Ground AI-GBL design in explicit learning-theory alignment and design AI feedback to promote active engagement rather than passive dependency
description: The review concludes that AI-GBL's "effectiveness rests on principled alignment between AI mechanisms and learning theory rather than algorithmic sophistication per se". For practitioners it recommends grounding adaptive mechanisms in explicit learning progression models, designing AI feedback to promote active engagement rather than passive dependency, treating affective-state monitoring as a first-class design requirement, and implementing bias auditing as standard in stealth assessment pipelines.
requirements: Explicit learning progression models underlying adaptive mechanisms
Validated outcome measurement and adequate sample sizes when evaluating AI-GBL
constraints: The review notes LLM latency introduces extraneous cognitive load and that findings on generative AI mechanisms may date quickly after publication
target_learning_goals: effective integration of AI mechanisms into game-based learning environments
examples: The four High-quality studies in the sample converge on design principles of explicit AI-instructional alignment, transparent adaptive mechanisms, validated outcome measurement, and adequate sample sizes
key_sources: Kaşarcı İsmail, Yurt Eyüp. (2026). Effectiveness of AI-Supported Game-Based Learning: A Systematic Review of Outcomes, Challenges, and Future Directions. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071050

article_title: From AI Intuition to AI Literacy: A Dual Framework for K-12 Education
citation: Beau, M., & Lazar, M. (2025). From AI Intuition to AI Literacy: A Dual Framework for K-12 Education. International School of Boston. https://resources.finalsite.net/images/v1760105856/isboston/njqucrdzeyxvmtjr4cla/WhitePaper_AI_October2025.pdf
title: AI intuition as experiential, inductive understanding developed through an iterative learning cycle
description: AI intuition is defined as "an experiential, inductive understanding of AI systems developed through exploration, trial-and-error, and reflective engagement, enabling learners to anticipate AI behavior, adapt strategies, and make context-dependent decisions". It is a structured form of tacit understanding, not guesswork, that emerges through repeated interaction, use, comparison, and failure. In classrooms it develops through an iterative cycle of exploration, observation, reflection, and adaptation, through which learners build heuristics about how prompts, constraints, and task contexts influence AI outputs.
requirements: Instructional designs that explicitly support the experiential learning cycle and make each phase visible and assessable
constraints: The concept is extended from Flechtner and colleagues' university-level design education work to K-12; the authors note it has not previously been extended to K-12 education
target_learning_goals: anticipating AI behavior and failure modes
developing rules of thumb for when to trust, verify, or disengage from AI
examples: In AI-assisted research activities using platforms such as NotebookLM, students explore through prompt variation, challenge systems with atypical or contradictory queries, and reflect on emerging patterns and limitations
key_sources: Beau, M., & Lazar, M. (2025). From AI Intuition to AI Literacy: A Dual Framework for K-12 Education. International School of Boston. https://resources.finalsite.net/images/v1760105856/isboston/njqucrdzeyxvmtjr4cla/WhitePaper_AI_October2025.pdf

article_title: The AI Literacy Heptagon: A Structured Approach to AI Literacy in Higher Education
citation: Veronika Hackl, Alexandra Elena Müller, Maximilian Sailer. (2025). The AI Literacy Heptagon: A Structured Approach to AI Literacy in Higher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.18900
title: The AI Literacy Heptagon: a seven-dimensional framework with four Bloom-based proficiency levels for AIL in higher education
description: The AI Literacy Heptagon is a framework structuring AIL in higher education around seven dimensions: Technical Knowledge and Skills, Application Proficiency, Critical Thinking Ability, Integration Skills, Legal and Regulatory Knowledge, Ethical Awareness and Reasoning, and Social Impact Understanding. It adds four competency levels (Unaware, Beginner, Intermediate, Expert) derived from Bloom's taxonomy, and distinguishes generic AIL (Beginner in all dimensions) from domain-specific extensions. The heptagonal shape represents the dimensions as equal, aiming to reduce cognitive load while not oversimplifying the construct.
requirements: Dimensions must be treated as interconnected and equal to foster perspectives beyond the dominant technical focus
constraints: Expert-level visualization lacks sufficient granularity, per expert validation feedback
The knowledge-skills-attitudes three-dimensional nature is not explicitly represented in the visual model

The final clause acknowledges variations in emphasis depending on the disciplinary context, connecting the definition to the adaptable Heptagon framework and addressing dimensions underrepresented in prior conceptualizations.

article_title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence-Supported Instruction on Student Learning in STEM: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Doğan Yunus, Kılıç Zeynep, Kalınkara Yusuf, Talan Tarık. (2026). The Impact of Artificial Intelligence-Supported Instruction on Student Learning in STEM: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence14060109
title: Treat AI as a pedagogical partner that extends, rather than replaces, the teacher
description: The article recommends conceptualizing AI-supported instruction as a complement to teaching rather than an autonomous instructional agent. It states: "AI should be conceptualized as a pedagogical partner rather than an autonomous instructional agent." The meta-analytic evidence of a moderate, heterogeneous effect underpins this: AI extends instructional capacity while teachers remain essential for guiding interpretation, facilitating deeper understanding, and supporting higher-order thinking.
requirements: Teacher involvement for guiding interpretation, facilitating deeper understanding, and supporting higher-order thinking processes
constraints: The article cautions that AI is not inherently effective but becomes effective under specific pedagogical and contextual conditions, and that its effectiveness depends on instructional design quality
target_learners: primary, secondary, high school, and university students in STEM education
examples: The meta-analysis of 35 experimental and quasi-experimental studies found a pooled g = 0.670 with high heterogeneity, which the authors read as evidence that AI amplifies effective pedagogy rather than substituting for it

article_title: Assessing AI-TPACK readiness in mathematics teacher education: The role of self-efficacy and teaching beliefs
citation: Meijuan Xie, Liling Luo. (2025). The Status Quo and Future of AI-TPACK for Mathematics Teacher Education Students: A Case Study in Chinese Universities. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13533
title: AI-TPACK framework: integrating artificial intelligence into TPACK
description: The AI-TPACK framework adapts the TPACK framework by adding artificial-intelligence elements to the technology dimension. As the article puts it, "It incorporates elements of artificial intelligence on top of TPACK in order to facilitate the integration of these technologies in education". Integrating AI into TK and intertwining it with PK and CK forms AI-TPK and AI-TCK, which combine with PCK to develop AI-TPACK. The framework demands deep integration of human instructors with AI technology, fostering tripartite co-creation of technological, content, and pedagogical elements through human and machine cognition, and obliges educators to master AI tools such as intelligent tutoring systems and robot teachers.
requirements: Teachers must possess proficiency in AI technology and integrate it with conventional pedagogical approaches and subject knowledge
target_learning_goals: integrating AI technology with mathematical content and pedagogy (AI-TK, AI-TCK, AI-TPK, AI-TPACK)
examples: The article operationalised the framework as a 24-item scale measuring AI-TK, AI-TCK, AI-TPK and AI-TPACK administered to 412 MTES in seven Chinese universities

description: A questionnaire scale the authors designed and validated to measure MTES competence on six variables: AI-TK, AI-TCK, AI-TPK, AI-TPACK, self-efficacy, and teaching beliefs. The revised instrument "contained six variables and 24 items and each variable hold four items", with "the options of each item is a 7-point Likert type ranged from “1: strongly disagree” to “7: strongly agree”". It was refined via a pre-test with 128 senior MTES using EFA and CFA (KMO = 0.937; Cronbach's alphas 0.899–0.934 across factors) before post-testing on 412 students.

citation: Alrazeeni, D. M., Alharrasi, M., Khan, R. M. K., Biswas, R. K., Tama, I. J., Halder, C. R., Deb, B., Bashar, F., & Akter, F. (2026). Transforming Nursing Education with Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review (2010–2025). SAGE Open Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1177/23779608261424597
title: Four-area taxonomy of AI integration in nursing education: personalized learning, simulation-based training, automated assessment, and institutional analytics
description: The review organizes its synthesis of 28 empirical studies into four thematic application areas of AI in nursing education. As the abstract states, "AI-enhanced nursing education in four main areas: (a) personalized learning systems tailored content to individual needs, (b) simulation-based training improved decision-making in high-acuity scenarios, (c) automated assessment tools provided immediate, unbiased feedback, and (d) at the institutional level, AI supported curriculum management and predictive analytics." The taxonomy structures the narrative synthesis, with studies grouped thematically under these focus areas.
requirements: Empirical studies of AI applications in academic, clinical, or hybrid nursing education contexts with measurable outcomes
constraints: Derived from 28 studies, most from middle- and high-income countries, which the review notes may limit generalizability
examples: The narrative synthesis grouped studies thematically under personalized learning, simulation-based training, automated assessment, clinical reasoning, administrative applications, and ethical considerations

description: An LLM-generated interactive pendulum simulation (Figure 1) with sliders for mass, length, initial angle, and angular velocity, and graphs of angle and angular velocity over time with the analytical small-angle solution overlaid. An enhanced version (Figure 2) adds "full rotations and non-periodic trajectories", a friction slider demonstrating damping, pendulum tension over time, and energy distribution bars. Generated with OpenAI's O1 or Claude 3.5 Sonnet.

constraints: The small-angle analytical overlay diverges from the numerical solution at larger initial angles, illustrating the limits of the approximation

examples: Physical tests confirmed the period matches T = 2π√(L/g) for small angles and that numerical and analytical solutions diverge as initial angle increases

It uses "Monte Carlo methods (Metropolis-Hastings)" and lets students observe phase transitions and the critical temperature.

article_title: AI-interaction literacy: reflections on how generative AI might be used to support self-regulated learning in higher education
citation: Linus Brunnström & Lisa Palmqvist. (2026). AI-interaction literacy: reflections on how generative AI might be used to support self-regulated learning in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2731261
title: AI-interaction literacy: the capacity to steer, evaluate, and learn from iterative GenAI interaction
description: AI-interaction literacy is the article's name for a specific capacity within broader AI literacy: "the ability to steer, evaluate, and learn from iterative interaction with GenAI". It concerns how self-regulatory processes are enacted with a system that responds fluently but not necessarily reliably or pedagogically, and includes formulating prompts, identifying when answers are too broad or complex, requesting clarification, comparing explanations, questioning claims, and deciding how to use or reject feedback. The authors position it as a specific enactment of broader AI literacy, particularly applying, evaluating, and integrating AI-generated output within a learning process.
requirements: The learner must possess self-regulatory skills in advance to tune the GenAI into a genuinely helpful partner, since the article found productive use demanded these skills.
constraints: The article notes it remains untested whether students could achieve the qualitative-phase progression using general, uninformed prompts alone, and that the emphasis on prompt quality may shift as GenAI systems develop.
examples: In the demonstration, enacting this literacy meant telling the system its answers were overwhelming, asking explicitly for simplification, and requesting the learning process be structured in smaller steps.

article_title: Building AI Companions that Prioritize Learning over Performance
citation: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816
title: AI learning companions framework: pedagogical, adaptive, and responsible design foundations
description: The paper introduces AI learning companions as "adaptive, pedagogically informed, LLM-powered agents designed for integration into learning environments" and proposes a design framework on three interrelated foundations. The pedagogical foundation addresses how students learn with AI; the adaptive foundation addresses how AI learns about students through modelling cognitive, affective, and behavioural data; and the responsible design foundation keeps systems "transparent, accountable, inclusive, and secure". The framework is illustrated through five case studies across educational contexts.
requirements: Companions must be deliberately engineered to prioritise durable learning over short-term performance rather than relying on prompt-level tutor roles
constraints: The paper states current tools' limitations are revealed by the case studies, and prompt-based approaches cannot match the adaptivity of ITSs
target_learners: students across diverse educational contexts and levels

title: Nine-dimension contrast between AI for work and AI for learning
description: Figure 1 formalises the contrast between AI designed for professional productivity and AI designed for learning across nine dimensions, including purpose, what AI does, nature of interaction, relationship to cognitive effort, relationship to error, measures of success, key failure mode, design principle, and theoretical grounding. In work contexts "AI performs or co-performs the cognitive task on behalf of the user, each interaction is transactional and stateless"; in learning contexts AI must scaffold and challenge the learner, with success measured by retention, transfer, and metacognitive growth.
requirements: Learning-oriented AI must preserve productive struggle and withhold direct answers as a deliberate design feature
constraints: The paper states the reorientation demands a fundamental reconceptualisation, not a minor adjustment to prompting strategy or interface design
target_learners: designers and educators building AI tools for education

article_title: AI-Powered Simulation for Nursing Education: Mixed Methods Systematic Review
citation: Jiang Hongzhan, Wang Ziyan, Shen Wanting, Meng Meiqi, Yang Dan, Li Xuejing, Hao Yufang. (2026). AI-Powered Simulation for Nursing Education: Mixed Methods Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/95167
title: Four-category taxonomy of AI-powered simulation modalities in nursing education
description: The review organizes AI-powered nursing simulations into four categories "distinguished by their technical architectures and pedagogical mechanisms": generative AI/large language models, AI-driven virtual patients/mannequins, AI-enhanced VR/mixed reality, and AI chatbots/tutors. Despite differing implementations, they share a common pedagogical mechanism of using AI to drive interactive, adaptive, real-time learning experiences distinct from static or rule-based simulations. The review uses this taxonomy for subgroup synthesis of differential effects by modality.
requirements: AI algorithms must actively drive patient behavior, physiological responses, scenario progression, feedback, or debriefing, rather than serving only rule-based or debriefing-analytics roles
constraints: Studies using AI only for debriefing analytics without real-time interaction, and rule-based manikins or static virtual patients, were excluded from the category
target_learners: practicing nurses in formal educational activities
examples: The review's subgroup analysis found GenAI/LLM interventions (n=7 studies) consistently improved knowledge, competence, communication, self-efficacy, and empathy, while chatbots (n=2) showed nonsignificant knowledge gains as adjuncts

title: AI-Augmented Learning System: a five-domain heuristic framework for GenAI-driven curricular and pedagogical reconfiguration
description: The AI-Augmented Learning System is the study's central theoretical contribution: a five-domain heuristic linking curriculum design, teaching, capability development, governance, and ecosystemic integration. It was developed through cross-case synthesis of the systematic review themes and interview-derived domains, interpreted through constructivism, connectivism, TPACK, SAMR, and constructive alignment. The article states it "develops the AI-Augmented Learning System framework a five-domain heuristic that links curriculum design, teaching, capability development, governance, and ecosystemic integration". It is positioned as an analytical lens and discussion device, not a prescriptive model.

AI literacy and educator capability development

article_title: The Evolution of Research on AI and Education Across Four Decades: Insights from the AIxEd Framework
citation: Sina Rismanchian & Shayan Doroudi. (2025). The Evolution of Research on AI and Education Across Four Decades: Insights from the AIxEd Framework. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35:2797–2820. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00483-9
title: AI×Ed framework: two axes (role of AI, end user) yielding four quadrants for categorizing AI-in-education research
description: AI×Ed is a categorization framework for research at the intersection of AI and education. Its vertical axis distinguishes "AI as an applied tool vs. AI as an analogy to HI" (human intelligence), and its horizontal axis distinguishes whether the primary end user is a researcher or a learner, with teachers, practitioners, policymakers, and parents in between. The two axes give rise to four quadrants, each highlighting a particular role AI can play in education, such as learner-facing intelligent tutoring systems (upper right), educational data mining (upper left), computational models of learning (lower left), and children writing AI programs to reflect on their own thinking (lower right). The authors use it to code and compare AIED and IJAIED papers across four decades.
requirements: Each paper is given a single point based on the main focus of the work as identified by the authors; multi-faceted works receive a holistic judgment positioning them between locations
constraints: The authors state the framework "may not be rich enough to capture all work in AIED or some work may be very difficult to situate in either or both axes"
The exact position of papers in relation to neighboring points is arbitrary; points within a small cluster are generally interchangeable
target_learners: AIED researchers and scholars categorizing AI-in-education research
target_learning_goals: Understanding and categorizing the diverse roles AI can play in education and learning research
examples: The authors located each paper in AIED proceedings (1985, 1993, 2021, 2024) and IJAIED volumes (2004, 2014, 2021) within the framework's quadrants, e.g., classifying VanLehn's Cascade as AI as an analogy for HI and OLAE as AI as an applied tool
key_sources: Sina Rismanchian & Shayan Doroudi. (2025). The Evolution of Research on AI and Education Across Four Decades: Insights from the AIxEd Framework. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35:2797–2820. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00483-9

The dataset covers papers from AIED proceedings (1985, 1993, 2021, 2024) and IJAIED volumes (2004, 2014, 2021), with each paper given a single point based on its main focus.

article_title: Faculty Readiness for AI-Supported Teaching and Scalable Online Program Delivery in Higher Education: The EPIQ-AI Framework for Epistemic Integrity
citation: Sangwa, S., Ndahayo, C., Dusengumuremyi, F., & Mutabazi, P. (2025). Faculty Readiness for AI-Supported Teaching and Scalable Online Program Delivery in Higher Education: The EPIQ-AI Framework for Epistemic Integrity. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/kj4vt_v1
title: AI-aware assessment patterns shift evaluation toward process evidence and demonstration of judgment
description: Because GenAI can produce plausible text at scale, the article argues that presented fluency no longer plausibly indicates individual mastery, so assessment validity must depend on task design, process evidence, and demonstration of judgment rather than product-only evaluation. The pattern is instantiated in the dashboard as "adoption of AI-aware assessment patterns such as authentic tasks, process artifacts, oral defenses, iterative drafts, and reflective disclosure", aligned with scoping-review recommendations and faculty calls for assessment transformation.

constraints: Assessment reform is positioned as necessary for durable academic integrity protection, not as a standalone fix
target_learning_goals: Valid assessment of student learning and self-regulated learning in AI-saturated environments
examples: Pedagogical readiness tracked through adoption of authentic tasks, process artifacts, oral defenses, iterative drafts, and reflective disclosure

article_title: AI as a cognitive partner in learning: Emerging epistemic practices of reflective thought
citation: Dalsgaard, C., & Prilop, C. N. (2026). AI as a cognitive partner in learning: Emerging epistemic practices of reflective thought. Journal of Research on Technology in Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/15391523.2026.2695013
title: One-year action and design-based research project on AI use across eight Danish upper secondary schools
description: The empirical basis of the study is a one-year action and design-based research project in which "59 teachers from eight upper secondary schools developed action plans for interventions in the form of teaching activities using AI". Teachers attended an initiating workshop introducing cognitive partnership and epistemic practices, completed five-month interventions, then revised plans in a second workshop cycle. Data consist of eight student group interviews with 48 students (28 male, 20 female), most aged 16–19, analyzed via reflexive thematic analysis. Outcomes were the research findings and teacher-designed teaching plans.
requirements: Teachers develop their own exploratory action plans; the project does not prescribe specific practices or AI use
constraints: Interviewed students were selected by teachers from the participating teachers' classes; findings are qualitative and from one national context
target_learning_goals: emerging epistemic practices with generative AI in schoolwork
examples: Four group interviews were conducted in December 2024 after the first cycle and four in March 2025 after the second cycle

article_title: 'Architecting an AI-Driven Decision Support System for Enhanced Online Learning and Assessment'
citation: Mahamad, S.; Chin, Y.H.; Zulmuksah, N.I.N.; Haque, M.M.; Shaheen, M.; Nisar, K. (2025). Technical Review: Architecting an AI-Driven Decision Support System for Enhanced Online Learning and Assessment. Future Internet 2025, 17, 383. https://doi.org/10.3390/fi17090383
title: Combined quantitative–qualitative evaluation framework and metric set for AI-DSSs
description: The review defines a balanced evaluation approach for AI-driven decision support systems combining technical metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, scalability, response time) with user-focused outcomes (user satisfaction via validated surveys drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, and engagement measured through interaction frequency, task completion rates, or time-on-task). Quantitative methods include k-fold cross-validation and statistical comparisons via t-tests or ANOVA; qualitative methods include surveys, interviews, and case studies. The article concludes that "By combining these complementary approaches, evaluations achieve a balance of technical precision and practical relevance, ensuring AI-DSSs meet both performance and user needs."
requirements: Both quantitative performance metrics and qualitative user-perspective data must be collected
Statistical methods such as t-tests or ANOVA for comparison against traditional systems
constraints: Trade-offs are inherent: high deep-learning accuracy (92%) increases latency (30–60%), and real-time response (<1 s) trades accuracy in complex tasks
target_learners: online learners in MOOCs, institutional LMSs, and adaptive learning environments
target_learning_goals: reliable evaluation of AI-supported learning and assessment systems

article_title: AI Mindset – An Empirically Tested Theoretical Framework on the Psychological Factors Shaping AI Competence and AI Use
citation: Feng, S., Koch, M. J., & Carolus, A. (2026). AI Mindset – An empirically tested theoretical framework on the psychological factors shaping AI competence and AI use. Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100402
title: AI Mindset framework: a triadic structure of dispositional factors, contextual and social facilitation, and technology-related appraisals explaining teachers' AI use
description: The AI Mindset framework integrates constructs from social-cognitive, socio-technical and motivation theories into three domains: dispositional factors (personality, basic psychological needs, self-efficacy, self-regulation), contextual and social facilitation (social influence, habit), and technology-related appraisals (attitudes, performance and effort expectancy, hedonic motivation). The article states it is "a cohesive triadic structure comprising dispositional factors, contextual and social facilitations, and technology-related appraisals" shaping tendencies to adopt AI. It extends technology-acceptance models by organising these domains jointly in relation to pedagogical AI competence and AI use.
requirements: Intended to supplement and integrate with, rather than replace, established models such as the Technology Acceptance Model, UTAUT2 and the Theory of Planned Behaviour
constraints: The article notes the incremental explanatory value of the framework requires further investigation because competing theoretical models were not directly compared
target_learning_goals: Understanding psychological factors associated with teachers' AI competence development and AI use in teaching practice
examples: The framework was operationalised as a mediation structural equation model tested with survey data from 224 teachers, with pedagogical AI competence specified as mediator between AI Mindset factors and AI use

article_title: 'AI-Supported Problem-Based Learning for Enhancing Computational Thinking'
citation: Ayanwale, M. A., & Omeh, C. B. (2026). AI-supported problem-based learning for enhancing computational thinking skills in STEM education. Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans 7 (2026) 100263. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100263
title: AI-PBL as Social Constructivist scaffolding: AI tools act as more capable peers within learners' Zone of Proximal Development
description: The study's theoretical framework grounds AI-supported PBL in Vygotsky's Social Constructivism, positioning intelligent systems as digital "more capable peers" within the learner's Zone of Proximal Development. AI supports learning through three functions the article names: "Problem formulation", "Exploration", and "Reflection" — AI agents help define problem parameters, intelligent tutoring systems and reinforcement learning agents simulate robotic behaviors and offer real-time debugging support, and chatbots and analytics tools prompt metacognitive dialogue. In resource-constrained Nigerian university settings, the framework is offered as a scalable, context-aware solution that promotes equity and bridges the digital divide.
requirements: AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Teachable Machine) embedded in inquiry-driven PBL instruction to provide adaptive scaffolding and feedback
constraints: Traditional PBL models rely heavily on instructor facilitation and may be constrained by limited resources, especially in developing contexts
target_learners: First-year undergraduate students in computer robotics programming courses
target_learning_goals: Computational thinking skills (abstraction, decomposition, algorithm design, debugging, metacognitive reflection)
Academic achievement in computer robotics programming
examples: In a search-and-rescue robot task, AI tools guided students in selecting sensors, simulated decision-making algorithms, and provided feedback on classifier accuracy.

citation: Ayanwale, M. A., & Omeh, C. B. (2026). AI-supported problem-based learning for enhancing computational thinking skills in STEM education. Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans 7 (2026) 100263. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100263
title: 14-week localized, adaptive AI-PBL intervention for computer robotics programming
description: The intervention integrated AI tools into problem-based learning over 14 weeks (42 instructional hours) for first-year computer education students. "Localized" emphasizes grounding projects in authentic, context-specific challenges such as maze navigation, assistive robotics, recycling, and search-and-rescue tasks. "Adaptive" highlights the dynamic role of AI tools—ChatGPT for idea generation, debugging, and decision logic, and Teachable Machine for training classifiers—that provided iterative feedback and cognitive scaffolding. Students designed a line-following robot, a service robot for visually impaired individuals, a recycling-sorting robot, and a search-and-rescue robot, with Arduino kits providing tactile programming experience.
requirements: Robotics kits and AI tools (ChatGPT, Teachable Machine) available; students shared in groups because the robotics tools would not be enough for each individual
constraints: The control group received traditional lecture-based teaching on the same content without AI integration
target_learners: First-year undergraduate students in a Computer Education programme
examples: Week 8: students used Teachable Machine to build classifiers distinguishing recyclables by shape and color, integrated into robotic arms for automated classification.

article_title: AI refusal in higher education: the right to refuse, the duty to understand and the diagnostic value of non-use
citation: Zagami, J. (2026). AI refusal in higher education: the right to refuse, the duty to understand and the diagnostic value of non-use. Higher Education Research & Development, 45(7), 2287-2294. https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2026.2694409
title: AI refusal as a role-structured spectrum of non-use, opt-out, restriction, bounded use and institutional delay
description: The article develops AI refusal as a conceptual and diagnostic category rather than a single measurable behaviour. It argues that 'refusal in higher education should be understood as a spectrum of non- use, opt-out, restriction, bounded use and institutional delay', whose meaning changes across roles because universities are role-structured and publicly accountable. Different AI systems (chatbots, analytics, proctoring, plagiarism detection) differ in visibility, risk and user control, so refusing one is not the same as refusing another. The theory draws on technology non-use scholarship that treats non-use as socially meaningful rather than a deficit.
requirements: Interpret refusal in relation to the specific AI system, the actor's role, and the conditions of agency, rather than as one behaviour
constraints: The article does not measure refusal prevalence or offer a systematic review; it is a conceptual and diagnostic category
target_learning_goals: defensible decision-making about when AI serves, compromises, or must be refused in learning and academic work
examples: A student choosing not to use a chatbot (personal); a course team prohibiting generative AI for a task evidencing unaided reasoning (pedagogical); a university delaying procurement pending privacy and accountability clarity (institutional)
key_sources: Zagami, J. (2026). AI refusal in higher education: the right to refuse, the duty to understand and the diagnostic value of non-use. Higher Education Research & Development, 45(7), 2287-2294. https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2026.2694409

article_title: Supporting Undergraduate Students' Learning in Practical Chemistry Courses through AI-Supported Experimental Design
citation: Yim, K.-H.; Lui, M. Y. (2026). Supporting Undergraduate Students' Learning in Practical Chemistry Courses through AI-Supported Experimental Design. Journal of Chemical Education. https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jchemed.5c01311
title: Integrate AI-supported experimental design with professional validation to make authentic inquiry manageable in undergraduate laboratories
description: The article presents an approach where students use AI to design lab manuals for real-world sample analysis, then implement them experimentally. AI's "rapid response and capacity to produce extensive information from user prompts" helps students narrow broad topics and develop manuals, making Level 3 authentic inquiry more accessible. Independent professional validation ensures safety and feasibility before implementation.
requirements: AI tools available to students with institutional guidance on ethical use
Professional validation team to verify safety and feasibility of student-designed manuals
Consultation sessions with instructor for safety protocols and practical guidance
Two draft submissions with instructor feedback before experimental sessions
constraints: Students need prior hands-on experience with relevant analytical instruments
Requires staff availability for increased supervision workload
Students need foundational knowledge to critically evaluate AI-generated content
examples: 38 students in 8 groups designed lab manuals across six topics (food, cosmetic, water analysis) using LC-DAD, GC-MS, UV-vis, fluorescence, and titration methods, then implemented them in two 3-hour lab sessions

title: AI-assisted lab manual design project in analytical chemistry laboratory course
description: A group-based project embedded in a third-year analytical chemistry laboratory course at Hong Kong Baptist University. Students selected from six broad everyday-life topics (food, cosmetic, water analysis using various instrumental techniques), used AI tools to design a complete lab manual (objectives, background, procedures, data analysis), submitted two drafts, consulted with instructors, implemented their manuals in two 3-hour sessions, and presented results. Manuals were validated by an independent professional team before release to students.

Instructor consultation sessions
Professional validation team (course instructor, project assistant, Chemical Testing Services representatives)
Two 3-hour laboratory sessions for implementation

Group size of 4-5 limited individual participation in all steps
Course constraints limited the study to a single iteration with small sample

article_title: Beyond Detection: Redesigning Authentic Assessment in an AI-Mediated World
citation: Kickbusch, S., Ashford-Rowe, K., Kemp, A., Boreland, J., & Huijser, H. (2025). Beyond Detection: Redesigning Authentic Assessment in an AI-Mediated World. Education Sciences, 15(11), 1537. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci15111537
title: AI-as-collaborator assessment patterns requiring critique, adaptation and verification of AI outputs
description: The paper offers discipline-agnostic learning design patterns that position AI as a collaborator rather than a cheating application. Patterns include "tasks that require students to critique, adapt and verify AI outputs", explicit process transparency (prompts, iterations, rationale), and assessable demonstrations of digital discernment and ethical judgement. Patterns are treated as design propositions—named solutions to recurrent problems under AI-present conditions—and are intended to scaffold local adaptation across disciplines.
requirements: A pattern must make student judgement and process evident and assessable, be adaptable across disciplines, and be generally feasible under typical higher education constraints
constraints: The set is intentionally compact and non-exhaustive and invites future empirical evaluation
examples: Business students interrogate a chatbot-generated market analysis; pre-service teachers evaluate AI-produced lesson plans for inclusivity and pedagogical soundness

article_title: New systems of learning for distance learning institutions? A six-study review of implementing AIDA
citation: Rienties, Bart; Coughlan, Tim; Domingue, John and Herodotou, Christothea (2026). New systems of learning for distance learning institutions? A six-study review of implementing AIDA. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100607
title: AIDA: the Open University's AI Digital Assistant with GraphRAG grounding and a pedagogical knowledge graph
description: AIDA is a human-centred GenAI digital assistant co-developed by the OU's Knowledge Media Institute, Institute of Educational Technology and Digital Services. Unlike generic LLM deployments, "AIDA was explicitly architected to prioritise provenance, transparency, and pedagogical intent": it uses a staged retrieval-augmented generation strategy extended to a GraphRAG architecture grounding all responses in curated OU content, with direct links back to originating resources so students can verify sources. A dedicated Knowledge Graph encodes the learning task, pedagogical approach, AIDA's role, domain, course level and interaction language, enabling scaffolding, reflection prompts, formative feedback and activity generation. It runs on the OU's Azure Enterprise platform, primarily using GPT-4o.
requirements: Grounding responses in curated institutional content with surfaced provenance links
Enterprise cloud platform providing governance, monitoring and data-management practices
Encoded pedagogical knowledge (task, approach, role, domain, level, language)
constraints: Despite substantial testing and student/staff support, upscaling as business as usual has not materialised; deployment so far is limited to non-credit-bearing OLC courses and one induction pilot
target_learners: distance learning students at the Open University, predominantly working adults
target_learning_goals: context-specific learning support, formative feedback, quiz practice, and study guidance
examples: Tested across six studies from December 2023 to July 2025 with 498 students and 20 staff, including a randomised trial on two OpenLearn Create courses and a 354-student induction pilot

article_title: Transforming clicks into critical thinking: An AI-based media literacy program for children
citation: Demir, R., & Akar, C. (2025). Transforming Clicks into Critical Thinking: An AI-Based Media Literacy Program for Children. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-6786882/v1
title: AI-integrated 5E learning cycle for critical media literacy in elementary grades
description: An 18-hour instructional pattern that maps each phase of the 5E learning cycle (Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate) onto specific AI and digital tools, activities, and national curriculum outcomes. The article states it involved "an 18-hour instructional intervention designed using the 5E learning cycle model—Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate—integrated with AI-based tools to foster critical media literacy among elementary school students." Tools such as ChatGPT, Perplexity AI, Canva AI, and Grammarly were embedded within pedagogical tasks rather than used as standalone applications, and the sequence was aligned with the Turkish Language and Social Studies curricula.
requirements: Alignment with national curriculum outcomes (Turkish Language and Social Studies programs)
Digital tools selected for pedagogical potency and technological accessibility in low-resource settings
constraints: The participating school had a socioeconomically disadvantaged profile, shaping tool choices toward accessible options

article_title: Enhancing Sustainability Consciousness in Higher Education: Impacts of Artificial Intelligence-Integrated Sustainable Engineering Education
citation: Feng Liu, Hua Wang, Yuntao Guo, Tianpei Tang. (2026). Enhancing Sustainability Consciousness in Higher Education: Impacts of Artificial Intelligence-Integrated Sustainable Engineering Education. Sustainability 18, 2124. https://doi.org/10.3390/su18042124
title: AI-SEE: a pedagogical framework integrating AI across the engineering curriculum as a cognitive scaffold and system-optimization resource
description: AI-SEE (Artificial Intelligence-Integrated Sustainable Engineering Education) is a pedagogical framework structured around an input-process-output logic, in which institutional conditions, learner characteristics, and external contexts feed a pedagogical process of four pillars whose intended outputs are sustainability-related knowledge, attitudes, and behavioral orientations. The article states that "The core pedagogical process is operationalized through four mutually reinforcing pillars—intelligence-driven, green-empowered, responsibility-leading, and practice-integrated—which together constitute an integrated learning system." AI is positioned not merely as an instructional aid but as a cognitive augmentation platform and scenario simulation engine supporting systems thinking, ethical trade-off analysis, and knowledge-to-action translation.
requirements: AI embedded across the educational lifecycle to support data-rich learning, iterative feedback, and adaptive instruction
human-AI collaboration positioning engineers and students as accountable agents of judgment rather than passive recipients of algorithmic outputs
constraints: designed for feasibility, scalability, and sustainability within resource-constrained, practice-oriented higher education contexts
tailored to application-oriented undergraduate institutions in China
target_learning_goals: systems thinking and ethical trade-off analysis in engineering decision-making
examples: implemented in transportation-related programs at Nantong University with a pilot cohort exposed to the model and a control cohort following a conventional curriculum
key_sources: Feng Liu, Hua Wang, Yuntao Guo, Tianpei Tang. (2026). Enhancing Sustainability Consciousness in Higher Education: Impacts of Artificial Intelligence-Integrated Sustainable Engineering Education. Sustainability 18, 2124. https://doi.org/10.3390/su18042124

article_title: Enhancing Sustainability Consciousness in Higher Education: Impacts of Artificial Intelligence-Integrated Sustainable Engineering Education
citation: Feng Liu, Hua Wang, Yuntao Guo, Tianpei Tang. (2026). Enhancing Sustainability Consciousness in Higher Education: Impacts of Artificial Intelligence-Integrated Sustainable Engineering Education. Sustainability 18, 2124. https://doi.org/10.3390/su18042124
title: Four-pillar curriculum pattern: intelligence-driven, green-empowered, responsibility-leading, and practice-integrated learning
description: The AI-SEE framework organizes the curriculum as four mutually reinforcing pillars. The intelligence-driven pillar embeds AI for data acquisition, modeling, feedback, and simulation; the green-empowered pillar embeds lifecycle assessment and carbon accounting as decision criteria; the responsibility-leading pillar makes engineering ethics a required component; the practice-integrated pillar connects classrooms with industry and communities. The article states that "AI-SEE therefore emphasizes that learning tasks should culminate in action within real contexts," and that the pillars "together form a dynamic system for cultivating the competencies required of sustainable engineering professionals in the AI era."
requirements: integration across curriculum design, teaching and learning activities, assessment, and continuous improvement
partnerships with industrial parks, enterprises, governments, and NGOs for authentic tasks
constraints: the article notes students perceived entry barriers to AI tools and limited hands-on time for methodological internalization
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students in application-oriented programs
target_learning_goals: ethical reasoning as a situated competence
examples: students used Python-based workflows on open datasets, applied machine learning to forecast building cooling loads, used digital twins for microgrid scenarios, and completed energy-efficiency diagnostics and photovoltaic site-selection projects with external partners

citation: Christ, O., Riedl, R., Schmid, J., Zürcher, P., & Thilo, F. (2026). Theoretical Perspectives on Teaching with Robots: From Interdisciplinary Prerequisites and Necessities in Today's Classrooms to Five Different Types of Robots. AI Educ. 2, 28. https://doi.org/10.3390/aieduc2030028
title: AI technology stack enabling adaptive and socially responsive educational robots
description: The article specifies the AI foundations underpinning the proposed robot types: 'natural-language processing (NLP) for dialogic interaction, affective computing for emotion recognition and expression, reinforcement learning for adaptive behaviour modulation, and behaviour-prediction models that support personalised engagement'. Integrated into multimodal sensor architectures, these components let robots interpret speech, gestures, facial expressions, and proxemics in real time. The article frames this as hybrid intelligence in which human and machine capabilities co-evolve.

constraints: AI is framed not as a substitute for the teacher but as a cognitive extension that amplifies human judgement and empathy

examples: Multimodal sensor architectures enable robots to interpret speech, gestures, facial expressions, and proxemics in real time, aligning with embodied and enacted cognition principles

citation: Venetsanos, D. T. (2026). A Tripartite Feedback Framework for AI-Assisted Assessment of Complex Reports in Higher Education. AI Educ. 2026, 2, 26. https://doi.org/10.3390/aieduc2030026
title: Frame AI as flagging issues for human review rather than as authoritative verification
description: This principle holds that AI systems in assessment should be positioned as surfacing potential issues for expert human review, with interfaces that "surface AI reasoning for review, not verdicts". It responds to the risk that LLMs perform statistical pattern-matching rather than logical verification, and it preserves human final authority over all feedback reaching students.
requirements: Hybrid architectures combining rule-based checks with language models, humans retained as final authorities, and interfaces surfacing AI reasoning for review
constraints: LLMs may accept incorrect work resembling correct patterns, reject unusual correct approaches, or miss uncommon errors
target_learners: higher education students submitting complex written reports
target_learning_goals: factual accuracy and procedural correctness in reports
examples: The article proposes AI-supported intermediate-level checking explicitly framed as flagging potential issues for expert human review rather than generating autonomous feedback

article_title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
citation: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7
title: Taxonomy of K-12 AI literacy approaches: learning experiences versus theoretical/implementation perspectives
description: The review organizes the K-12 AI literacy field into two broad thematic categories: learning experiences and theoretical perspectives on implementation. Learning experiences cover understanding AI concepts, how AI works, tools for AI, and living with AI; the implementation category covers curriculum design, AI as a subject, student perspective, teacher training, support resources, and gender diversity. The review states: "the papers were classified into two broad thematic categories according to the type of educational approach, namely, learning experience and theoretical perspective." Each main category was further subdivided to structure the field (Fig. 6).
requirements: Documents must concern AI literacy or AI education at the K-12 level, excluding computer-based learning and intelligent tutoring systems
constraints: Based on Scopus-indexed documents only; search conducted between 21 October 2021 and 9 March 2023
examples: Figure 6 shows the full taxonomy of identified categories and subcategories

article_title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
citation: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7
title: K-12 AI literacy requires a competency framework to guide didactic proposals and define a sequenced, modular, personalized curriculum
description: The review concludes that a competency framework is needed to guide didactic proposals for AI literacy in K-12 and to define a curriculum reflecting sequence and academic continuity. It states: "These studies highlight the need for a competency framework to guide the design of didactic proposals for AI literacy in K-12 in educational institutions." Such a curriculum "should be modular and personalized" and adjusted to the conditions of the schools, and learning experiences should be based on clearly defined competencies within an AI literacy framework.

Curriculum adjusted to the conditions of the schools
constraints: The review notes AI teaching at K-12 is not yet prevalent in formal settings and is considered challenging

examples: Van Brummelen et al. (2021a) designed a five-day online workshop based on the AI competencies proposed by Long and Magerko (2020)

article_title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
citation: Crompton, H., & Burke, D. (2023). Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00392-8
title: Five usage codes for AI in higher education: Assessment/Evaluation, Predicting, AI Assistant, Intelligent Tutoring System, and Managing Student Learning
description: This systematic review used grounded coding of 138 articles to let uses of AI in higher education emerge from the data rather than fitting them to pre-existing frameworks. The review reports that "Five usage codes emerged from the data: (1) Assessment/Evaluation, (2) Predicting, (3) AI Assistant, (4) Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS), and (5) Managing Student Learning." Each code has axial codes as subcategories, e.g. automatic assessment, prediction of dropouts, chatbots, adaptive tutoring, and learning analytics.
requirements: Grounded coding of primary studies' descriptions of AI use, with in vivo codes and constant comparison until codes are theoretically saturated
constraints: Derived from peer-reviewed journal articles published 2016–2022 in English; conference proceedings and gray literature excluded
target_learning_goals: understanding how artificial intelligence is used across higher education contexts
examples: The review delineated each code with a figure of codes and axial codes, e.g. six axial codes under Assessment/Evaluation and ten axial codes under Predicting

article_title: Assessing student perceptions and use of instructor versus AI ‐generated feedback
citation: Er, Erkan; Akçapınar, Gökhan; Bayazıt, Alper; Noroozi, Omid; Banihashem, Seyyed Kazem. (2024). Assessing student perceptions and use of instructor versus AI-generated feedback. British Journal of Educational Technology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13558
title: AI should not be the sole source of feedback; human expertise remains crucial
description: The article's practitioner implication is that AI-generated feedback should not replace instructor feedback. Its experiment showed students receiving AI feedback had significantly lower score improvements, and the authors conclude that "AI should not be the sole source of feedback, as human expertise is crucial." They attribute this to instructors' contextual awareness and AI's risk of hallucination and generic feedback.

target_learning_goals: improving programming work based on feedback
examples: Students in the AI-feedback condition improved lab scores significantly less than the instructor-feedback condition after controlling for midterm scores

article_title: The impact of AI-assisted pair programming on student motivation, programming anxiety, collaborative learning, and programming performance: a comparative study with traditional pair programming and individual approaches
citation: Fan, G., Liu, D., Zhang, R., & Pan, L. (2025). The impact of AI-assisted pair programming on student motivation, programming anxiety, collaborative learning, and programming performance: a comparative study with traditional pair programming and individual approaches. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00537-3
title: Integrate AI coding assistants to complement rather than replace human pairing in programming education
description: The article concludes that AI-assisted pair programming enhances motivation, reduces anxiety, and improves performance, yet does not match the collaborative depth and social presence of human–human pairing. Educators should therefore "integrate such tools thoughtfully, ensuring that technology complements rather than replaces the interpersonal dynamics and skill development central to effective programming education". The principle pairs AI support for outcomes with preserved human interaction for social engagement.
