Training on effectively using the AI assistants as programming partners, as Group A received
constraints: AI-assisted pairing did not fully replicate the collaborative and social benefits of human–human pairing, per the article's own conclusion

article_title: Envisioning AI for K-12: What Should Every Child Know about AI?
citation: Touretzky, D.; Gardner-McCune, C.; Martin, F.; and Seehorn, D. (2019). Envisioning AI for K-12: What Should Every Child Know about AI? The Thirty-Third AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-19). https://www.aaai.org
title: Five thematic strands ('big ideas') organizing K-12 AI guidelines
description: The AI for K-12 working group frames its guidelines around five big ideas in AI: computers perceive the world using sensors; agents maintain models/representations of the world and use them for reasoning; computers can learn from data; making agents interact comfortably with humans is a substantial challenge; and AI applications can impact society in both positive and negative ways. The authors state the guidelines "will unpack AI's 'Big Ideas' along five thematic strands, and organize them by four grade bands". They chose this formulation over a traditional division into application areas because it "better meets the needs of K-12 students and teachers".
requirements: Guidelines are developed via a collaboration between AI experts and K-12 teachers
constraints: The authors note others might frame the field differently and welcome community feedback
target_learners: K-12 students in grade bands K-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-12
target_learning_goals: Understanding core AI concepts: perception, representation and reasoning, machine learning, human-AI interaction, and societal/ethical impacts of AI
examples: The current draft lists each big idea with grade-band expectations, e.g., K-2 students interact with voice-based agents while grades 9-12 students train perceptual classifiers
key_sources: Touretzky, D.; Gardner-McCune, C.; Martin, F.; and Seehorn, D. (2019). Envisioning AI for K-12: What Should Every Child Know about AI? The Thirty-Third AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-19). https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33019795

description: For each big idea, the draft guidelines specify what students should know and be able to do in four grade bands: K-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-12. The progression moves from experiencing and examining AI (e.g., interacting with voice agents, examining "the world map created by Calypso for Cozmo") toward modifying applications, then creating complex applications, and finally demonstrating limitations and training systems, e.g., grades 9-12 students "should be able identify and demonstrate the limitations of machine perception systems and use machine learning tools".
requirements: Age-appropriate AI tools and programming frameworks with AI primitives at each band
target_learning_goals: Progressively deeper understanding of machine perception, representation, machine learning, natural language interaction, and AI ethics
examples: Grades 6-8 students measure how well a trained system generalizes to novel inputs and understand how training-data biases affect performance

title: Taxonomies of artificial intelligence: thinking/acting like humans versus rationally, and five methodological tribes
description: The report notes there is no single universally accepted definition of AI and surveys expert taxonomies. A popular AI textbook's taxonomy distinguishes "systems that think like humans," "systems that act like humans," systems that think rationally, and systems that act rationally. It also reports Pedro Domingos's five tribes of AI researchers — symbolists, connectionists, evolutionaries, Bayesians, and analogizers — and Frank Chen's five problem categories, illustrating the field's diversity of problems and solutions.

constraints: The report states the diversity of AI problems and solutions makes it difficult to define a bright-line distinction between what constitutes AI and what does not

examples: The report quotes the Russell and Norvig four-category taxonomy and Domingos's five tribes as differing expert taxonomies

citation: Zawacki-Richter, O., Bond, M., & Gouverneur, F. (2019). Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators? International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-019-0171-0
title: Four areas of AIEd applications in higher education
description: This systematic review of 146 articles on AI in higher education organizes the literature into four application areas derived through iterative coding: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems. The framework maps AI-based services onto the student life-cycle, spanning institutional and administrative services as well as academic support for teaching and learning. It provides a shared vocabulary for educators navigating a fragmented field where terminology varies widely across studies.

constraints: The taxonomy emerged from literature published between 2007 and 2018 and may not capture newer AIEd developments

article_title: Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education
citation: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y
title: AI-GLM framework for generative learning in AI-mediated mathematics education
description: The AI-Enhanced Generative Learning in Mathematics (AI-GLM) framework is a conceptual framework specifying how generative AI reshapes the conditions of Wittrock's generative learning theory in mathematics. The article states: "I propose the AI-Enhanced Generative Learning in Mathematics (AI-GLM) framework, which identifies three roles AI can occupy in relation to learners' generative processes". It comprises a three-role typology, a role determination mechanism combining tool design, task design, learner orientation, and teacher mediation, and five design principles, with propositions stated with operationalizations and falsification conditions.
requirements: Propositions require operationalizations and falsification conditions for empirical testing, as the article states
constraints: The framework is developed for mathematics learning specifically, addressing its representational, symbolic, and justificatory demands
target_learners: mathematics learners in AI-mediated learning environments
target_learning_goals: generative learning and deep mathematical understanding
examples: The framework was derived by coding each of the eight generative learning strategies for the cognitive process affected, the direction of change, and the condition of dependence, retaining themes supported by more than one form of generative work
key_sources: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y

article_title: Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education
citation: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y
title: Role determination mechanism: task design, tool design, learner orientation, and teacher mediation
description: The mechanism specifies how four factors combine to determine which AI role obtains in a given episode. "Task design is logically prior: it designates which generative work is the target and thereby fixes the referent against which a role is defined". Tool and task design jointly establish an opportunity structure; learner orientation is the proximal determinant selecting among permitted assignments; teacher mediation is distal, operating through the other three. Learner expertise and instructional context moderate the weights.
requirements: Role assignment must be identifiable independently of the learning outcome, from the task specification and the interaction record, for the framework's predictions to be falsifiable
constraints: In unsupervised settings such as homework, tool defaults and learner orientation dominate; where activity is supervised and teacher-designed, task design and teacher mediation dominate
target_learners: mathematics learners across expertise levels; teachers mediating AI use
target_learning_goals: predicting and steering AI role assignment in instructional episodes
examples: A task asking students to explain why the quadratic formula works and then test that explanation against AI output makes the explanation the target and the AI output an object of evaluation, a Catalyst assignment
key_sources: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y

citation: Skulmowski, A. (2024). AI-Related Threats to Information Sovereignty and Challenges for Research Ethics. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09939-1
title: Table of AI-related and cloud-based functionalities, participant risks, and solutions
description: Table 1 of the article enumerates concrete functionalities that threaten participant privacy during research: browser spell checking using cloud services, malware scanners using cloud databases, word processors using AI assistants, and user tracking in operating systems. For each it names the risk, such as "Transfer of user input to clouds and AI training databases", and a solution or workaround, such as recommending participants disable spell checking or AI assistants, or boot alternative operating systems for high-risk studies.
requirements: Researchers must communicate the recommended workarounds to participants, e.g., in informed consent forms.
constraints: The listed workarounds depend on participants changing settings or software on their own devices, which may not be feasible in every context.
target_learning_goals: mitigating AI- and cloud-related privacy risks during data collection
examples: One row recommends disabling cloud-based malware scanners during the time of diary studies, since scanners may transfer user files containing identifiable information.

article_title: The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development
citation: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5
title: The AIR framework characterizes epistemic thinking as three interdependent components: epistemic aims, epistemic ideals, and reliable epistemic processes
description: The AIR framework provides a structure for analyzing epistemic thinking in terms of three interdependent components. Epistemic aims are goals involving developing a representation of the world, such as models, theories, explanations, and beliefs. Epistemic ideals are the standards or criteria people use to evaluate whether epistemic aims have been achieved. Reliable epistemic processes are the individual and collective strategies or methods people use to try to achieve their epistemic aims in light of the associated ideals. The article states that "epistemic aims, ideals, and reliable processes are inextricably interconnected in the AIR framework" and that people "deploy aims, ideals, and reliable processes in concert when engaged in epistemic thinking."
requirements: Researchers or educators analyzing epistemic thinking must attend to how aims, ideals, and processes interact rather than treating them in isolation
constraints: The interdependence of the AIR components does not mean that researchers must always study all three together; researchers may focus on one component when seeking a rich and detailed portrait of it
target_learners: elementary through university students and teachers engaged in inquiry, argumentation, and fact-checking tasks
target_learning_goals: growth in epistemic thinking including evaluating online claims, constructing knowledge from multiple documents, and model-based inquiry in science
examples: Table 1 presents examples of aims, ideals, and processes expressed by ninth graders constructing knowledge from multiple historical documents and seventh graders constructing and evaluating scientific models
key_sources: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5

article_title: When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education
citation: Peng Wang, Olga Viberg, Effie Lai-Chong Law, Samuel Greiff. (2026). When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10202-y
title: Eight validity criteria determine when an AI system should count as a cognitive model of learning
description: The review's central contribution is an evaluative framework of eight criteria that an AI system must satisfy before its cognitive-model status is granted rather than assumed: theoretical grounding, construct validity, mechanistic transparency, alignment with human learning trajectories, error-signature matching, causal-intervention tests, ecological validity, and instructional usefulness. The framework shifts the question from whether AI can model cognition to when it should be allowed to count as one, treating the criteria as "a structured set of validity criteria that together determine when an AI system should be allowed to count as a cognitive model of learning".
requirements: Internal components must be transparent enough to support meaningful mappings to theory, and these mappings must be empirically validated rather than asserted by intuition
constraints: The cognitive status of any virtual-learner proxy must be earned through the validity criteria rather than assumed from the label
target_learners: Educational researchers using computational models of learners
target_learning_goals: Mechanistic explanation of learning processes such as memory, strategy use, motivation, and self-regulation
examples: The review uses a running example of math anxiety and problem solving, operationalized as an anxiety signal that narrows attention or pre-empts working memory, tested via representation analysis and targeted ablation against human error trajectories
key_sources: Peng Wang, Olga Viberg, Effie Lai-Chong Law, Samuel Greiff. (2026). When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10202-y

article_title: When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education
citation: Peng Wang, Olga Viberg, Effie Lai-Chong Law, Samuel Greiff. (2026). When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10202-y
title: Four AI model families as complementary lenses on educational cognition, organized by learning flexibility and mechanistic transparency
description: The review organizes AI approaches to modeling educational cognition into four families treated as different lenses rather than a formal taxonomy: neural networks, reinforcement learning agents, cognitive architectures, and large language models. It situates them along two dimensions, learning flexibility and scale, and mechanistic transparency and construct alignment, arguing that "neural networks emphasize learning from experience through gradual parameter change; reinforcement learning formalizes adaptation through feedback and incentives; cognitive architectures enforce psychologically motivated structure and capacity limits; and large language models bring broad, pretrained competence for language-mediated tasks". The families are complementary and increasingly integrable through hybrid approaches.
requirements: Model choice should be theory-driven, depending on whether the target phenomenon is practice-driven skill acquisition, sequential decision making under feedback, structured procedure under capacity limits, or language-mediated reasoning
constraints: The four families are neither mutually exclusive nor strictly parallel, and figure placements are illustrative rather than exact, intended for qualitative comparison only
target_learners: Educational psychology researchers and learning scientists selecting computational modeling approaches
target_learning_goals: Explaining learning trajectories, error patterns, strategy selection, cognitive load, self-regulation, and transfer
examples: Figure 2 places LLMs in the high-flexibility, low-transparency region and cognitive architectures in the opposite region, with neural networks and RL agents between the poles
key_sources: Peng Wang, Olga Viberg, Effie Lai-Chong Law, Samuel Greiff. (2026). When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10202-y

article_title: When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education
citation: Peng Wang, Olga Viberg, Effie Lai-Chong Law, Samuel Greiff. (2026). When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as Cognitive Models in Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10202-y
title: Comparative guide table of AI model families mapping phenomena, interpretability risks, and validity checks
description: The review provides a summary table (Table 1) comparing the four major AI model families as cognitive models for educational psychology. For each family it lists best-suited phenomena, internal variables, explanatory strengths, key limitations and risks, and priority validity checks mapped to the review's criteria. The table is described as "a compact guide to what each modeling family naturally represents (e.g., practice-driven learning, feedback-driven decisions, capacity limits, language-mediated reasoning), the main interpretability/construct-validity risks, and the evaluation checks that strengthen mechanistic claims".
requirements: The final column maps recommended checks to the review's validity criteria: construct validity, trajectory alignment, error-signature matching, and causal-intervention tests
constraints: The table summarizes family-level trade-offs and recommended checks rather than quantitative rankings of model families
target_learners: Educational researchers choosing among AI modeling approaches
target_learning_goals: Selecting and validating AI models for explaining memory, strategy use, cognitive load, and language-mediated learning
examples: For neural networks the table lists representation probing, learning-curve fitting, structured error patterns, and ablations or counterfactuals as priority validity checks

article_title: Emotional Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Heng Zhang, Yuhan Liu, Meilin Jiang, Juanjuan Chen, Minhong Wang, Fred Paas. (2025). Emotional Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10086-4
title: Taxonomy of eight AI-based cognitive support types and five AI-based emotional support types in education
description: From 172 included articles, the review identified "eight types of AI-based cognitive support and five types of AI-based emotional support." Cognitive support types include providing individualized feedback (65 articles), real-time task guidance (45), simulating human conversations for communication skills (32), personalized learning resources (31), answering questions (26), prompting questions (13), metacognitive advice (10), and translating images/text (5). Emotional support types include tailored affective responses (34), emotional interaction without monitoring (22), reminders to relax or regulate emotions (4), instructing teachers to demonstrate empathetic behaviors (1), and grouping students with similar knowledge levels (1). This taxonomy maps the intervention space of emotional AI in education and underpins the three-category meta-analytic comparison.
requirements: Interventions must be classifiable as AI-based cognitive support, AI-based emotional support, or an integration of both, based on the nature of the support provided
constraints: The taxonomy reflects the 172 articles included in this review (2000–2025); support types were identified from the included literature rather than proposed a priori
target_learners: students across pre-school, elementary, secondary, and tertiary education
examples: Table 4 lists all support types with article counts, e.g., CS1 providing feedback based on individual circumstances (65 articles) and ES1 offering affective responses tailored to individual circumstances (34 articles)

article_title: Moving Beyond Reflection: Reflexivity and Epistemic Cognition in Teaching and Teacher Education
citation: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180
title: Chinn and colleagues' AIR model of epistemic cognition: Aims, Ideals and Reliable processes
description: The article describes the AIR model as a comprehensive, philosophically-driven framework for epistemic cognition developed by Chinn and colleagues, which re-conceptualizes aspects of existing frameworks. An earlier version focused on five components: epistemic aims and epistemic value; structure of knowledge and other epistemic achievements; sources and justification of knowledge; epistemic virtues and vices; and reliable and unreliable processes for achieving epistemic aims. 'Its current version, the AIR model, focuses specifically on epistemic Aims, Ideals and Reliable processes to better understand and explain the nature of knowledge and processes of knowing.'
requirements: Application requires attention to all three components—aims, ideals and reliable processes—rather than beliefs alone
constraints: The article presents the model as described by Chinn et al. (2011, 2014) and does not evaluate it empirically
target_learning_goals: understanding and explaining the nature of knowledge and processes of knowing
examples: Bråten, Muis and Reznitskaya's special-issue article uses the framework's aims and reliable processes constructs to analyze dialogic teaching for deep understanding
key_sources: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180

article_title: Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity
citation: Jo Lunn Brownlee, Leila E. Ferguson & Mary Ryan (2017). Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 242–252. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1333430
title: The AIR framework models epistemic cognition as epistemic Aims, Ideals, and Reliable processes
description: The article describes the AIR framework, developed by Chinn and colleagues from an extensive review of educational and philosophical literature, as a model with three components. Epistemic aims and values cover goals such as developing true beliefs, understanding, or wisdom; epistemic ideals are "criteria or standards that must be met" for judging that aims have been achieved; and reliable processes are strategies, procedures, and activities for achieving epistemic aims, such as argumentation or logical reasoning. The 3R-EC Framework draws specifically on this AIR model to relate epistemic cognition to reflexivity in teaching contexts.
requirements: Epistemic aims, ideals, and reliable processes must be identified within specific teaching and learning contexts
constraints: The article notes that understanding reliable processes includes explicating the conditions in which processes may be considered reliable, a focus it says is not present in other epistemic cognition frameworks
target_learning_goals: Understanding the components of epistemic cognition
Developing justified true beliefs, understanding, and explanations
examples: In the active citizenship example, reliable processes for promoting understanding and explanation include accountable talk, argumentation, scaffolds, epistemic categories, and classroom norms
key_sources: Jo Lunn Brownlee, Leila E. Ferguson & Mary Ryan (2017). Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 242–252. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1333430

article_title: Pragmatic AI in education and its role in mathematics learning and teaching
citation: Gabriel, F., Kennedy, J.P., Marrone, R. & Leonard, S. (2025). Pragmatic AI in education and its role in mathematics learning and teaching. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00315-4
title: Conceptual model of learning mathematics with balancing and reinforcing emotion feedback loops
description: Figure 1 presents "a much simplified and sharply focussed model of the process of learning mathematics" in which the educational goal is socio-emotional learning and mathematics activities are the means. It includes a balancing loop where emotional self-regulation dampens maths anxiety, and reinforcing loops in which success builds perceived control, and perceived control reduces anxiety, which further increases control; the authors note that perceived loss of control can also escalate anxiety. The model marks points of teacher influence and potential AI contribution.
requirements: Students experience both successes and difficulties, since each causes different emotional responses in the larger system
constraints: The authors stress the model is incomplete, omitting factors such as resilience, and is not a complete representation of the process of learning
target_learners: Students of mathematics in schools and universities
examples: The model identifies loops B1, R1 and R2, with AI able to mediate the emotion-related loops at autonomous or supervised points
key_sources: Gabriel, F., Kennedy, J.P., Marrone, R. & Leonard, S. (2025). Pragmatic AI in education and its role in mathematics learning and teaching. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00315-4

article_title: Development and validation of a multidimensional scale for AI tutoring acceptance in higher education
citation: Zhang, Z., Katayoun, M., Tan, L., & Wei, G. (2026). Development and Validation of a Multidimensional Scale for AI Tutoring Acceptance in Higher Education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00431-9
title: AITAQS four-dimensional framework of AI tutoring acceptance quality
description: The framework conceptualizes AI tutoring acceptance quality as a higher-order learner-perceived construct with four constitutive dimensions: "Feedback Quality", "Instructional Effectiveness", "Interaction Experience", and "User Trust". Each dimension captures a distinct domain — pedagogical, functional, interactional, relational — and none is sufficient alone; a system may be easy to use yet instructionally weak. The dimensions are treated as internal content of the construct rather than antecedents, correlates, or distal outcomes, and the construct is explicitly bounded away from satisfaction, motivation, behavioural intention, and academic achievement.
requirements: All four dimensions must be assessed together, since none is sufficient on its own to capture the construct
constraints: The scale is not intended to measure downstream outcomes such as actual academic achievement, learner motivation, behavioral intention, or global satisfaction
target_learning_goals: evaluating the perceived quality of AI tutoring as instructional support (feedback, instruction, interaction, trust)
examples: The 12-item AITAQS operationalizes the framework with three items per dimension, validated with undergraduate students at five universities in Shanxi Province, China.
key_sources: Zhang, Z., Katayoun, M., Tan, L., & Wei, G. (2026). Development and Validation of a Multidimensional Scale for AI Tutoring Acceptance in Higher Education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00431-9

article_title: A systematic review of AI literacy scales
citation: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4
title: Consensus core competencies of AI literacy: technical understanding, societal impact, and AI ethics, with contested creation and evaluation
description: The review synthesizes the scale authors' conceptualizations of AI literacy and finds broad agreement on three foundational competencies: "they emphasize the technical understanding of AI", "the societal impact of AI as a critical component", and "AI ethics is acknowledged as an essential aspect". The authors disagree, however, on whether higher-order skills — creating and critically evaluating AI — belong in AI literacy: MAILS found creation of AI a separate construct while AILQ includes it as core. The review suggests these skills may become core competencies of functional AI literacy in the near future.
requirements: Scale conceptualizations should specify which of the core competencies (technical understanding, societal impact, ethics) and higher-order skills (creation, evaluation) they measure
examples: Ng et al.'s conceptualization proposes four aspects: know and understand, use, evaluate, and understanding of ethical issues related to the use of AI
key_sources: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4

article_title: A systematic review of AI literacy scales
citation: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4
title: AI literacy test: a performance-based scale of 30 multiple-choice items and one sorting item for university students
description: The AI literacy test is a performance-based scale assessing AI-related knowledge through 30 multiple-choice questions with single correct options plus one sorting question, validated with IRT on 1286 university students (mean age 23.6). It draws on Long & Magerko's conceptualization of 17 AI competencies in five areas. The review found limited evidence for content validity and high evidence for structural validity, internal consistency, and construct validity, and calls it the only performance-based scale targeting higher education students.
requirements: Available in German and English, though the English version has not yet been revalidated
constraints: The review notes some questions dealing with atypical use of AI in practice may become obsolete due to developments in AI
target_learners: professionals who encounter AI in their work
target_learning_goals: AI-related knowledge: what AI is, can do, how it works, and how it should be used
examples: Items range from specialized knowledge such as distinguishing supervised from unsupervised learning to recognizing areas of daily life where AI is used
key_sources: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4

article_title: Speech connectedness predicts reading performance three months in advance: a longitudinal experiment
citation: Bárbara Malcorra, Marina Ribeiro, Giovanna Jensen, Tamara Meletti & Natália Bezerra Mota. (2024). Speech connectedness predicts reading performance three months in advance: a longitudinal experiment. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00248-4
title: Scalable AI-based narrative collection and screening application
description: The authors describe a narrative collection application that displays three positive-content images, records children's spoken stories, and "transcribed automatically using an AI-based algorithm." Each narrative is converted into a word recurrence graph analyzed to determine academic development, and results can be plotted "on a normative curve representing the evolution of oral narrative complexity throughout the school years" to compare a child's communication-skill development with peers. The article presents this as "a safe and scalable way to evaluate public educational policies" and "a valuable, language-independent tool for education professionals."
requirements: Automatic AI-based transcription of recorded narratives; normative curves of narrative complexity across school years for comparison
constraints: Graph attributes indicate academic development in children without signs or symptoms of mental distress, per the cited prior work
target_learners: elementary school children in large-scale school settings, e.g., public education systems in Brazil
target_learning_goals: monitoring oral narrative development and reading acquisition on a large scale
examples: The study's own protocol: five 15-minute individual sessions across the 2022 school year, with storytelling tasks and reading performance tasks administered in regular class hours
key_sources: Bárbara Malcorra, Marina Ribeiro, Giovanna Jensen, Tamara Meletti & Natália Bezerra Mota. (2024). Speech connectedness predicts reading performance three months in advance: a longitudinal experiment. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00248-4

article_title: Training the Body: The Potential of AIED to Support Personalized Motor Skills Learning
citation: Olga C. Santos. (2016). Training the Body: The Potential of AIED to Support Personalized Motor Skills Learning. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:730–755. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0103-2
title: Two AIED research directions for personalized motor skills learning: modelling psychomotor interaction and providing personalized psychomotor support
description: The paper organizes its forward-looking agenda in Table 2 around two AIED directions: modelling psychomotor interaction (detecting the learner's physical interaction, modelling expert movements, diagnosing the learner-expert mismatch) and providing personalized psychomotor support (modelling the intervention, deciding the intervention strategy and timing, delivering the intervention). The author argues these "pose familiar AIED problems, but in novel and challenging new forms" and maps them to novel approaches: wearable devices, big data processing, 3D modelling, TORMES methodology, ambient intelligence, and 3D printing.
requirements: Detecting physical interaction requires collecting movement data via wearable sensors and processing data streams with big data mining to extract movement indicators in time for just-in-time feedback.
constraints: The agenda is a proposal for future AIED research, not a tested system.
target_learners: Learners training motor skills, e.g., musical instrument, handwriting, surgery, sports and martial arts, sign language, dance
target_learning_goals: Acquisition and automatization of motor skills through practice
examples: Table 2 maps each research issue to a challenge and a novel approach, e.g., diagnosing mismatch between learner and expert movements is addressed with 3D modelling.
key_sources: Olga C. Santos. (2016). Training the Body: The Potential of AIED to Support Personalized Motor Skills Learning. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:730–755. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0103-2

article_title: The Future Trajectory of the AIED Community: Defining the ‘Knowledge Tradition’ in Critical Times
citation: Rebecca Eynon. (2024). The Future Trajectory of the AIED Community: Defining the ‘Knowledge Tradition’ in Critical Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 105–110. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00354-1
title: AIED as a knowledge tradition characterised by an engineering view of education
description: Eynon characterises AIED as a distinctive knowledge tradition whose work “tends to be broadly characterised by a desire to use technology as the primary way to address perceived problems in education”. She calls this an “engineering view of education” in which AI systems are seen as relatively neutral tools designed to achieve specific learning outcomes, typically tested with randomised control trials and other experimental designs. The underlying belief that appropriately designed technology can make learning more efficient and effective persists even as learning theories and AI techniques have shifted.
requirements: Researchers and systems explicitly framed within this tradition, with technology treated as a designed means to specified learning outcomes
constraints: The author notes it is highly risky for an outsider to capture the tenets of a field and offers the characterisation as a short-essay representation
target_learners: Researchers and practitioners in artificial intelligence in education
target_learning_goals: Understanding the epistemological framing of AIED research and its methods
examples: The author points to the typical use of randomised control trials and other experimental designs to test causal models as the tradition's most typical research methods
key_sources: Rebecca Eynon. (2024). The Future Trajectory of the AIED Community: Defining the ‘Knowledge Tradition’ in Critical Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 105–110. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00354-1

article_title: AI as a Methodology for Supporting Educational Praxis and Teacher Metacognition
citation: Kaśka Porayska-Pomsta. (2016). AI as a Methodology for Supporting Educational Praxis and Teacher Metacognition. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:679–700. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0101-4
title: AI as a methodology: knowledge representation and elicitation as a front-end technology for educators' metacognition in praxis
description: The article proposes viewing AI not only as back-end functionality of educational technology but as a "front-end technology-of-the-mind" through which educators represent, experiment with and compare their practices at fine-grained detail. AI's knowledge representation acts as a surrogate of the world, forcing ontological commitments that expose multiple perspectives, and as a medium of human expression that leaves a trace of one's views over time. Knowledge elicitation engages teachers in externalising tacit knowledge, which the exemplar projects (LeAM, TARDIS) show scaffolds critical reflection on their own practices.
requirements: Educators must make a conscious effort to represent the what, the why and the how of their thinking; methods, tools and common knowledge representation standards are needed so practitioners can generate evidence independently of researchers
constraints: Neither exemplar project evaluated the effectiveness of these methods, so no objective measures can be offered; existing systems such as ASSISTments and Learning Designer lack explicit support for teachers' metacognitive enquiry or fine-grained reflection on momentary decisions
target_learners: teachers, tutors, coaches and other front-line educational practitioners
target_learning_goals: reflective practice and continuous professional development
examples: LeAM used Wizard-of-Oz studies where tutors talked aloud about feedback decisions and selected situational factors, directly implementing a Bayesian network; TARDIS used knowledge elicitation across three stages to build practitioners' self-observation skills culminating in an annotation schema
key_sources: Kaśka Porayska-Pomsta. (2016). AI as a Methodology for Supporting Educational Praxis and Teacher Metacognition. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:679–700. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0101-4

article_title: Preface to the Special Issue on K-12 AI Education
citation: Ning Wang · James Lester. (2023). Preface to the Special Issue on K-12 AI Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00363-0
title: AI4K12 Five Big Ideas in AI as an organizing framework for K-12 AI learning progressions
description: The preface identifies the AI4K12 initiative's Five Big Ideas in AI as an organizing framework for K-12 AI learning progressions, used by Touretsky et al. with a focus on machine learning. The editors write that "Based on the AI4K12 initiative, they discuss how the Five Big Ideas in AI provide an organizing framework for K-12 AI learning progressions with a focus on machine learning." The framework thus structures how machine learning is sequenced for K-12 learners.
requirements: Learning progressions must be developed around the Five Big Ideas, adapted to grade bands
key_sources: Ning Wang · James Lester. (2023). Preface to the Special Issue on K-12 AI Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00363-0

article_title: Twenty Years on: Reflections on “Supporting the Use of External Representations in Problem Solving”…
citation: Richard Cox & Paul Brna. (2015). Twenty Years on: Reflections on "Supporting the Use of External Representations in Problem Solving". Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:193–204. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0054-z
title: AIED systems for external-representation reasoning: switching, synchrony, selection guidance and effective use
description: The article articulates a framework of roles that AIED systems can play in supporting learners who reason with external representations. The roles are: enabling learners to "move easily from one ER to a different one (switching ERs)"; using AI to keep several forms of ER in synchrony as the student works on one of them; guiding the student to the ER form most likely to be of use; and helping the student use an ER effectively. The switchER2 system embodied these roles, providing feedback on errors of omission and commission during representation building.
requirements: Empirical results were needed to determine factors that help learners select, construct and make use of an ER, as the authors state.
constraints: The authors note that systems that intelligently parse and respond to input graphics or support ER switching remain relatively rare.
target_learning_goals: Selecting, constructing, using and switching between external representations during problem solving
examples: switchER2 provided feedback on errors of omission (leaving part of a problem unrepresented) and errors of commission (mistakes in the diagram), plus attention-drawing, hinting and suggesting interventions.
key_sources: Richard Cox & Paul Brna. (2015). Twenty Years on: Reflections on "Supporting the Use of External Representations in Problem Solving". Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:193–204. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0054-z

article_title: AIED—Coming of Age?
citation: Wayne Holmes. (2024). AIED—Coming of Age?. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00352-3
title: AI literacy curricula should give the human dimension of AI equal billing with the technological dimension
description: The author argues AI curricula typically focus on how AI works and how to create it while treating ethics as an afterthought. He argues 'the human dimension of AI should be given equal billing to the technological dimension of AI, and that the two dimensions should be interwoven throughout any course', for example studying emotion detection's impact on people alongside how it works.
requirements: Interweaving must occur throughout any course, not as a separate ethics unit
constraints: Existing curricula such as AI4K12 and MIT's DAILy Workshop currently emphasise the technological dimension
target_learning_goals: Understanding AI's impact on humans and society, including ethical questions of power and political motivation
examples: If a student studies how emotion detection works, they should simultaneously study its potential impact on people, including surveillance in classrooms
key_sources: Wayne Holmes. (2024). AIED—Coming of Age?. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00352-3

article_title: Editor’s Note: Special Issue on AIED in the Global South
citation: Seiji Isotani, Ig Ibert Bittencourt, César A. Collazos, Maria Mercedes T. Rodrigo, Diego Dermeval, Lu Yu. (2024). Editor’s Note: Special Issue on AIED in the Global South. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00445-7
title: AIED Global South special issue with papers available via the journal's Collections link
description: The International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education published a special issue on AIED in the Global South, guest edited by Seiji Isotani, Ig Ibert Bittencourt, César A. Collazos, Maria Mercedes T. Rodrigo, Diego Dermeval, and Lu Yu. The editors state that "The papers are available via the “Collections” link on the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education homepage." The note functions as an access point for the collection rather than describing the papers' content. This element records the collection itself as a citable artifact of research dissemination on AIED in Global South contexts.
requirements: Access to the papers requires navigating to the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education homepage and using its Collections link.
target_learners: researchers and practitioners in artificial intelligence in education, particularly those working in Global South contexts
target_learning_goals: advancing and disseminating research on AI in education in the Global South
examples: The guest editors acknowledge their editorial work on the special issue, listing six editors from institutions in Brazil, Colombia, the Philippines, the USA, and China.
key_sources: Seiji Isotani, Ig Ibert Bittencourt, César A. Collazos, Maria Mercedes T. Rodrigo, Diego Dermeval, Lu Yu. (2024). Editor’s Note: Special Issue on AIED in the Global South. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00445-7

article_title: How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences
citation: Eglington, L.G., Pavlik, P.I. (2022). How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00296-0
title: Adaptive instructional systems should include online mechanisms that adjust for systematic learner-model error
description: The article's central design recommendation: because individual student parameters are frequently unavailable, learner models assuming equal learning rates will make systematic errors, so AIS should "include mechanisms to adjust predictions to account for them". The recommended mechanisms adjust online in a running system using data already present in most AIS — prior correctness and prior learner model predictions — rather than requiring pretests or student clustering.
requirements: Prior correctness outcomes and prior learner model predictions must be logged and available in the running system
constraints: The authors do not claim the suggested model adjustments completely resolve the issue and state experiments are needed to verify tractability in practice
target_learners: students in adaptive instructional systems, especially new students with no prior data
target_learning_goals: efficient practice sequencing and accurate mastery decisions
examples: The authors implemented PEV and student-level proportional decay adjustments that improved model accuracy in all six tested datasets
key_sources: Eglington, L.G., Pavlik, P.I. (2022). How to Optimize Student Learning Using Student Models That Adapt Rapidly to Individual Differences. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00296-0

article_title: Examining AI Use in Educational Contexts: A Scoping Meta-Review and Bibliometric Analysis
citation: Yao Fu, Zhenjie Weng, Jiaxi Wang. (2024). Examining AI Use in Educational Contexts: A Scoping Meta-Review and Bibliometric Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00442-w
title: Thematic map of AIED organized around AI's impact on learning, teaching, and administration
description: The article's thematic analysis of the 126 systematic reviews generated "three major themes and nine subthemes related to AI's impact on learning, teaching, and administration", presented as a thematic map (Fig. 10) capturing relationships between themes and subthemes. The learning theme covers domains of learning, adaptive and personalized learning, and AI-based assessments; the teaching theme covers instructional pedagogies and instructor role recalibration, curriculum design, and teacher professional development; the administration theme covers student performance analysis and support, administrative efficiency, and research priorities. The map serves as the organizing framework for the meta-review's synthesis of the AIED field.
requirements: Built from systematic reviews of AI use in educational contexts, coded inductively via thematic analysis with a codebook and inter-rater agreement of 91.6%
constraints: The authors note selected reviews on AIED emphasize more on the strengths of AI use in education, with limited reviews mentioning negative or neutral impact
target_learners: learners across PreK-12 and higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding the state of AI integration across learning, teaching, and administration in education
key_sources: Yao Fu, Zhenjie Weng, Jiaxi Wang. (2024). Examining AI Use in Educational Contexts: A Scoping Meta-Review and Bibliometric Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00442-w

article_title: Constructive Criticism? Working with (Rather than Against) the AIED Back-Lash
citation: Neil Selwyn. (2023). Constructive Criticism? Working with (Rather than Against) the AIED Back-Lash. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00344-3
title: Approach AIED as a political project and make underpinning values explicit
description: The article contends critics remind the field that "AIED needs to be approached as a political project", since AI in education is entangled with power, disadvantage and marginalisation, and tends toward centralisation of power. Everyone working in AIED should be ready to examine and make explicit the values and ideologies driving debates, reflect on their own positionality, and reject claims that AI is non-political and neutral.
requirements: Explicit examination of the values and ideologies underpinning AIED work
Acknowledgement that claiming neutrality tacitly supports the status quo
constraints: The article notes these political issues rarely drive discussions in technical venues such as IJAIED
target_learners: AIED researchers, developers, and the academic AIED community
target_learning_goals: Political awareness of how educational AI is designed and deployed
examples: The article asks how complicit AIED researchers are prepared to be with commercial marketing of AIED products and their deployment in institutions built around different values
key_sources: Neil Selwyn. (2023). Constructive Criticism? Working with (Rather than Against) the AIED Back-Lash. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00344-3

article_title: Mapping Artificial Intelligence in Education Research: a Network-based Keyword Analysis
citation: Shihui Feng & Nancy Law. (2021). Mapping Artificial Intelligence in Education Research: A Network-based Keyword Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 277–303. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00244-4
title: Dataset of 1830 AIED articles from five major publication sources, 2010–2019
description: The corpus comprises all available research articles from five prominent AIED publication venues: AIEDC, IJAIED, EDM, L@S and ITS conferences/journal, from 2010 to 2019. "In total, there are 1830 articles in the final dataset for analyzing the research topics and their evolution within the AIED field." After keyword standardization (singularization, de-hyphenation, lowercasing, abbreviation avoidance, redundancy removal), the articles yield 3800 distinct keywords used to build the KCNs. Twenty-eight EDM 2010 articles lacking keywords were excluded.
requirements: Articles with listed keywords, and keyword pre-processing to eliminate duplicates
constraints: Excludes articles without listed keywords (e.g., 28 EDM 2010 articles)
target_learning_goals: bibliometric mapping of AIED research topics and their evolution
examples: Sources include AIEDC: 328 full and short papers; EDM: 518 full and short papers; L@S: 396 articles; ITS: 420 articles
key_sources: Shihui Feng & Nancy Law. (2021). Mapping Artificial Intelligence in Education Research: A Network-based Keyword Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 277–303. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00244-4

article_title: Pedagogy, Cognition, Human Rights, and Social Justice
citation: Benedict du Boulay. (2024). Pedagogy, Cognition, Human Rights, and Social Justice. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 34:116–121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00355-0
title: Distinction between aied (the broad commercial and academic field) and AIED (the academic society)
description: The article distinguishes the overall applications of AI in education, designated "aied", from the academic research community embodied in the International Society for Artificial Intelligence in Education, designated "AIED". It argues that criticism conflated the two: the quotation presented to the AIED 2022 panel "conflated "aied" – the broad field of commercial and academic activity – with "AIED" the largely academic activities of the International Society for Artificial Intelligence in Education".
requirements: Users of the distinction must keep the commercial and academic strands of the field separate when attributing blame or credit
constraints: AIED is described as "a relatively small academic society" with limited regulatory power over the commercial market
target_learners: education researchers and policymakers evaluating AI in education
target_learning_goals: accurate attribution of pedagogical and ethical practices in AI in education
examples: The commentary uses the distinction to argue that the implied claim that AIED championed poor pedagogy misdirects criticism aimed at commercial rollout
key_sources: Benedict du Boulay. (2024). Pedagogy, Cognition, Human Rights, and Social Justice. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 34:116–121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00355-0

article_title: Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement
citation: Bhimdiwala, A., Neri, R. C., & Gomez, L. M. (2022). Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00278-8
title: Taxonomy of AIEd design approaches by user involvement, positioning continuous improvement as an expansion
description: Table 1 of the article provides "an overview of current approaches in AIEd with attention to their characteristics and differences in user involvement", organizing the field along a continuum from in-vivo classroom studies (designed in a lab, evaluated via pre/post-tests or student models), through participatory/co-design and design-based research, to continuous improvement. Continuous improvement is characterized by "iterative cycles of inquiry to address user-problem-specific needs" and building "user capacity, ownership, and trust of the system"; the authors state it expands, not replaces, prior approaches.
requirements: Users and their expertise leveraged in design, implementation, and evaluation stages
constraints: The article prints challenges for each approach: in-vivo work lacks user voice and sociocultural factors; co-design cannot capture variation during implementation; DBR is siloed in single settings; continuous improvement is labor/time intensive and hard to sustain
target_learners: K-12 teachers and learners in AIEd-supported classrooms
target_learning_goals: Selecting and organizing design approaches for developing AIEd systems
key_sources: Bhimdiwala, A., Neri, R. C., & Gomez, L. M. (2022). Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00278-8

article_title: Redefining Literature Education: The Role of ChatGPT in Undergraduate Courses
citation: Andrea Roxana Bellot, Mar Gutiérrez-Colón Plana, Katarzyna Agnieszka Baran. (2025). Redefining Literature Education: The Role of ChatGPT in Undergraduate Courses. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00497-3
title: Educators integrating AI into literature teaching should account for AI's Western-centric cultural bias and deliberately include diverse global perspectives
description: The article argues that because ChatGPT's training data comes largely from English-language and Western sources, its outputs may reinforce Western ideas, values and storytelling traditions and limit students' exposure to non-Western literary traditions. It advises that "educators need to be aware of these cultural limitations when integrating AI into the literature classroom and intentionally include diverse, global perspectives." The principle rests on cited reviews of AI bias (Messeri and Crockett; Resnik and Hosseini; Roe) rather than on data from this study.
requirements: Educator awareness of training-data origins of the AI tool in use
Curricular effort to bring in non-Western texts and perspectives alongside AI-generated material
constraints: Evidence for the bias is drawn from prior literature the article cites, not from the study's own data
target_learning_goals: critical engagement with a diverse range of literary texts
examples: The authors propose future studies on AI's cultural biases in students' understanding of different literary traditions and on applying AI to non-Western traditions and non-English literature
key_sources: Andrea Roxana Bellot, Mar Gutiérrez-Colón Plana, Katarzyna Agnieszka Baran. (2025). Redefining Literature Education: The Role of ChatGPT in Undergraduate Courses. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00497-3

article_title: The Birth of IJAIED
citation: John Self. (2015). The Birth of IJAIED. Int J Artif Intell Educ (2016) 26:4–12. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0040-5
title: AIED's two distinctive characteristics: precision in describing vague educational terms, and real-time analysis of learner interaction to adapt it
description: The author describes what he considered the two distinctive characteristics of the AIED field. The first is "the striving towards some kind of precision, derived from AI or computation generally, in the description of otherwise vague terms (such as metacognition, collaboration, even learning itself)" of importance to educationalists. The second is that AIED systems carry out significant real-time analysis of interaction with learners in order to adapt that interaction, responding in ways that are not pre-specified, which the author calls the essential difference between AI programs and general computer programs. The account is the author's own later characterization of the field.
requirements: The account presumes AIED research involves computational or AI-derived descriptions of educational phenomena, as the author frames the field's identity.
constraints: The author states he has no idea whether his 1997 'scope and standards' wording applies to today's field, doubting that it does.
target_learners: learners interacting with AIED (intelligent tutoring) systems
target_learning_goals: adaptation of instructional interaction based on real-time analysis of learner interaction
examples: The author cites his 'scope and standards' webpage for JAIED as his best attempt to pin down the field's AI flavour.

article_title: Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue
citation: Monique Grandbastien, Rosemary Luckin, Riichiro Mizoguchi, Vincent Aleven. (2016). Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0092-6
title: AIED as a mature research community whose history shapes future research directions
description: The preface frames Artificial Intelligence in Education as a research community with a traceable history: the journal's early years "coincided with the coalescing of the research community in Artificial Intelligence and Education", alongside the start of the International Conference on AI in Education (first held in 1987) and the Intelligent Tutoring Systems conference (first held in 1988). The editors emphasize the staying power of featured projects, which "often over many years reached a state of substantial maturity and produced sharable and reusable results, surviving— often capitalizing on— rapid changes in the underlying technologies used". They hold that a research field needs a sense of its history, and that this history influences current exploration of new ways technology can impact education.
requirements: A research field needs a sense of its history, which the anniversary issue provides
constraints: The editors explicitly declined to synthesize general trends and lessons from the set of articles, judging that too daunting a scholarly task
target_learners: researchers new to the AIED field
target_learning_goals: understanding the historical development, milestones and future directions of AI in education as a research field
examples: The journal was titled the Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education from 1989 to 1995, renamed in 1995 with volume numbers continuing in sequence; John Self's article on the birth of IJAIED in this issue records the Society's history

article_title: An AI-Based System for Formative and Summative Assessment in Data Science Courses
citation: Pierpaolo Vittorini, Stefano Menini, Sara Tonelli. (2021). An AI-Based System for Formative and Summative Assessment in Data Science Courses. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00230-2
title: AI-based automated grading system for R assignments with NLP comment classification
description: A tool that automatically grades assignments consisting of R commands and Italian-language comments. It performs static code analysis to extract commands, outputs, and comments, then uses a Python NLP server (fastText embeddings, 300 dimensions) and an R classification engine (CARET/E1071 SVM) to judge comment correctness. The distance calculator module combines missing commands, differing outputs, and comment correctness into a final grade converted to the Italian 0–31 scale.
requirements: Requires a professor-provided correct solution with commands, outputs, and gold standard comments
Requires a set of sentence pairs from previous exams to tune the classifier for each specific topic
constraints: Developed and tested only for statistical analysis of health data in R with Italian-language comments
Can return false pass/fail outcomes, especially near the pass threshold
target_learners: Master's degree students in Medicine and Surgery, Prevention Sciences, and Nursing Sciences
target_learning_goals: Statistical analysis of health data in R
Correct interpretation of statistical test results
examples: Used for formative assessment during homework and for summative assessment in exams, with exams randomly corrected manually or through the automated system

article_title: Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue, Part 2
citation: Lane, H. C., McCalla, G., Looi, C., & Bull, S. (2016). Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue, Part 2: The Next 25 Years: How Advanced Interactive Learning Technologies will Change the World. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 539–543. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0109-9
title: AIED as an interdisciplinary research community combining AI with education and the learning sciences
description: The editorial characterizes AIED as a fundamentally interdisciplinary field in which the journal's creation 25 years ago corresponded with the formal emergence of the field itself. It states that "A good AIED research project was seen to be one in which both the technological frontier and the pedagogical frontier were being challenged in novel and interesting ways." The framework holds that AIED research draws on AI together with data mining, personalization, human-computer interaction, the semantic web, recommender systems, multi-agent systems, information visualization, computational linguistics, and simulation, and uses social-science methods for theoretical insight and empirical validation. It is used in the preface to frame the special issue's forward-looking papers.
requirements: AIED research must engage both the technological frontier and the pedagogical frontier
target_learners: learners supported by advanced learning technologies across the AIED field
target_learning_goals: interdisciplinary design of advanced learning technologies
examples: The preface cites the wide diversity of IJAIED papers spanning affective computing, collaborative learning, educational games, and immersive technologies as evidence of the field's interdisciplinary scope.

citation: Lane, H. C., McCalla, G., Looi, C., & Bull, S. (2016). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 539–543. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0109-9
title: Three core characteristics of AIED research with a learner-first core value
description: The editorial identifies three key characteristics that have emerged in AIED research over its first 25 years: "(i) aggressiveness in asking hard and deep questions; (ii) openness to an eclectic range of ideas; and (iii) a learner-first perspective." It further states that the most defining core value of AIED research is placing the learner at the focus of the field's work, driven by important problems for which AI and other perspectives create advanced learning technologies that "care" for the learner (Self 1998). This framework frames the special issue's vision papers.
requirements: Research problems must be important to learners, with AI used in conjunction with other disciplines to create technologies that care for the learner
target_learning_goals: design of learning technologies centered on learner needs
examples: The preface invokes Self's (1998) call for systems that care for the learner as the field's defining core value.

article_title: K-12 Education in the Age of AI: A Call to Action for K-12 AI Literacy
citation: Ning Wang · James Lester. (2023). K-12 Education in the Age of AI: A Call to Action for K-12 AI Literacy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00358-x
title: AI literacy defined as the ability to readily engage with AI by leveraging AI tools, systems, and frameworks to effectively and ethically solve problems in a wide range of sociocultural contexts
description: The article defines AI literacy as "the ability to readily engage with AI by leveraging AI tools, systems, and frameworks to effectively and ethically solve problems in a wide range of sociocultural contexts." It frames this as a component-based definition with three key parts: understanding AI capabilities, utilizing AI for problem solving, and applying AI in sociocultural contexts. This definition serves as the organizing framework for the article's call for K-12 AI literacy curricula and research.
requirements: AI literacy education should not require all students to engage with advanced concepts or mathematical foundations of AI
constraints: The definition is a conceptual framing by the authors, not an empirically tested construct
key_sources: Ning Wang · James Lester. (2023). K-12 Education in the Age of AI: A Call to Action for K-12 AI Literacy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00358-x

article_title: K-12 Education in the Age of AI: A Call to Action for K-12 AI Literacy
citation: Ning Wang · James Lester. (2023). K-12 Education in the Age of AI: A Call to Action for K-12 AI Literacy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00358-x
title: Introduce AI literacy across all grade bands, with learning progressions from elementary examples of AI in everyday software through middle-school technical concepts to universal high-school AI education with elective advanced coursework
description: The article recommends that "K-12 education should introduce all K-12 students to the fundamentals of AI as well as provide an on-ramp to advanced AI education through a series of learning progressions." Beginning in elementary grades, students develop AI literacy through examples of AI in widely used software and social issues in AI; middle school focuses on age-appropriate AI technical concepts; high school AI education should be universal, with advanced coursework available for students pursuing AI careers.
requirements: A series of learning progressions that provide an on-ramp to advanced AI education for students who wish to pursue technical careers in AI
constraints: AI literacy does not entail requiring all students to engage with advanced concepts or mathematical foundations of AI
examples: Elementary students begin developing AI literacy through examples of how AI manifests in widely used software and being introduced to social issues in AI

title: AI literacy should require all students to develop a solid understanding of AI capabilities, their limits, their application, and the ethical considerations bearing on their use
description: The article states that "AI literacy, however, should require all students to develop a solid understanding of AI capabilities, their limits, their application, and the ethical considerations bearing on their use." This principle positions AI literacy as universal education for all students, not just those pursuing R&D AI careers, and explicitly excludes requiring advanced concepts or mathematical foundations of AI for every learner.
requirements: Curricula designed to support all students, not just those who will pursue R&D AI careers
constraints: AI literacy does not entail requiring all students to engage with advanced concepts or mathematical foundations of AI

article_title: Adaptive and Intelligent Web-based Educational Systems
citation: Peter Brusilovsky, Christoph Peylo. (2003). Adaptive and Intelligent Web-based Educational Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197315v1
title: Five groups of AIWBES technologies classified by their field of origin
description: The article organizes the variety of adaptive and intelligent Web-based educational systems into five technology groups: adaptive hypermedia, adaptive information filtering, intelligent class monitoring, intelligent collaborative learning, and intelligent tutoring. It states that "An earlier review (Brusilovsky, 1999) identified five major technologies used in AIWBES" and that these technologies have roots in Adaptive Hypermedia and Intelligent Tutoring Systems, with newer Web-inspired technologies subdivided into the other three groups. Table 1 lists technologies and sample systems for each group.
requirements: The taxonomy requires distinguishing technologies by their field of origin, as the article groups them according to whether they originated in Adaptive Hypermedia, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, Information Retrieval, CSCL, or Machine Learning/Data Mining.
constraints: The article notes that at the time of the earlier review, the lack of examples of Web-inspired technologies did not allow further classification, and that the borders between intelligent and non-intelligent systems are not clear-cut.
target_learners: students and teachers in Web-based education
target_learning_goals: understanding the landscape of adaptive and intelligent educational technologies

article_title: Adaptive and Intelligent Web-based Educational Systems
citation: Peter Brusilovsky, Christoph Peylo. (2003). Adaptive and Intelligent Web-based Educational Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197315v1
title: Three major AI-Ed development paradigms: AI-CAI, ITS, and AIWBES
description: The article distinguishes three major development paradigms in AI-Ed since 1970, compared in Table 2 across time span, goal, context, learning material, technologies, system completeness, and platform. The AI-CAI paradigm (1970s) aimed to replace primitive CAI in transferring knowledge; the ITS paradigm (1980s-1990s) aimed to "Support problem solving"; and the AIWBES paradigm (late 1990s-2000s) aims at "Comprehensive support" in a context of independent self-study with rich on-line learning material.
requirements: The paradigm comparison requires analyzing systems across multiple dimensions including goal, application context, learning material, technologies, system completeness, and platform.
constraints: The article states that "If we analyze the variety of adaptive and intelligent educational systems developed since the birth of the AI-Ed field in 1970, we can distinguish at least three major development paradigms."
target_learning_goals: understanding the historical development of AI in Education paradigms

article_title: ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem
citation: Nye, B. D. (2016). ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0098-8
title: AI-controlled experimental sampling: multi-armed bandit and adaptive design optimization methods for running education experiments at scale
description: The article frames the experimental process itself as an efficient search problem that AI can play a major role in. It notes that educational data mining research "has already started looking at dynamically assigning subjects to different learning conditions based on multi-armed bandit models," that cognitive model-comparison experiments have used adaptive design optimization, and that adaptive sampling is common in medical research. In the long term, automated experimentation may compare the effectiveness of different services or content modules by randomly selecting them from open repositories, allowing direct comparison of theories and exploration of interactions between theoretically-grounded constructs.
requirements: Methods must output interpretable statistics grounded in theories and concepts comparable across systems; efficient-search problems in AIED experiments need fundamental framing and solution
constraints: Trace- and path-based models are often too granular to generalize and may tailor instruction so tightly to specific problems that theoretical implications are hard to infer; model-comparison approaches require pre-existing hypothesized models; integrating expert knowledge with statistically-sampled information (e.g., as Bayesian priors) remains an open problem
target_learners: researchers studying learning on large-scale online platforms
target_learning_goals: estimating relative importance and boundary conditions of learning principles across contexts
examples: Multi-armed bandit models treat each treatment condition like a slot machine with different payout distributions, e.g., student learning gains

article_title: Navigating Ethical Benefits and Risks as AIED Comes of Age
citation: Ken Koedinger. (2024). Navigating Ethical Benefits and Risks as AIED Comes of Age. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00350-5
title: Frame AI in education as replacing unsupported homework with deliberate practice at the edge of competence, not as replacing teachers
description: This principle holds that the productive framing of AI in education is not replacing teachers but replacing doing homework without any available support. It works by using AI to automate assessment of where a student's competence is, select an appropriate next task, and provide feedback and instruction just when needed, grounding this in the author's statement that "A key principle of effective learning and expertise development is deliberate practice." The article uses this framing to answer criticism that AI aims to replace human workers, arguing instead that active learning with a guide on the side can be scaled with a technology component.
requirements: Assessment of where the student's competence is, so that tasks can be selected at the edge of that competence
Feedback and reactive instruction so students can learn from failure
constraints: The author frames this as a framing and argument, not a tested result; the article reports no data on it
target_learners: K-12 and college students doing homework assignments
target_learning_goals: Deliberate practice at the edge of competence
Active learning with just-in-time feedback and instruction
examples: The author describes homework assignments becoming more interactive than a passive piece of paper, with interaction data informing teachers and parents about progress and needs
