citation: Filippo Sciarrone, Carla Limongelli, Olga C. Santos, Marco Temperini. (2021). Preface to the Special Issue AI4MOOCs: Artificial Intelligence, Sensoring, Modeling and Assessment for MOOCs. A Step Beyond. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00255-1
title: AI4MOOCs special issue of IJAIED (three peer-reviewed papers on AI for MOOC learning processes)
description: The special issue "AI4MOOCs: Artificial Intelligence, Sensoring, Modeling and Assessment for MOOCs. A Step Beyond" was designed to explore recent developments and applications of Artificial Intelligence in MOOCs, "ranging over different aspects of MOOCs learning processes and management, including Artificial Intelligence and Embodied Learning, Deep Learning, and Adaptive Learning". The call attracted fifteen papers, of which three were accepted after at least two rounds of reviews. The editors state the issue shows AIED in MOOCs as an emerging research field and addresses assessment in science courses, human simulated responses and drop-out prediction.
requirements: Papers addressing AI aspects related to MOOCs learning processes, reviewed by experienced IJAIED reviewers
target_learning_goals: student modeling, personalization/adaptation of learning activities, and assessment and prediction of individual learning outcomes in MOOCs
examples: The three accepted papers: an AI-based formative and summative assessment system for data science MOOCs; deep-learning natural language generation to support MOOC learners; and deep-learning prediction of student purchasing behaviour in MOOCs.

article_title: A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education
citation: Kaśka Porayska‑Pomsta. (2024). A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 73–83. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00346-1
title: AIED as a human-centred sub-discipline of AI whose technologies aim to strengthen, not substitute, human capacities
description: The article characterises AIED as a distinctive sub-field of AI: rather than compensating for or bypassing user abilities, its technologies are interventions "to enhance and change human thinking and behaviour" and "to emphasise, help train and strengthen the capacities with which we are biologically endowed." Because of this, fidelity to human cognition is central: AIED applications must support learning "in cognitively congruent, efficacious and socio-culturally desirable ways." The theory explains why AIED cannot be evaluated only by task performance but must consider user experience, context, culture, affect and motivation as integral to learning, and why the field is intertwined with wider social, cultural, economic and political contexts.
requirements: Fidelity of AIED applications to human cognition and behaviour, so support is cognitively congruent and socio-culturally desirable
constraints: The account is the author's characterisation of the field's ambitions and does not report empirical tests
target_learners: all learners addressed by AIED technologies
target_learning_goals: strengthening learners' innate cognitive and behavioural capacities
examples: The article cites the field's early adoption of participatory, user-centred design and action research integrated with engineering as reflecting this human-centred perspective

article_title: Transforming EFL Teaching with AI: A Systematic Review of Empirical Studies
citation: Arnab Kundu, Tripti Bej. (2024). Transforming school EFL teaching with AI: A Systematic Review of Empirical Studies. Research Square preprint. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4805086/v1
title: Eight-category functional taxonomy of AI technologies in school EFL teaching
description: The review categorizes the AI tools used across the 22 studies into eight functionality-based classes: NLP, chatbots and virtual tutors, gamification, adaptive learning platforms, speech and pronunciation tools, content creation and management tools, AI-powered assessment tools, and VR/AR. It reports that "NLP appears as a popular and e cient AI technology in EFL education, providing tailored, interactive experiences for students," supporting grammar correction, pronunciation feedback, and vocabulary building. The taxonomy organizes which tool types serve which language-learning aspects.
requirements: Tools must be matched to specific EFL learning aspects and functionalities as the review's categorization does
constraints: The review's data are concentrated in Southeast Asian school contexts rather than global
target_learning_goals: EFL vocabulary, grammar, speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills
examples: Google Assistant, ChatGPT, and Google Dialogflow are classified under NLP or chatbots/virtual tutors; Jungle Animals Game under gamification
key_sources: Arnab Kundu, Tripti Bej. (2024). Transforming school EFL teaching with AI: A Systematic Review of Empirical Studies. Research Square preprint. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4805086/v1

article_title: Transforming EFL Teaching with AI: A Systematic Review of Empirical Studies
citation: Arnab Kundu, Tripti Bej. (2024). Transforming school EFL teaching with AI: A Systematic Review of Empirical Studies. Research Square preprint. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4805086/v1
title: Four-component conceptual framework for AI-enabled language learning: technology, pedagogy, linguistic, and learning components
description: The review proposes a conceptual framework (Fig. 1) examining AI-enabled language learning at the intersection of four components. As the article states, "It examines AI-enabled language learning by examining the intersection of technology, pedagogy, linguistic, and learning components." The technology component covers AI tools' capabilities, limitations, and data privacy; the language component covers phonetics, morphology, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics; the learning component covers learner interaction with AI tools and outcomes. The framework structures the review's analysis of the included studies.
requirements: Combining insights across all four components to develop effective AI-enabled EFL learning solutions
target_learning_goals: EFL language acquisition across linguistic subsystems
examples: Tables 2 and 3 of the review classify each included study by technology component, linguistic component, and pedagogical component
key_sources: Arnab Kundu, Tripti Bej. (2024). Transforming school EFL teaching with AI: A Systematic Review of Empirical Studies. Research Square preprint. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4805086/v1

article_title: Transforming EFL Teaching with AI: A Systematic Review of Empirical Studies
citation: Arnab Kundu, Tripti Bej. (2024). Transforming school EFL teaching with AI: A Systematic Review of Empirical Studies. Research Square preprint. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4805086/v1
title: Eight pedagogical approaches evolving in AI-enabled school EFL teaching
description: The review identifies eight pedagogical approaches that evolved in AI-enabled EFL teaching: "personalized learning, blended learning, gami cation, project-based learning, collaborative learning, inquiry-based learning, competency-based learning, and task-based language teaching (Table 5)." Each is instantiated with AI-specific practices, e.g., adaptive difficulty levels in gamification, AI-driven research assistants in project-based learning, and AI-driven role-playing and simulation environments in task-based language teaching. The pattern describes how AI capabilities support these approaches in school EFL classrooms.
requirements: Teachers need pedagogical expertise in using AI tools for approaches such as collaborative learning with ChatGPT
constraints: The review notes these approaches shift practice from traditional teacher-centered methods toward student-centered, adaptive pedagogy
target_learning_goals: Communicative competence and engagement in EFL learning
examples: Table 5 lists nuanced practices such as learning analytics to monitor progress and adjust instruction under personalized learning

article_title: An Educational System for Learning Search Algorithms and Automatically Assessing Student Performance
citation: Grivokostopoulou, F., Perikos, I., & Hatzilygeroudis, I. (2016). An Educational System for Learning Search Algorithms and Automatically Assessing Student Performance. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0116-x
title: AITS: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Teaching Search Algorithms
description: AITS is an intelligent tutoring system developed to help students learn and tutors teach search algorithms, a fundamental AI topic. It consists of six main units: Student Interface, Tutor Interface, Automatic Assessment, Test Generator, Learning Analytics, and Domain Knowledge & Learning Objects. Learning is achieved through a wide range of learning activities including theory, examples, visualizations, interactive exercises, and tests. The system adapts test difficulty to individual students using a rule-based expert system.
requirements: Requires domain knowledge structured as subject-topic-concept hierarchy with learning objects
Requires an automatic assessment mechanism integrated into the system
constraints: Designed for AI curriculum topics, particularly search algorithms (blind and heuristic)
target_learners: Undergraduate computer science students in an AI course
target_learning_goals: Understanding and applying search algorithms (blind and heuristic)
examples: Used in real class conditions in the AI course at the University of Patras department

article_title: Designing Game-Based Learning for High School Artificial Intelligence Education
citation: Leitner, M., Greenwald, E., Wang, N., Montgomery, R., & Merchant, C. (2023). Designing Game-Based Learning for High School Artificial Intelligence Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 33, 384–398. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00327-w
title: Three-category taxonomy of K-12 AI learners: AI Consumers, AI Operators, and AI Developers
description: The article organizes high school AI learners into three categories drawn from the K-12 AI education research community: "those who will be AI end-users in their everyday lives and careers, those who will need to implement AI algorithms, and those who will research and advance AI algorithms." AI Consumers (all students) need to learn what is possible with AI and its impact; AI Operators need to understand algorithm varieties, strengths and weaknesses to make informed decisions; AI Developers need deep algorithmic understanding including estimating space and time complexity. ARIN-561's design targets appropriate takeaways for each category.
requirements: Designs must provide takeaways appropriate to each learner category, as the article's game does by exposing algorithm tradeoffs for Operators and step-by-step algorithm mechanics for Developers
target_learning_goals: selecting appropriate AI algorithms for tasks
understanding how search algorithms work in detail
examples: ARIN-561 gives Consumers a glimpse of how task-specific information enables more efficient approaches, Operators comparisons of algorithms on memory usage and runtime, and Developers introductory ways to calculate time and space complexity

citation: Sarah K. Howard, Jo Tondeur. (2023). Higher education teachers' digital competencies for a blended future. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10211-6
title: AI digital competencies framework extending DigCompEdu and revising P21
description: A concept paper by Tsz Kit Ng, Ka Lok Leung, Jiahong Su, Chi Wui Ng, and Kai Wah Chu addresses AI digital competencies for higher education teachers. It explores opportunities and challenges of employing AI systems for teaching, learning, and assessment, and "complemented the DigCompEdu framework and revised the P21's framework to accommodate AI technologies in order to provide an overview of the necessary AI digital competencies." The framework aligns AI-specific competencies with generic digital competence frameworks.

title: AI-in-PCK stage framework mapping AI adoption trajectory
description: The AI-in-PCK stage framework maps the trajectory of AI adoption, illustrating how teachers' concerns and practices evolve from initial exploration and experimentation to strategic integration and ongoing learning while responding to classroom realities and student feedback. It applies the Concern-Based Adoption Model as a conceptual lens, capturing shifts from self-oriented considerations to task-related and impact-driven concerns across seven concerns-based stages.

description: AICO_edu (AI Competence Educators) is a self-report questionnaire developed to assess teachers' perceived AI competence. "Each dimension was captured through six to eight items (TH: 8; LF: 6; IP: 8; AT: 8; TL: 8; PF: 7), which were answered on a five-point Likert scale." It focuses on perceived AI competence rather than general digital competence, and is intended for use by school leaders and educators in teacher training.

article_title: AI-assisted data extraction for systematic reviews in education
citation: Schroeder, N. L., Jaldi, C. D., Zhang, S., & Yamoah, K. (2025). AI-Assisted Data Extraction for Systematic Reviews in Education. https://osf.io/nraxf/?view_only=879654690be249cc9237525ed7f86ec2
title: AIDE: AI-Assisted Data Extraction tool (R package and web version)
description: AIDE is a free, open-source tool for human-in-the-loop LLM-based data extraction in systematic reviews, available as an R package (https://github.com/noah-schroeder/AIDE) and a web version (https://noah-schroeder.github.io/AIDE-Web/). It sends a PDF's full text and coding-form prompts to an LLM API, auto-populates responses in a user interface, shows the LLM's reasoning and source page, and requires the user to press Record after reviewing or editing each answer. The web version stores API keys in sessionStorage and uses structured JSON response parsing.
requirements: Requires an API key from Google AI Studio, Mistral AI, or Open Router, or a local model via Ollama
constraints: The R-based pilot version runs locally and should not be hosted on an external-facing website because API keys would not be secure
target_learning_goals: Accurate, efficient data extraction for research synthesis
examples: The analysis page presents the PDF on the left and LLM answers, source text, and record buttons on the right

citation: Darmawansah, D., Hwang, G.-J., Lin, C.-J., & Febiyani, F. (2025). An artificial intelligence-supported GFCA learning model to enhance L2 students' role-play performance, English speaking and interaction mindset. Education Tech Research Dev (2025) 73:1451–1479. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10453-6
title: The AI-GFCA learning model: four scaffolding stages (generalization, formulation, correction, appreciation) supported by an AI speaking app
description: The AI-GFCA learning model is a four-stage scaffolding framework for technology-supported role-play in L2 learning. As the article states, "the study employed generalization, formulation, correction, and appreciation strategies by integrating AI speaking learning by proposing the AI-GFCA learning model to scaffold students' performance in role-play tasks, English speaking skills, L2 errors, and interaction mindset." Generalization clarifies task goals and success criteria from O'Donnell and Topping's objectives-and-criteria approach; formulation builds collaborative readiness; correction conducts intergroup corrective feedback with internal and external monitoring; appreciation fosters positive appraisal to reduce tension. The model was tested against AI-supported conventional learning lacking the pedagogical theory.
requirements: An AI-based speaking learning app providing real-time speaking feedback
A platform for sharing role-play recordings and conducting intergroup corrective feedback
Scaffolding stages delivered in sequence across role-play tasks
constraints: The study used semi-scripted role-plays combining closed role-play practice with open role-play flexibility
Tested with first-year university EFL students at A1-B1 CEFR levels in Taiwan
target_learners: First-year university EFL students with A1-B1 CEFR English proficiency
examples: Students performed a tourist-information-center role-play (T1) and a traditional-English-restaurant role-play (T2), with intergroup corrective feedback exchanged through a formative assessment platform

article_title: AI-enhanced legal pedagogy: a case study of generative AI integration in property law courses
citation: Haifang Liu. (2026). AI-enhanced legal pedagogy: a case study of generative AI integration in property law courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10698-9
title: AI-Enhanced Legal Pedagogy Framework integrating constructivism, TAM, and TPACK
description: The article proposes an integrated framework in which constructivist learning theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, and the TPACK framework are not parallel layers but "constrain and inform one another at specific theoretical junctures". Constructivism governed the staged 16-week intervention design via the ZPD trajectory from other-regulated to self-regulated performance; TAM governed the measurement framework and SEM analysis; TPACK governed instructor preparation and implementation consistency. Cross-constraints include TPACK's Technological Content Knowledge shaping TAM's Perceived Usefulness, and TAM's Behavioral Intention feeding back into constructivist engagement.
requirements: Instructors need integrated technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge, which the article says requires deliberate professional development rather than developing automatically from any single domain
constraints: The framework is offered as a preliminary conceptual contribution subject to refinement through replication across diverse legal education settings
target_learners: third-year undergraduate law students in civil-law higher education
target_learning_goals: discipline-specific critical evaluation of AI-generated legal analysis
examples: The 16-week intervention shifted GenAI roles from information provider (Weeks 1–4) to Socratic dialogue partner (Weeks 5–8), writing assistant and feedback provider (Weeks 9–12), and strategic planning assistant and opposing counsel simulator (Weeks 13–16)

citation: Donghwa Lee, Hong-hyeon Kim, Seok-Hyun Sung. (2023). Development research on an AI English learning support system to facilitate learner-generated-context-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10172-2
title: AI web-based English learning support system with four functional modules
description: The developed system is an AI web-based English learning support system usable in web and mobile environments. "The system has four functional modules: (1) learning content management, (2) learning management, (3) personalized English language learning, and (4) content curation." The content management module uses a passage wizard (OCR plus Google Cloud Natural Language API, translation and text-to-speech APIs) and a video wizard that time-stamps and repeats YouTube dialogue segments; the personalized module generates practice and test questions from learner-selected content with speech recognition feedback.
requirements: Built on open-source AI community APIs including natural language analysis, translation, text-to-speech, and optical character recognition
constraints: The content curation module's functionality was limited because insufficient data existed for it to learn users' preferences, and it has no content recommendation function
examples: Haru photographed school textbook pages and the passage wizard converted them into vocabulary lists with Korean translations and voice data

citation: Pozdniakov, S., Brazil, J., Banihashem, S. K., Noroozi, O., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., & Khosravi, H. (2026). AI assistance in peer feedback provision: Pedagogically sound, but minimally adopted. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105591
title: Design AI assistance in peer feedback platforms to preserve student autonomy by positioning AI as a guide rather than a replacement for student voice
description: The article recommends that AI assistance in peer feedback should act as a guide, offering advice students can adopt, revise, or ignore, rather than replacing the student voice. This human-led approach scaffolds students' evaluative judgment and feedback literacy in real-time. The article states that "Rather than replacing the student voice, AI-A acts as a guide, offering advice students can adopt, revise, or ignore."
requirements: Students must first write peer feedback before receiving AI assistance (human-led model)
constraints: Grades did not depend on whether students incorporated suggestions from AI assistance
examples: Students could submit their initial peer review without making any changes; AI-A was provided for every peer feedback instance before submission but revision was not required.

article_title: AI for Clinical Competency Assessment: Scoping Review of Methods and Applications.
citation: Zhang Wenjia (Stella), Daniels Benjamin B, Mita Carol, Nguyen Hoang, Duong David B. (2026). AI for Clinical Competency Assessment: Scoping Review of Methods and Applications. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/92826
title: Three-category taxonomy of AI-SSP intended use: deliberate-practice educational tools, hybrid training-plus-assessment tools, and explicit assessment systems
description: The review organizes the 20 unique AI-SSP systems by their primary intended use into three categories: educational tools for deliberate practice, hybrid training-and-assessment tools, and systems focused explicitly on assessment. It reports that "The largest group, 9 (45%) of 20 systems, framed AI-SSPs primarily as deliberate practice or educational tools", that six (30%) were hybrid training and assessment tools combining SP interaction with structured feedback and scoring, and that the remaining five systems focused explicitly on assessment. The taxonomy shows that even systems with scoring components have most often been introduced as formative learning environments, with an increasing subset emphasizing automated scoring and performance analytics.
requirements: Systems must produce some form of quantitative score to be classified in this review, even when assessment is not the primary purpose
constraints: Classification reflects the studies' stated primary purposes as charted by the reviewers, not independent functional testing of the systems
target_learners: nursing, pharmacy, physiotherapy, and physician assistant trainees
examples: USC Standard Patient, CureFun, SOPHIE, AMTES, Turing Interactive Case Learning, 2-Sigma, VR-AI-ECS, and MedSimAI were among the named platforms mapped in Table 2
key_sources: Zhang Wenjia (Stella), Daniels Benjamin B, Mita Carol, Nguyen Hoang, Duong David B. (2026). AI for Clinical Competency Assessment: Scoping Review of Methods and Applications. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/92826

article_title: AI for Clinical Competency Assessment: Scoping Review of Methods and Applications.
citation: Zhang Wenjia (Stella), Daniels Benjamin B, Mita Carol, Nguyen Hoang, Duong David B. (2026). AI for Clinical Competency Assessment: Scoping Review of Methods and Applications. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/92826
title: Deploy AI-SSPs to pursue scalable, more standardized clinical competency assessment, but treat validity and reliability across diverse learner groups as unproven
description: The review positions AI-SSPs as emerging infrastructures for clinical competency assessment rather than merely educational simulations, motivated by the resource intensity of OSCEs and documented evaluator-related bias, including halo and contrast effects, "with examiner stringency alone accounting for up to 29% of score variation in some OSCE settings". It concludes AI-SSPs could make assessment more scalable and potentially more standardized, while cautioning that more evidence is needed on validity and reliability across diverse learner or practitioner groups before large-scale deployment.
requirements: Quantitative scoring with comparability within a learner over time or across learners, as the review's own eligibility definition requires
constraints: The review states more evidence is still needed to determine whether AI-SSPs achieve validity and reliability across diverse learner or practitioner groups; the evidence base is concentrated in high-income countries
target_learners: nursing, pharmacy, and other health professions trainees
examples: The review's included studies spanned single-arm pilots, randomized controlled trials such as Brugge et al and Haut et al's SOPHIE trial, and a multisite quasi-experimental evaluation of MedSimAI with 410 unique learners across 3 US institutions

article_title: Artificial intelligence generated virtual patients in health professions education: a scoping review.
citation: Fang Eric Kin Meng, Boon Yuru, Ho Jin Yang, Tey Natasha, Low Matthew Jian Wen. (2026). Artificial intelligence generated virtual patients in health professions education: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10028-w
title: Use AI-generated virtual patients as an adjunct to, not a replacement for, real-life clinical experiences given current limitations
description: Based on reported limitations in clinical accuracy, conversational flow and nonverbal cues, the review recommends positioning AI-generated virtual patients alongside rather than in place of authentic clinical experience. The review reports that "learners suggested that AI generated virtual patients would be best used as an adjunct in the curriculum without replacing real life history taking experiences". This positions the technology as supplementing, not substituting, live patient contact while limitations persist.
requirements: Availability of real-life clinical experiences to which the virtual patient work complements
constraints: Grounded in learner suggestions within included studies; the review also notes physical examination training showed significant limitations and poorer performance versus human standardized patients in one study.
target_learners: Health professions students learning communication and clinical reasoning skills
examples: One included study of breast examination training with screen-based virtual patients found poorer performance and higher anxiety compared with human standardized patients despite higher satisfaction.

article_title: Use of artificial intelligence-enhanced virtual patients in educational approaches to medical interview training: a systematic review.
citation: Gilbert Valentin, Philip Pierre, Llorca Pierre-Michel, Samalin Ludovic. (2026). Use of artificial intelligence–enhanced virtual patients in educational approaches to medical interview training: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08804-9
title: Five-domain outcome taxonomy for AI-VP interview training research
description: The review organizes its synthesis of heterogeneous AI-VP studies around five inductively identified outcome domains. As the authors state, domains "included communication and interviewing performance, empathy and interpersonal skills, learner self-efficacy and engagement, feedback and evaluation mechanisms, and transfer to actual practice." This taxonomy structures the narrative synthesis, maps each included study's outcomes, and highlights where evidence is strongest (interview structure, questioning, feedback-supported empathy) and weakest (transfer to real practice). It serves as an organizing framework for future AI-VP evaluation studies.
requirements: Studies must report outcomes in terms that can be mapped to the five domains for cross-study comparison
constraints: Domains were identified inductively by two review authors from the eleven included studies; the quantitative synthesis was not performed due to marked heterogeneity between studies
examples: The review's narrative synthesis sections are organized under these five outcome-domain headings

article_title: Artificial intelligence augmented tutoring vs expert instruction on learning simulated general surgical skills: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Hanna Fouad et al. (2026). Artificial intelligence augmented tutoring vs expert instruction on learning simulated general surgical skills: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09606-9
title: AI-augmented tutoring defined by two integration models: AI-substitutive and AI-augmentative
description: The review defines an AI tutoring (intelligent tutoring) system as "an educational platform driven by computer algorithms" that integrates performance assessment with personalized, goal-oriented feedback to guide surgical skill acquisition in a training context. It distinguishes two integration models: an AI-substitutive model, in which AI delivers feedback in place of an expert, and an AI-augmentative model, in which AI-derived performance data is used by or supplements a human expert educator. The framework organizes the review's PICOS comparator structure and its framing of AI as augmentation rather than replacement.
requirements: The system must analyze trainee performance data from a simulator, generate automated personalized feedback, and be designed to guide skill acquisition in a training context
constraints: Systems using AI only for skill classification, phase recognition, or intraoperative guidance without a tutoring/feedback component were excluded from the meta-analysis

article_title: AI-Powered Problem- and Case-based Learning in Medical and Dental Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
citation: Wei H, Dai Y, Yuan K, Li KY, Hung KF, Hu EM, Lee AHC, Chang JWW, Zhang C, Li X. (2025). AI-Powered Problem- and Case-based Learning in Medical and Dental Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. International Dental Journal. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.identj.2025.100858
title: Taxonomy of AI technologies applied to PBL/CBL in medical and dental education
description: The review organises AI-powered PBL/CBL implementations into intelligent tutoring systems (COMET, CC-Cruiser, LearnGuide, ChatGPT), intelligent information access systems, AI-generated decision-making systems such as Watson for Oncology, and generative and immersive technologies. It describes ITSs as "computer-based educational platforms which utilise AI and adaptive technologies to mimic human tutoring by providing real-time, customised and interactive feedback to learners". Generative models including LLMs, GANs, VAEs and diffusion models create synthetic multimodal cases, while VR, AR and haptic systems support virtual patients for practising communication, diagnosis, decision-making and treatment.
requirements: AI tools must be integrated into PBL/CBL with an appropriate comparison group for effectiveness evaluation
constraints: The review notes drawbacks such as slow annotation processes and presence of irrelevant information for information-access systems, and high hardware requirements for some platforms
examples: COMET generated tutoring hints via Bayesian networks displayed in a discussion pane; METEOR reduced problem-scenario development time from 1 month to 4-5 hours per person using the UMLS Semantic Network

citation: Wei H, Dai Y, Yuan K, Li KY, Hung KF, Hu EM, Lee AHC, Chang JWW, Zhang C, Li X. (2025). AI-Powered Problem- and Case-based Learning in Medical and Dental Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. International Dental Journal. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.identj.2025.100858
title: Combine AI technology with skilled facilitators who verify AI-provided information and give personalised feedback
description: The review concludes that AI-powered PBL/CBL works best when human facilitators remain central: tutors educate students on using the AI system, verify the accuracy of AI-provided information, and provide personalised feedback. The authors state that "AI technology should be combined with skilled facilitators" to realise the full potential of the approach, positioning facilitators as accuracy checkers and feedback providers rather than replacements.
requirements: Facilitators must be trained to educate students on utilization of the AI-powered system/platform and verify the accuracy of the information provided by AI
constraints: The article frames this as a discussion-level recommendation, not a manipulated or tested condition
target_learning_goals: safe and accurate use of AI tools in PBL/CBL
examples: In the included RCTs, tutors/instructors verified AI-provided information and provided personalised feedback alongside ChatGPT-generated questions, simulated patients and interviews

article_title: Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges
citation: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661
title: Ainsworth's three functions of multiple representations: complementary information, limiting interpretation, constructing deeper understanding
description: The review describes Ainsworth's theory of multiple representations as an account of how external representations such as AR visualizations support learning. Multiple representations can support learning in three ways: by allowing for complementary information or processes, by limiting the room for interpretation, and by providing the opportunity for constructing deeper understanding. The review illustrates the first function with light intensity distribution graphs paired with an image of a diffraction pattern, and the second with a video of motion alongside a corresponding real-time graph. It warns that "If not introduced carefully, learning with multiple representations may result in cognitive overload."
requirements: Multiple representations must be introduced carefully; otherwise learning with them may result in cognitive overload.
constraints: The theory is presented as relevant for reasoning about learning with visualizations generally, including AR-based learning.
target_learners: physics learners working with AR overlays combining graphs, images, videos and 3D objects
target_learning_goals: interpreting multiple coordinated representations of physical phenomena, e.g., motion videos with real-time graphs
examples: The review's example: a video of the motion potentially prevents the interpretation of a graph as the image of motion, illustrating the interpretation-limiting function.

article_title: Air Reading: A Randomized Evaluation of a Virtual Tutoring Model in Louisiana and Texas Schools
citation: Neitzel, A.J., Storey, N., & Wang, X. (2026). Air Reading: A randomized evaluation of a virtual tutoring model in Louisiana and Texas schools. Center for Research and Reform in Education, Johns Hopkins University. https://education.jhu.edu/crre
title: Air Reading: assessment-driven virtual tutoring program for foundational reading skills in grades K-8
description: Air Reading is an assessment-driven virtual tutoring program designed to improve students' foundational reading skills in Kindergarten through 8th grade. Students receive live virtual instruction from consistent tutors in small groups of up to four, in 30-minute sessions four times each week. The program is grounded in the Science of Reading, uses one-on-one diagnostics to inform group placement and bi-weekly progress assessments, and delivers explicit, skill-based instruction from a systematic reading curriculum by paid tutors meeting qualification requirements (bachelor's degree, K-3 teaching experience, state certification). Sessions are tracked on the program's proprietary platform.
requirements: Tutors must meet minimum requirements including a bachelor's degree, prior teaching experience at the K-3 level, and state certification
constraints: Logistical barriers, such as session cancellations due to school-level conflicts, remain a challenge
target_learners: Students in grades 1-4 performing below grade level in reading (Tier 2 or Tier 3 intervention)
target_learning_goals: Foundational reading and early literacy skills
examples: In the evaluation, eligible students flagged for Tier 2 or Tier 3 intervention were randomized to tutoring during the school day or business-as-usual instruction, with group sizes ranging from 1:1 to 1:4
key_sources: Neitzel, A.J., Storey, N., & Wang, X. (2026). Air Reading: A randomized evaluation of a virtual tutoring model in Louisiana and Texas schools. Center for Research and Reform in Education, Johns Hopkins University. https://education.jhu.edu/crre

description: A CD-distributed computer application that functioned on the internet and allowed students to study English outside class in a self-directed manner. Students chose difficulty levels from 1 (least difficult) to 20 (most difficult). It was the experimental treatment in the SSRUIC study.

article_title: Simulation- and AI-supported technical troubleshooting training for biomedical device technology students in intensive care equipment education.
citation: İnan Onur; Akyüz Ali. (2026). Simulation- and AI-supported technical troubleshooting training for biomedical device technology students in intensive care equipment education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09952-8
title: Position AI feedback as a supervised cognitive scaffold, not an authority
description: The article states the AI layer's purpose "is not to act as an authority that directly provides the correct answer, but rather to serve as a cognitive scaffold that encourages systematic thinking grounded in technical findings." Students formulate an initial hypothesis before consulting AI feedback, the model is guided to avoid absolute statements, and the instructor remains responsible for guiding and contextualizing the activity.
requirements: Students formulate an initial technical fault hypothesis before using AI feedback; instructor supervision and contextualization

These features collectively enable repeatable, controllable simulated scenarios for communication training.

Affective computing module for emotional cue identification

citation: Jia Chuanlin; Qi Lulu. (2026). Digital Standardized Patients: Conceptual Framework for Generative AI–Empowered Medical Education. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/91050
title: Kolb's experiential learning cycle and deliberate practice as theoretical foundations for AI-SP design
description: The article grounds AI-SP design in two core pedagogical theories. Kolb's experiential learning theory comprises "4 stages: concrete experience → reflective observation → abstract conceptualization → active experimentation," which AI-SPs can fully embody through simulated consultations, generated feedback reports, internalization of feedback, and improved strategies in subsequent scenarios. Ericsson's deliberate practice theory emphasizes "clear goals, immediate feedback, sufficient repetition, and gradually increasing difficulty," which AI-SPs support through selectable skill goals, consistent feedback, unlimited scenario repetition, and teacher-adjusted complexity.
requirements: System-generated formative assessment reports for reflective observation
Teacher adjustment of scenario parameters for gradually increasing difficulty
constraints: The cycle can be repeated at low cost and high frequency, which is difficult to achieve with traditional SPs
examples: Learners can select specific communication skill goals such as 'practice empathic expression' or 'practice bad news disclosure'

The personality and communication stance modulation module integrates the Big Five personality model and Satir communication stance theory. The safety guardrail and content filtering module ensures responses "do not contain inappropriate content, do not provide medical advice beyond the SP role."

description: The article proposes an integrated 'future learning' framework explaining how AI-SPs integrate into medical education practice. title: AI-assisted PBL-CBL combined teaching model integrating pre-class preparation, in-class simulation, and post-class consolidation phases
description: The article describes a teaching model that "combines AI-assisted PBL with CBL," structured across three phases: pre-class preparation with AI-supported preview tasks, in-class implementation where "teacher-verified simulated patients are generated based on PHN cases" and students conduct simulated diagnosis and treatment in groups with AI evaluation, and post-class summary where groups present learning outcomes reviewed by teachers. Clinical skills in diagnosis and treatment planning

title: Complementary-mechanism account of AI-assisted PBL-CBL effectiveness: AI standardization plus PBL inquiry plus CBL immersion rationalizes cognitive resource distribution
description: The article proposes an explanatory account of why the combined model works: "The core advantage of this teaching model lies in the complementary advantages of AI technology combined with PBL-CBL teaching methods." AI provides "standardized clinical simulation scenarios and real-time accurate feedback," PBL contributes problem-oriented inquiry and thinking training, and CBL contributes immersive teaching with real cases. The article further states that the integration "rationalizes cognitive resource distribution during learning," cutting down invalid cognitive interference and concentrating learning resources on absorption of key clinical competencies, while AI-generated virtual patient scenarios allow repeated clinical training that strengthens clinical pattern recognition without the restrictions of limited teaching resources.
requirements: Requires integration of problem-based inquiry, authentic clinical cases, and personalized AI guidance working in synergy rather than isolation
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation offered in the discussion; the study tested the combined model as a package, so the contribution of each mechanism was not separately manipulated.

target_learning_goals: Efficient transformation and flexible application of professional knowledge

The knowledge graph contains "89 core knowledge points, 356 weighted relations" built from a standard textbook and validated by five senior pathology professors. The AI assistant comprises a knowledge-aware recommendation module, a pathology-adapted BERT QA module, and a dynamic path planning module; the AI feeds students' high-frequency errors back to the graph to adjust relation weights.

Personalized learning and understanding of complex pathological mechanisms

article_title: AI-Assisted Formative Assessment in Clinical Education: From Algorithms to Agency.
citation: Quang Thanh Nguyen, Thuy Minh Ha, Tina Mai. (2026). AI-Assisted Formative Assessment in Clinical Education: From Algorithms to Agency. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/93710
title: AI-assisted formative assessment is the intentional use of AI tools to generate, organize, and support interpretation of performance information for learning rather than grading
description: The article defines AI-assisted formative assessment as "the intentional use of AI tools to generate, organize, and support interpretation of performance information for the purpose of improving learning rather than grading". It distinguishes this from automated feedback, automated scoring, and AI-generated comments, arguing that AI output becomes formative only when learners and educators use it to understand performance and decide what to do next. The framework positions AI-assisted formative assessment as a strategy for developing feedback agency rather than simply increasing feedback volume.
requirements: Learners and educators must interpret AI-generated information critically and translate it into focused subsequent learning actions
constraints: Not synonymous with automated feedback, automated scoring, or AI-generated comments
target_learners: Clinical educators, assessment leaders, curriculum committees, faculty developers, and institutional leaders in health professions education
target_learning_goals: Improving learning through formative assessment rather than grading

article_title: AI-Assisted Formative Assessment in Clinical Education: From Algorithms to Agency.
citation: Quang Thanh Nguyen, Thuy Minh Ha, Tina Mai. (2026). AI-Assisted Formative Assessment in Clinical Education: From Algorithms to Agency. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/93710
title: AI tools in formative assessment fall into three categories: analytic/predictive, generative/LLM, and agentic systems
description: The article proposes a taxonomy distinguishing three types of AI relevant to formative assessment. Analytic or predictive systems "process learner performance data to generate scores, classifications, patterns, or recommendations" but generally lack open-ended interactivity. Generative AI and LLMs "produce text, dialogue, explanations, simulated patient responses, or feedback narratives" with educational value lying in interactivity. Emerging agentic AI systems "may pursue goals across multiple steps, select tasks, call external tools, retrieve resources, and personalize learning pathways with greater autonomy" but remain prospective in medical education.
requirements: Different AI systems create different educational possibilities, risks, and responsibilities and should not be treated as interchangeable
constraints: Agentic AI systems remain more prospective than established in medical education
target_learners: Clinical educators and curriculum committees in health professions education
target_learning_goals: Selecting appropriate AI tool types for formative assessment purposes
key_sources: Quang Thanh Nguyen, Thuy Minh Ha, Tina Mai. (2026). AI-Assisted Formative Assessment in Clinical Education: From Algorithms to Agency. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/93710

article_title: Susceptibility of Assessment Types to AI-Generated Content in Digital Health and Health Information Management Education: Quasi-Experimental Pilot Study.
citation: Wani Tafheem Ahmad, Liem Michael, Prasad Natasha, Robinson Kerin, Nexhip Abbey, Tassos Melanie, Gjorgioski Stephanie, Khan Urooj Raza, Boyd James, Riley Merilyn. (2026). Susceptibility of Assessment Types to AI-Generated Content in Digital Health and Health Information Management Education: Quasi-Experimental Pilot Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/82988
title: Task-category taxonomy of assessment susceptibility to AI-generated content
description: The article organizes its findings by grouping DIGHIM assessments into broader task categories to locate where generative AI shows relative strengths versus persistent limitations. As printed, "performance grouped into broader task categories (objective, reflective, descriptive analytical, scenario-based analytical, communication/referencing, and programming)". The taxonomy ranks objective and reflective tasks as most susceptible, descriptive and communication tasks as moderately susceptible, and programming and scenario-based coding as least susceptible, providing a design lens for deciding which assessment formats need redesign.
requirements: Assessments must be classifiable into the article's task categories by their dominant cognitive and technical demands
constraints: Derived from a small pilot sample in one institution's DIGHIM programs; the authors state findings are preliminary and larger-scale studies are needed
target_learners: undergraduate and master's-level digital health and health information management students
examples: The pilot marked 33 submissions (18 AI-generated, 15 student) across the five assessment types and synthesized scores into the six task categories
key_sources: Wani Tafheem Ahmad, Liem Michael, Prasad Natasha, Robinson Kerin, Nexhip Abbey, Tassos Melanie, Gjorgioski Stephanie, Khan Urooj Raza, Boyd James, Riley Merilyn. (2026). Susceptibility of Assessment Types to AI-Generated Content in Digital Health and Health Information Management Education: Quasi-Experimental Pilot Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/82988

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Chatbots as Virtual Patients in Dental Education: A Constructivist Approach to Classroom Implementation.
citation: B. Jones, A. Desu, and C. D. F. Honig. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Chatbots as Virtual Patients in Dental Education: A Constructivist Approach to Classroom Implementation. European Journal of Dental Education 30(2): 447–456. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.13135
title: Five-element AI role-play structure mirroring the dental clinic workflow
description: The role-play activity was "structured into multiple elements, mirroring the typical workflow in the dental hospitals teaching clinics": patient history taking with the AI-simulated patient, information synthesis into a preliminary assessment, diagnostic planning with a rationale for each test, supervisor interaction with an AI-simulated clinical supervisor, and test retrieval and interpretation with embedded multimedia such as radiographs, photographs, and videos of cold and percussion tests. This sequence let students experience the initial patient interaction through to diagnostic planning and supervisor consultation, adding realism and contextual interpretation of clinical data.
requirements: Two interconnected chatbots with prompt engineering limiting patient information per reply
Retrievable diagnostic tests embedded in the supervisor chat interface
constraints: The identification of the neuropathic pain root cause was outside the scope of practice for the students in the designed scenario
target_learners: oral health students transitioning from simulation to patient care and final-year students consolidating skills
examples: Students documented concise summaries of findings and test interpretations in a Google document used by the educator to inform tutorial discussion
key_sources: B. Jones, A. Desu, and C. D. F. Honig. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Chatbots as Virtual Patients in Dental Education: A Constructivist Approach to Classroom Implementation. European Journal of Dental Education 30(2): 447–456. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.13135

article_title: Voices of Innovation: Reflective Report on Integrating Artificial Intelligence-Simulated Mental Health Patient Scenarios Into Undergraduate Nursing Education in the United Arab Emirates.
citation: Amina Ahmad, Janisha Kavumpurath, Raheesa Kader, Muna Altamimi, Monia El Hajj, Fatma Refaat Ahmed Ahmed, Muhammad Arsyad Subu, Taliaa Yafei, Hind Rashed Ali, Idil Saleh, Nabeel Al-Yateem. (2026). Voices of Innovation: Reflective Report on Integrating Artificial Intelligence–Simulated Mental Health Patient Scenarios Into Undergraduate Nursing Education in the United Arab Emirates. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/78161
title: AI-integrated objective structured clinical examination with three simulation-based stations plus care-plan writing
description: An OSCE structure embedding the AI-simulated patient across stations: a live voice interaction assessing therapeutic communication with a structured rubric, a viva voce on clinical presentation and management, and a voice-only guided full mental status examination using behavioral cues such as "fidgets with hands" and "avoids eye contact". Students received 5 minutes of preparation per randomly assigned case and 30 minutes afterward to record findings and formulate a nursing care plan. The authors present this as ensuring assessment consistency.
requirements: A pool of prepared case scenarios containing presenting problem, history, diagnosis, medications, and risk factors
constraints: The current implementation included no formal validation, reliability testing, or outcome comparisons
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students in mental health practicum
examples: Figure 1 presents a flowchart of the AI-integrated OSCE structure in mental health nursing education
key_sources: Amina Ahmad, Janisha Kavumpurath, Raheesa Kader, Muna Altamimi, Monia El Hajj, Fatma Refaat Ahmed Ahmed, Muhammad Arsyad Subu, Taliaa Yafei, Hind Rashed Ali, Idil Saleh, Nabeel Al-Yateem. (2026). Voices of Innovation: Reflective Report on Integrating Artificial Intelligence–Simulated Mental Health Patient Scenarios Into Undergraduate Nursing Education in the United Arab Emirates. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/78161

article_title: Development and validation of a competency-based evaluation framework for clinical medical trainees in the era of artificial intelligence: a mixed-methods study in China.
citation: Li Feiyan, Zhao Haojing, Huang Qiqiao, Zhang Chunhui, Chen Geyu. (2026). Development and validation of a competency-based evaluation framework for clinical medical trainees in the era of artificial intelligence: a mixed-methods study in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08779-7
title: Three operational subdomains for AI-related clinical competency
description: The framework operationalizes AI-related competency in practice-facing terms rather than abstract digital literacy, organized around three interrelated subdomains: interaction with AI-enabled decision-support tools, critical appraisal of AI-generated outputs, and risk awareness and governance. Interaction descriptors require trainees to 'formulate clinically meaningful prompts or queries, specify relevant patient parameters, and interpret AI outputs within real-world clinical workflows.' Appraisal descriptors emphasize cross-checking AI recommendations against guidelines and patient data; risk-governance descriptors address algorithmic bias, hallucinated content, privacy, and human accountability.
requirements: Items must be drafted in a tool-agnostic manner to ensure applicability across different AI platforms
constraints: No model-specific technical validation was conducted as part of this educational study; item content was aligned with contemporary guidance on safe AI use in healthcare
target_learning_goals: safe and accountable AI-assisted clinical reasoning
examples: The risk-governance subdomain explicitly requires maintaining human accountability for all diagnostic and therapeutic decisions, and descriptors cover over-reliance on automated suggestions and limitations of training datasets
key_sources: Li Feiyan, Zhao Haojing, Huang Qiqiao, Zhang Chunhui, Chen Geyu. (2026). Development and validation of a competency-based evaluation framework for clinical medical trainees in the era of artificial intelligence: a mixed-methods study in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08779-7

article_title: Artificial Intelligence in Couple and Family Therapy: Introduction of the AI Competencies.
citation: Hertlein Katherine M. and Springer Paul. (2026). Artificial Intelligence in Couple and Family Therapy: Introduction of the AI Competencies. Journal of Marital and Family Therapy. https://doi.org/10.1111/jmft.70121
title: AICMFT: a six-domain competency framework for AI in couple and family therapy
description: The article introduces the AI Competencies for Couple and Family Therapy (AICMFT), a framework of "six proposed domains for AI Competencies for CMFT" that provide "a comprehensive skill set for therapists seeking to responsibly engage with AI in relational contexts." Specific competencies under each domain are worded using Bloom's taxonomy and mapped in a logic model to three informing frameworks.
requirements: Each domain must reflect the three informing frameworks — the condensed CMFT competencies, the interprofessional TBH competencies, and the AI competencies for healthcare professionals — and specific competencies are worded using Bloom's taxonomy so they can be observed.
constraints: The authors state the competencies are versioned, not final: "We fully expect and invite as AI changes, so, too, will these competencies," and they invite scholars, practitioners, and trainees to revise, refine, and adapt them.
target_learning_goals: responsibly integrate AI into relational therapy
apply systemic thinking to AI-mediated practice
key_sources: Hertlein Katherine M. and Springer Paul. (2026). Artificial Intelligence in Couple and Family Therapy: Introduction of the AI Competencies. Journal of Marital and Family Therapy. https://doi.org/10.1111/jmft.70121

article_title: Trustworthy AI-Augmented Objective Structured Clinical Examinations in Nursing Education: Taiwan-Japan Viewpoint on 5 AI Roles, Governance, and Cross-Border Implementation.
citation: Kubota Kazumi, Nishimura Ayako, Seto Ryoma, Li Liu. (2026). Trustworthy AI-Augmented Objective Structured Clinical Examinations in Nursing Education: Taiwan-Japan Viewpoint on 5 AI Roles, Governance, and Cross-Border Implementation. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/87830
title: Governance artifact set: machine-readable rubrics, persona cards, versioned prompts, and explainability-by-design logs
description: The article specifies a set of concrete governance artifacts that operationalize its pillars: machine-readable rubrics seeded with blueprint metadata, standardized patient persona cards specifying "history, affect, cultural considerations, difficulty, and response boundaries," versioned prompt libraries, evidence-linking rules with uncertainty flags, and audit-ready logs. Explainability-by-design logging links every AI suggestion to specific utterances or events so raters can verify, edit, or reject suggestions, with transparency artifacts such as model cards and data sheets documenting intended use, data sources, and limitations.
requirements: Institutions should prefer tools that publish model cards and data sheets, expose APIs for log capture, support role-based access, and report subgroup performance
constraints: Data governance and procurement constraints such as contractual access to logs, model cards, and version histories may limit transparency when third-party vendors are involved
target_learners: faculty raters and standardized patient trainers
target_learning_goals: auditable, fair AI-assisted scoring and feedback in OSCEs
examples: A worked example shows the system highlighting a time-stamped utterance mapped to a rubric item which the rater verifies and accepts, while another suggestion is rejected with the reason no evidence, and both actions are logged for audit
key_sources: Kubota Kazumi, Nishimura Ayako, Seto Ryoma, Li Liu. (2026). Trustworthy AI-Augmented Objective Structured Clinical Examinations in Nursing Education: Taiwan-Japan Viewpoint on 5 AI Roles, Governance, and Cross-Border Implementation. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/87830

article_title: Application of DeepSeek-based AI teaching assistant in teaching anesthesiology theories.
citation: Fan Hao, Du Wenqin, Yan Jia, Jiang Hong. (2025). Application of DeepSeek-based AI teaching assistant in teaching anesthesiology theories. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08494-9
title: Add AI teaching-assistant support on top of, not instead of, traditional lectures and clinical rotations
description: The article's design keeps the traditional instructional core — lectures, Q&A, and supervised clinical rotations — and layers AI capabilities over it: "The experimental group received traditional teaching (same as the control group) plus 24/7 online support, personalized learning plans, and real-time performance analysis from the AI assistant." This additive arrangement lets AI provide individualized pacing and feedback while faculty retain responsibility for core instruction.
requirements: Instructors with standardized teaching content and assessment criteria so the comparison isolates the AI's contribution
constraints: The trial design could not identify which AI component (24/7 support, personalized plans, etc.) produced the gains; the authors call for trials comparing passive versus active AI arms
target_learners: Residents in specialty rotations outside the taught field
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of dense theoretical knowledge within limited curriculum time
examples: Four senior lecturers were randomly assigned to both groups and received uniform training on the study protocol, standardized teaching content, and assessment criteria
key_sources: Fan Hao, Du Wenqin, Yan Jia, Jiang Hong. (2025). Application of DeepSeek-based AI teaching assistant in teaching anesthesiology theories. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08494-9

article_title: Application of DeepSeek-based AI teaching assistant in teaching anesthesiology theories.
citation: Fan Hao, Du Wenqin, Yan Jia, Jiang Hong. (2025). Application of DeepSeek-based AI teaching assistant in teaching anesthesiology theories. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08494-9
title: AI teaching assistants intended to support durable learning should incorporate spaced repetition and active recall
description: Because the AI system improved immediate scores but not 1-month retention, the authors conclude that "the AI system—designed primarily for 24/7 online support and targeted practice—lacked core evidence-based strategies for durable learning, such as spaced repetition and active recall, which are critical for long-term retention." They recommend building these retention-oriented features into AI teaching assistants and providing post-course reinforcement.
requirements: Spaced-repetition and active-recall functionality plus post-course reinforcement to support long-term consolidation
constraints: Evidence for this recommendation comes from a null retention result in a sample powered only to detect large effects, so the principle rests on the authors' interpretation rather than a tested AI-with-repetition arm
target_learning_goals: Long-term knowledge retention after course completion
examples: The article recommends future trials with larger samples and longer observation periods, and suggests embedding incentive mechanisms and gamification to lift interest and satisfaction
key_sources: Fan Hao, Du Wenqin, Yan Jia, Jiang Hong. (2025). Application of DeepSeek-based AI teaching assistant in teaching anesthesiology theories. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08494-9

article_title: Towards scalable psychological first aid training: an autoethnographic exploration of the potential of large language models in simulation-based learning.
citation: Figueroa Rodrigo A., Bernales Margarita, Hoeboer Chris M., Olff Miranda. (2026). Towards scalable psychological first aid training: an autoethnographic exploration of the potential of large language models in simulation-based learning. European Journal of Psychotraumatology. https://doi.org/10.1080/20008066.2026.2616976
title: Integrate AI-based PFA training with human oversight and psychological safeguards to protect trainee well-being
description: Because controlled simulations can create false self-efficacy and intense traumatic content can trigger distress, the article holds that AI-based training must be embedded in instructional design with human supervision. It states that "Implementing psychological safeguards – such as explicit opt-out options, immediate access to emotional support, and structured debriefing sessions – is essential to protect trainees' well-being". Privacy risks on external AI platforms require strictly fictional scenarios, anonymised information, and secure, privacy-compliant platforms.
requirements: Explicit opt-out options, immediate access to emotional support, and structured debriefing sessions
Strictly fictional scenarios, anonymised information, and secure privacy-compliant platforms
constraints: Intense traumatic content can trigger psychological distress without adequate human supervision
target_learners: Trainees practising PFA with simulated traumatic content
target_learning_goals: Safe acquisition of PFA helping skills without overconfidence or psychological harm
examples: The article cites simulation literature showing high-fidelity simulation can lead to overconfidence in medical students
key_sources: Figueroa Rodrigo A., Bernales Margarita, Hoeboer Chris M., Olff Miranda. (2026). Towards scalable psychological first aid training: an autoethnographic exploration of the potential of large language models in simulation-based learning. European Journal of Psychotraumatology. https://doi.org/10.1080/20008066.2026.2616976

article_title: Comparative performance evaluation of ChatGPT-4 Omni and Gemini Advanced in the Turkish Dentistry Specialization Exam.
citation: Dundar Sari Makbule Buse, Sezer Berkant. (2026). Comparative performance evaluation of ChatGPT-4 Omni and Gemini Advanced in the Turkish Dentistry Specialization Exam. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08621-0
title: Use AI chatbots in dental education as supervised supplementary tools, not replacements for formal education and professional expertise
description: The article recommends that advanced LLMs, given their high but discipline-variable accuracy on exam questions, serve as supplementary tools for exam preparation and knowledge reinforcement while clinical judgment remains central. It states that "LLMs hold promise as supportive resources, they should be regarded as complementary to—rather than replacements for—formal education and professional expertise." This follows directly from the observed higher error rates in clinically oriented subjects.
requirements: Cautious and supervised use, particularly in clinically oriented subjects requiring complex reasoning and contextual interpretation
constraints: Higher error rates in clinically oriented subjects limit suitability as replacements for human decision-making despite comparable scores
target_learners: dental students preparing for specialization exams
examples: The study benchmarked both chatbots on 1,504 DUS questions and found overall accuracies above 80%, supporting their use for rapid, structured information retrieval in exam preparation.
key_sources: Dundar Sari Makbule Buse, Sezer Berkant. (2026). Comparative performance evaluation of ChatGPT-4 Omni and Gemini Advanced in the Turkish Dentistry Specialization Exam. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08621-0

article_title: An Alternative Approach in Anatomy Education: Design of a Learning Environment Based on Artificial Intelligence-Supported Virtual Manipulatives and Investigation of Its Effectiveness.
citation: Bolatli, G., S. Birisci, and Z. Bolatli. 2026. An Alternative Approach in Anatomy Education: Design of a Learning Environment Based on Artificial Intelligence‐Supported Virtual Manipulatives and Investigation of Its Effectiveness. Clinical Anatomy 39, no. 1: 30–44. https://doi.org/10.1002/ca.70008
title: Web-based anatomy learning module integrating 3D virtual manipulatives with a ChatGPT sidebar
description: A web system integrating seven 3D virtual manipulation models (e.g., medulla spinalis, cortex cerebri, cranial nerves) sourced from AnatomyTOOL and Sketchfab under Creative Commons licensing, with ChatGPT 3.5 accessed via the Sider Chrome plug-in. The article states it was "integrated into a web system (https://sanalanatomi.my.canva.site/anatomisanal) to provide access to virtual learning materials featuring two main components: 3D virtual manipulatives on the left and ChatGPT interactions on the right." The SML+AI group asked questions and received immediate AI-generated feedback; the SML group used the same site without the sidebar.
requirements: Computer-based access for each student; a user manual and instructional videos were distributed to ensure platform proficiency
Sample keywords and prompt guidance embedded on the web page
constraints: Virtual manipulations were limited to the AnatomyTOOL and Sketchfab web-based interfaces
ChatGPT 3.5 free version was used, trained on data only up to September 2021
target_learners: first-year junior nursing students studying the nervous system
target_learning_goals: understanding nervous system anatomy structure and function
examples: SML+AI students used the ChatGPT sidebar to ask questions during 4 h of practical sessions; SML and C groups had the instructor answer questions directly
