article_title: The reliability of answers from four different AI chatbots on periodontology theoretical exam questions: an evaluation in dental education.
citation: Koyuncuoglu Cenker Zeki, Selcuker Ahmet Hamdi, Ozyilmaz Erdem. (2025). The reliability of answers from four different AI chatbots on periodontology theoretical exam questions: an evaluation in dental education. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-025-07387-z
title: Use AI chatbots in dental education only as a supervised, complementary tool with critical evaluation of their answers
description: The article recommends that AI chatbots support rather than replace expert instruction in dental education. It states "AI chatbots should be considered as a complementary tool for students" and that "their use should be carefully guided and complemented by clinical experience, critical appraisal of information sources, and academic oversight". It further recommends chatbots develop information verification mechanisms so students can use them in accordance with academic standards.
requirements: Academic oversight and guidance of chatbot use by educators
Students' critical appraisal of AI-provided information and its literature support
Complementation by clinical observations and practical work
constraints: The study found accuracy rates of only about 56–75% on periodontology exam questions, underscoring the need for critical evaluation before adoption
examples: The study evaluated 125 closed-ended periodontology exam questions from 2018–2023 exams, posed twice with a one-month interval to ChatGPT-4o mini, ChatGPT-4o, Gemini Advance, and CoPilot Pro with cleared histories and fresh email addresses
key_sources: Koyuncuoglu Cenker Zeki, Selcuker Ahmet Hamdi, Ozyilmaz Erdem. (2025). The reliability of answers from four different AI chatbots on periodontology theoretical exam questions: an evaluation in dental education. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-025-07387-z

article_title: Mechanism of an integrated PBL-KAP-AI spiral health education model for breast cancer patients.
citation: Li Heyu, Lu Yang, Tian Yang, Zhou Li, Wang Danna. (2025). Mechanism of an integrated PBL-KAP-AI spiral health education model for breast cancer patients. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1687956
title: AI platform for personalized health education delivery
description: The AI platform is the core technological component of the intervention, responsible for personalized task delivery, emotion and state recognition, behavior prediction, and dynamic feedback. It integrates initial surveys, behavioral data from mobile applications and wearables, emotional data from facial expression analysis and speech recognition, and physiological data. It uses "collaborative filtering and natural language processing algorithms" to deliver personalized tasks such as micro-courses, case simulations, and group discussions, and employs reinforcement learning to adjust delivery frequency, content, and intensity.
requirements: Requires multi-source data: initial surveys, behavioral, emotional, and physiological data
Requires mobile applications and wearable devices for real-time data collection
constraints: The specific algorithmic details and the assurance of fairness have not been thoroughly explored, per the authors
target_learners: female breast cancer patients in hospital care
examples: The platform pushed micro-lectures, case simulations, group discussions, and real-time feedback questionnaires during the 3-month trial.
key_sources: Li Heyu, Lu Yang, Tian Yang, Zhou Li, Wang Danna. (2025). Mechanism of an integrated PBL-KAP-AI spiral health education model for breast cancer patients. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1687956

article_title: Comparing ChatGPT and DeepSeek for Assessment of Multiple-Choice Questions in Orthopedic Medical Education: Cross-Sectional Study.
citation: Anusitviwat C, Suwannaphisit S, Bvonpanttarananon J, Tangtrakulwanich B. (2025). Comparing ChatGPT and DeepSeek for Assessment of Multiple-Choice Questions in Orthopedic Medical Education: Cross-Sectional Study. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/75607
title: Use AI assessment tools under human supervision as a complement to, not a replacement for, expert clinical judgment
description: The article argues that although LLMs offer efficiency and consistency in evaluating MCQs, "human supervision is necessary to guarantee that AI functions as a helpful tool rather than a substitute for professional judgment", particularly in high-stakes educational or health care settings. Educators are advised to carefully combine AI with conventional teaching techniques and evaluation procedures to maintain academic integrity while students continue refining their decision-making abilities.
requirements: Human oversight of AI-generated assessments
Combination of AI tools with conventional teaching and evaluation techniques
constraints: The study's cross-sectional design captured LLM performance at a single point in time, and models are continually updated, so performance may vary over time; explanation quality was not formally assessed
target_learning_goals: Maintaining valid, fair summative assessment of clinical reasoning while preserving academic integrity
examples: Both models showed residual variability despite strong reliability, and errors clustered in complex domains such as complications, pediatrics and anomalies, and pelvic and spine injuries.
key_sources: Anusitviwat C, Suwannaphisit S, Bvonpanttarananon J, Tangtrakulwanich B. (2025). Comparing ChatGPT and DeepSeek for Assessment of Multiple-Choice Questions in Orthopedic Medical Education: Cross-Sectional Study. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/75607

article_title: A research roadmap for AI opportunities in student assessment for medical education.
citation: Rezaei-Zadeh M, Cerbin-Koczorowska M. (2025). A research roadmap for AI opportunities in student assessment for medical education. BMC Medical Education 25:1653. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08078-7
title: Pair AI assessment adoption with algorithmic transparency, bias-free training data, and human oversight
description: The article argues that AI-driven assessment innovations must be governed responsibly, not merely deployed effectively. It calls for "establishing clear policies for algorithmic transparency, ensuring datasets used for model training are free from bias, and providing robust mechanisms for human oversight and appeal". These safeguards are framed as fundamental to fairness and trustworthiness, particularly where AI touches high-stakes summative assessment.
requirements: Institutional policies for algorithmic transparency, unbiased training datasets, and human oversight and appeal mechanisms must exist before AI is used in high-stakes assessment
constraints: The article frames these as necessary conditions for trustworthy AI in assessment, especially in high-stakes summative contexts
target_learners: medical students in summative and formative assessment
target_learning_goals: fair, equitable, and trustworthy AI-driven assessment governance
examples: The conclusion advocates this safeguard set alongside the phased roadmap, citing accuracy and fairness scrutiny recommended in recent UK Parliament policy guidance
key_sources: Rezaei-Zadeh M, Cerbin-Koczorowska M. (2025). A research roadmap for AI opportunities in student assessment for medical education. BMC Medical Education 25:1653. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08078-7

article_title: Ten tips to harnessing generative AI for high-quality MCQS in medical education assessment.
citation: Magzoub Mohi Eldin, Zafar Imran, Munshi Fadi, Shersad Fouzia. (2025). Ten tips to harnessing generative AI for high-quality MCQs in medical education assessment. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2025.2532682
title: AIG and AI-based item generation as distinct but interlinked approaches to MCQ development
description: The article distinguishes automatic item generation (AIG), which relies on predefined algorithms and templates to generate items systematically, from AI-based item generation using machine learning models that adapt more flexibly to diverse educational contexts. It argues the two are closely interlinked: AI enhances the capabilities of traditional AIG, adding creativity and adaptability while both methods reduce the time and cost of item generation. This framing underpins the article's tips on how generative AI can be harnessed for assessment creation.
requirements: Successful integration requires careful consideration of AI's limitations and consensus-based guidelines to govern its use
constraints: AI-generated content carries potential biases and accuracy issues that educators must understand and manage
target_learners: medical educators and item writers in undergraduate and graduate medical education
examples: The article contrasts template-driven AIG consistency with the flexible adaptation of generative AI models like ChatGPT
key_sources: Magzoub Mohi Eldin, Zafar Imran, Munshi Fadi, Shersad Fouzia. (2025). Ten tips to harnessing generative AI for high-quality MCQs in medical education assessment. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2025.2532682

article_title: Proposing core competencies for physicians in using artificial intelligence tools in clinical practice.
citation: Scott IA, Shaw T, Slade C, Wan TT, Barmanray R, Coorey C, Johnson SLJ, Bell L, Herd M, Sullivan CM. (2025). Proposing core competencies for physicians in using artificial intelligence tools in clinical practice. Internal Medicine Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/imj.70112
title: Match the methodological rigour required of AI tool evidence to the risk level of the task the tool performs
description: The article recommends that the evidence standard demanded of an AI tool scale with the risk of the task it performs. High-risk applications such as decision support warrant the strongest designs, while low-risk tasks may be supported by weaker evidence. The article states: 'The required level of methodological rigour should be proportionate to the level of risk inherent to the task the tool is performing.' It gives the examples of randomised controlled trials for decision support and observational studies for documentation or data retrieval.
requirements: Physicians must be able to judge the risk level of the task a tool performs and appraise the study designs behind it
constraints: Many studies comparing AI tools with standard clinical practice use retrospective designs and highly curated settings, with high risk of bias or irrelevance to routine care
target_learning_goals: critical appraisal of AI tool evidence
examples: The article states a decision support tool will in most cases require a randomised controlled trial, while for less critical documentation tasks or data retrieval, observational studies may suffice
key_sources: Scott IA, Shaw T, Slade C, Wan TT, Barmanray R, Coorey C, Johnson SLJ, Bell L, Herd M, Sullivan CM. (2025). Proposing core competencies for physicians in using artificial intelligence tools in clinical practice. Internal Medicine Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/imj.70112

article_title: RCFLA-YOLO: a deep learning-driven framework for the automated assessment of root canal filling quality in periapical radiographs.
citation: Ayhan Muhammed, Kayadibi İsmail, Aykanat Berkehan. (2025). RCFLA-YOLO: a deep learning-driven framework for the automated assessment of root canal filling quality in periapical radiographs. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07483-2
title: Use AI-based assessment in preclinical dental education as a decision-support tool that standardizes evaluation and frees educators for higher-quality instructional tasks
description: The article argues that computer-aided, AI-based assessment of student procedures provides a standardized and objective alternative to subjective, time-consuming educator evaluation in crowded preclinical settings. It states that "AI-driven student assessment reduces the workload of educators, allowing them to focus on higher-quality instructional tasks, such as providing personalized guidance and support". Applied to root canal filling assessment, such systems can save instructors time and give students instant feedback, supporting a data-driven educational environment.
requirements: Human oversight in borderline or ambiguous cases, given the model's false positive and false negative predictions
constraints: The article suggests the system be used as a decision-support tool rather than as an independent evaluator; the dataset's single-institution origin may limit generalizability to other settings
target_learners: dental students in preclinical endodontics laboratory training
target_learning_goals: development of motor skills and clinical experience in root canal treatment before treating actual patients
examples: The RCFLA-YOLO model used for length determination in RCFs during endodontic preclinical training may offer objective and consistent assessments in crowded preclinical settings

article_title: Application of AI-assisted multi-advisor system combined with BOPPPS teaching model in clinical pharmacy education.

title: AI-assisted multi-advisor BOPPPS teaching model for clinical pharmacy education
description: A hybrid teaching model for clinical pharmacy training at Xiangya Hospital combining a multi-advisor system, staged rotations, BOPPPS sessions, and supervised ChatGPT use. The article reports that "a teaching model was developed that consists of five components: advisor system, teaching strategy, teaching method, teaching mode, and assessment methods," implemented across a staged learning process from theoretical course through TDM and genetic testing to clinical practice, with periodic assessment plus OSCE replacing a traditional final examination.

A staged curriculum bridging the theoretical course and clinical practice, with all groups belonging to the pharmacy department
constraints: The article states the proposed teaching approach "may not work out as well in other professional training contexts" beyond organ-transplant clinical pharmacy
target_learners: advanced students with work experience seeking additional professional knowledge
examples: Implemented in the Pharmacy Department of Xiangya Hospital from spring 2023 to spring 2024, with kidney transplantation clinical pharmacy as the test case

article_title: A pilot study on the application of a digital dental teaching evaluation system in Class II cavity preparation teaching.
citation: Zhang Yuejiao, Li Xiaolan, Wei Xi, Xiao Jiexuan, Zhang Qi, Mai Sui. (2025). A pilot study on the application of a digital dental teaching evaluation system in Class II cavity preparation teaching. BMC Oral Health 25, 372. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-025-05695-y
title: Aizhixing Digital Real-Time Evaluation System DHC210 for real-time Class II cavity preparation training
description: The Aizhixing DHC210 is a real-time dental evaluation system using infrared navigation to track operator movements on realistic artificial teeth. The article states it "provides real-time spatial positioning and instantaneous grading of all preparation details through a combination of a phantom head and dentoform, dental instruments, infrared sensors, infrared cameras, and computer system". Operators monitor preparation on screen, compare it with standard morphological guidelines, and adjust cutting volume using graphical tips in practice mode; a step-by-step playback function supports targeted faculty feedback. It was used with four practice-examination cycles in this pilot.
requirements: Requires the Aizhixing-specific handpiece and instrument calibration by engineers prior to each use
constraints: The handpiece was reported heavier than clinical handpieces, causing some discomfort, and the standard cavity depth setting was judged too deep
target_learners: clinicians preparing for preclinical operative dentistry teaching
dental students in preclinical simulation training
target_learning_goals: G.V. Black Class II cavity preparation skill
examples: Eighteen clinicians alternated practice mode and 15-min examination mode four times on a left mandibular first molar resin tooth model

article_title: Digital and artificial intelligence-assisted cephalometric training effectively enhanced students' landmarking accuracy in preclinical orthodontic education.
citation: Lin Jiayu, Liao Zhihao, Dai Jingtao, Wang Manyi, Yu Ruixue, Yang Hong, Liu Chufeng. (2025). Digital and artificial intelligence-assisted cephalometric training effectively enhanced students’ landmarking accuracy in preclinical orthodontic education. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-025-05978-4
title: AI as a complementary tool to clinical expertise rather than a replacement in dentistry
description: The article frames the role of AI in dental education and practice as assistive rather than substitutive. It reports that researchers generally agree human expertise remains irreplaceable in areas such as empathy, ethical considerations, and interpreting complex information, and that "the current consensus is that AI will serve as a complementary tool to clinical expertise and skills, rather than a replacement." This account underpins the study's positioning of digital tools as supplements to instructor-led training and students' preference that instructors assess their technical skills.
requirements: Human instructors retain responsibility for transmitting experiential insights and serving as professional role models
constraints: AI accuracy depends on the choice of AI model, radiograph clarity, and training data quality; integration raises ethical concerns about patient privacy and data security
target_learning_goals: safe and responsible use of AI tools in dental diagnosis and education
examples: The article notes that 56.1% of North American orthodontic program directors had implemented or planned AI-related teaching, while students disagreed that AI can replace dentists.

citation: Wu Shangdi, Tang Ming, Liu Jie, Qin Dian, Wang Yuxian, Zhai Siwei, Bi Enxu, Li Yichuan, Wang Chunrong, Xiong Yong, Li Guangkuo, Gao Fengwei, Cai Yunqiang, Gao Pan, Wu Zhong, Cai He, Liu Jian, Chen Yonghua, Fang Chihua, Yao Li, Jiang Jingwen, Peng Bing, Wu Hong, Li Ang, Wang Xin. (2024). Impact of an AI-based laparoscopic cholecystectomy coaching program on the surgical performance: a randomized controlled trial. International Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1097/JS9.0000000000001798
title: Digitization-plus-visualization framework: two prerequisites for applying AI to surgical education
description: The article proposes that practical AI application in surgical education requires two things: sufficiently accurate algorithms that digitize surgery (recognizing surgical phases, disease severity, critical duct division actions, and CVS scores, which SurgSmart achieves at over 90% average accuracy), and a visual platform for coach-learner interaction. The authors state that "the successful development and implementation of the two key technologies, 'digitization' and 'visualization' of surgeries, have paved the way for the successful implementation of this AI-assisted SmartCoach" and that no comparable visualization platforms had been reported worldwide.
requirements: Accurate AI algorithms capable of digitizing surgery, and a visual platform that facilitates interaction between coaches and learners
constraints: The AI analyzes multidimensional metrics but a human coach is still necessary to synthesize the data, devise a coaching plan, and communicate with coachees
target_learning_goals: objective assessment and personalized feedback on surgical performance and safety
examples: SurgSmart generates postoperative reports with quantified CVS scores and surgical phase information, and the SmartCoach platform supports video playback with a key information timeline for postoperative review.

article_title: Application of AI-empowered scenario-based simulation teaching mode in cardiovascular disease education.
citation: Zheng Koulong, Shen Zhiyu, Chen Zanhao, Che Chang, Zhu Huixia. (2024). Application of AI-empowered scenario-based simulation teaching mode in cardiovascular disease education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05977-z
title: AI-empowered scenario-based simulation teaching mode for cardiovascular disease education
description: A teaching mode in which generative AI (ChatGPT 3.5) and Midjourney are used to produce animated scenario simulation videos of cardiovascular cases, integrated with teacher-led theoretical explanation, role-play during video viewing, group discussions capped at six students grouped by GPA, and thinking questions answerable with ChatGPT help. The experimental group receiving this mode "were divided into 6 groups" and the authors conclude the mode "is an effective and feasible teaching model, which is worthy of promotion in other courses."
requirements: Teachers and teaching assistants trained in scenario simulation teaching and proficient in using ChatGPT, with AI outputs reviewed for scientific validity and alignment with teaching objectives
constraints: Implemented with ChatGPT version 3.5, which the authors note does not fully represent the highest computing power of AI technology; the study sample was small with limited follow-up duration
examples: Thirty-four experimental-group students experienced the mode while thirty-two control students received traditional lecture-and-demonstration teaching with standardized patients, with all clinical practice processes except theoretical learning identical between groups.

article_title: Assessment of ChatGPT-4 in Family Medicine Board Examinations Using Advanced AI Learning and Analytical Methods: Observational Study.
citation: Goodings Anthony James DEC, Kajitani S, Chhor A, Albakri A, Pastrak M, Kodancha M, Ives R, Lee YB, Kajitani K. (2024). Assessment of ChatGPT-4 in Family Medicine Board Examinations Using Advanced AI Learning and Analytical Methods: Observational Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/56128
title: Three-category taxonomy of AI answer errors: logical fallacy, informational fallacy, and explicit fallacy
description: The article classifies errors made by humans or AI when answering questions into three categories. A logical fallacy "occurs when the response demonstrates a stepwise process but ultimately fails to correctly answer the question"; an informational fallacy misinterprets or omits key information from the stem; an explicit fallacy combines incoherent reasoning with misapplied information. The taxonomy is used as the output indicator for labeling incorrect answers in the study, with two collectors assigning types independently and a third adjudicating disagreements.
requirements: Errors must be classified by independent raters, with a third evaluator resolving disagreements
constraints: The taxonomy was applied to multiple-choice medical examination questions in this study
target_learners: medical students preparing for board examinations
AI system developers in medical education
target_learning_goals: diagnosing why AI or human respondents answer examination questions incorrectly
examples: Incorrect answers on the 300 AAFP practice questions were labeled logical, informational, or explicit fallacy and compared across the two ChatGPT-4 versions

citation: Goodings Anthony James DEC, Kajitani S, Chhor A, Albakri A, Pastrak M, Kodancha M, Ives R, Lee YB, Kajitani K. (2024). Assessment of ChatGPT-4 in Family Medicine Board Examinations Using Advanced AI Learning and Analytical Methods: Observational Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/56128
title: AI Family Medicine Exam Expert: a customized ChatGPT-4 configured to take the ABFM Certification Examination
description: The AI Family Medicine Exam Expert is a specialized version of ChatGPT-4 programmed to take the ABFM Certification Examination. It was instructed to adopt the persona of a final-year family medicine resident, prioritize three family medicine textbooks loaded into its configuration, fall back on web browsing of scholarly sources such as UpToDate, and finally use its own medical knowledge for educated guesses, explaining its reasoning and resources for each answer. Questions came from the AAFP Family Medicine Board Review Questions, presented one at a time as stand-alone tasks.
requirements: Access to the three configured textbooks (Rakel, Baldor, Al-Gelban et al.)
Prompt instructions specifying persona, resource hierarchy, and output format
constraints: The textbook knowledge base is static and may not capture the evolving nature of medical knowledge, per the authors' limitations section
target_learners: medical students preparing for board examinations
examples: The custom GPT was run on 300 AAFP practice questions and its responses recorded in a Microsoft Excel sheet for analysis

article_title: AIxSuture: vision-based assessment of open suturing skills.
citation: Hoffmann Hanna, Funke Isabel, Peters Philipp, Venkatesh Danush Kumar, Egger Jan, Rivoir Dominik, Röhrig Rainer, Hölzle Frank, Bodenstedt Sebastian, Willemer Marie-Christin, Speidel Stefanie, Puladi Behrus. (2024). AIxSuture: vision-based assessment of open suturing skills. International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-024-03093-3
title: AIxSuture dataset of 314 expert-rated open suturing videos with OSATS-based three-level skill labels
description: The AIxSuture dataset is a released video corpus for open surgery skill assessment research. It "is comprised of 314 videos of approximately 5 min each taken at 30 fps", recorded with a GoPro Hero 5 from a bird's-eye-view in a standardized simulated suturing setting. Each video carries OSATS ratings from three independent raters, whose eight category scores sum to a global rating score from 8 to 40, and the authors released the data publicly.
requirements: Videos must be rated by independent raters using the OSATS scale with eight skill categories to yield a global rating score
constraints: Videos were recorded before and after one hour of training, so the dataset is composed mainly of good and very bad performances and lacks intermediate and expert (GRS >32) recordings
target_learners: medical and dental students learning open suturing
target_learning_goals: open surgical suturing skill acquisition and assessment
examples: The data originated from a randomized controlled trial comparing virtual reality head-mounted display-guided training to e-learning and tutor-based approaches, with pre- and post-training videos rated per student

(2024). AIxSuture: vision-based assessment of open suturing skills. International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-024-03093-3

article_title: AI in Surgical Curriculum Design and Unintended Outcomes for Technical Competencies in Simulation Training.
citation: Fazlollahi AM, Yilmaz R, Winkler-Schwartz A, Mirchi N, Ledwos N, Bakhaidar M, Alsayegh A, Del Maestro RF. (2023). AI in Surgical Curriculum Design and Unintended Outcomes for Technical Competencies in Simulation Training. JAMA Netw Open. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.34658
title: AI-enhanced curricula require ongoing cost-benefit evaluation by subject matter experts before acceptance in formal training
description: Because an AI-selected curriculum produced both beneficial (safety) and detrimental (movement, efficiency) unintended outcomes, the article recommends that adopting AI in course design requires ongoing assessment to maintain transparency and that "assessment of AI-enhanced curricula requires a cost-benefit evaluation by subject matter experts to determine their acceptance in formal training". It also suggests the curriculum "may benefit from contextual and timely feedback either from a live instructor or a real-time performance assessment system".
requirements: Ongoing assessment of unintended outcomes across the full metric set, not only the taught objectives; expert cost-benefit judgment; contextual and timely feedback from a live instructor or real-time assessment system
constraints: Unintended effects were observed in one simulated bimanual neurosurgical task with post-hoc feedback only; the authors note post-hoc feedback lacks contextual and directional components and that long-term effects warrant longitudinal study
target_learners: medical students in simulation-based surgical skills training
target_learning_goals: technical competency acquisition balanced across safety, movement, and efficiency domains
examples: The VOA curriculum taught 4 AI-selected objectives via post-hoc audiovisual feedback and stepwise competency assessment, improving safety metrics while slowing dominant-hand movement and reducing tumor removal rate
key_sources: Fazlollahi AM, Yilmaz R, Winkler-Schwartz A, Mirchi N, Ledwos N, Bakhaidar M, Alsayegh A, Del Maestro RF. (2023). AI in Surgical Curriculum Design and Unintended Outcomes for Technical Competencies in Simulation Training. JAMA Netw Open. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.34658

article_title: Artificial intelligence in laparoscopic simulation: a promising future for large-scale automated evaluations.
citation: Belmar Francisca, Gaete María Inés, Escalona Gabriel, Carnier Martín, Durán Valentina, Villagrán Ignacio, Asbun Domenech, Cortés Matías, Neyem Andrés, Crovari Fernando, Alseidi Adnan, Varas Julián. (2022). Artificial intelligence in laparoscopic simulation: a promising future for large-scale automated evaluations. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-022-09576-1
title: AI assessment algorithm for basic laparoscopic simulation exercises (U-net and YOLO v4)
description: An AI algorithm developed with the CRISP-DM methodology in Python and PyTorch, using "U-net for segmentation, allowing clamp tracking, and YOLO v4 for element, receptacle, and pin detection". It detects object movement, identifies fallen objects, tracks grasper clamp location, and measures exercise time, providing two main outputs: falling objects and time to complete the exercise. Times are manually categorized as pass or fail against established passing times (BD < 24 s, PT < 55 s) and compared to expert evaluators.
requirements: An expert group of AI labelers labels random video frames and provides Pascal VOC files for the labeling process
constraints: The algorithm can only measure the time it takes to complete the exercise and does not replace experts' feedback; fallen-object detection was not considered among the pass or fail criteria due to technical limitations
target_learners: surgery trainees performing basic laparoscopic simulation exercises
target_learning_goals: automated pass/fail assessment of basic laparoscopic technical skills
examples: The algorithm was trained on 400 bean drop and 480 peg transfer videos and tested on 64 and 43 videos respectively
key_sources: Belmar Francisca, Gaete María Inés, Escalona Gabriel, Carnier Martín, Durán Valentina, Villagrán Ignacio, Asbun Domenech, Cortés Matías, Neyem Andrés, Crovari Fernando, Alseidi Adnan, Varas Julián.
